title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or on landlords sharing rent or occupancy data with each other. That does not make coordinated pricing safe. Alaska's general antitrust law makes every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade unlawful, and federal antitrust law also applies. If you use a pricing tool that recommends rents from competitors' nonpublic data, or agree with other landlords on rents or lease terms, get legal advice first. Setting your own rent from public market information is not restricted by any Alaska statute.

title: No Application Fee Rules
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on rental application or screening fees: no cap, no required refund, no rule on holding fees while earlier applicants are screened, and no tenant screening act. Two limits still shape your application. Alaska's fair housing law makes it unlawful to ask about or record an applicant's sex, marital status, changes in marital status, race, religion, physical or mental disability, color or national origin, so leave those questions off the form (this does not apply when you rent a room in a home you live in and share common living areas). Federal fair housing and consumer reporting law also apply. A cautious practice is to charge no more than your actual screening cost and refund the fee if you never process the application. Money you hold as security for rent or damage is a deposit, whatever you call it, and counts toward the deposit limit where that limit applies (rent of $2,000 a month or less).

title: Collection Fees
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule that authorizes, caps or bans a fee for collecting a tenant's past-due debt, and the library does not offer a collection-fee clause. Three rules point away from one. A lease may not make the tenant agree to pay your attorney fees, and a provision that does is unenforceable. When you win a case under the landlord-tenant act or the lease, the court allows attorney fees to the prevailing party by statute, without any lease clause. For a tenant's breach you recover your actual damages; whether a collection agency's commission counts as actual damages is not settled by statute. If you collect your own debts you need no collection agency license; an agency you hire must be licensed to collect for others.

title: No Fee Transparency Law
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rental fee transparency or all-in pricing law. Nothing requires you to advertise a single total price including mandatory fees, to state a total monthly payment on the lease's first page, or to follow a set fee disclosure sentence, and no auto-renewal rule reaches residential leases. Alaska's general consumer protection act bans unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce, including saying an agreement gives rights or obligations it does not; whether that act reaches residential leases is unsettled, and a successful claim can bring three times actual damages or $500. The cautious course is to list every required fee, with its amount and purpose, in your advertising and in the lease, and to charge none that the lease does not state.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no general rule barring a residential landlord from charging a fee for a service that is not provided. (A similar rule exists only for mobile home park fees, which this library does not cover.) Related rules still apply. If the lease promises a service and you do not provide it, the tenant may recover damages for your breach of the rental agreement. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat, sanitary facilities or other essential services the lease or the law requires, the tenant may, after written notice, buy the service and deduct its reasonable cost from rent, recover reduced-value damages, or move to substitute housing. Charge only for services you actually deliver, and describe each one in the lease.

title: Which Charges Count as Rent
bodyText: Under Alaska's landlord-tenant act, rent is the uniform periodic payment due to you, whatever the lease calls it. A fixed charge paid every period with the rent, such as a set monthly pet or parking charge, may therefore be rent. One-time or variable charges, such as late fees, repair costs or a returned-check fee, are not uniform periodic payments, and calling them additional rent in the lease does not clearly change that. This matters for eviction: the seven-day nonpayment notice covers unpaid rent, and the court's notice form tells you to leave out late fees and interest because a tenant can't be evicted for unpaid late fees. Collect other charges by agreement or as a damages claim in court. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, the deposit may be applied only to accrued rent and to damage to the premises beyond normal wear and tear that the tenant caused, so do not deduct late fees or returned-check fees from it. Never make legal fees additional rent: a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees.

title: Government Fees on Your Property
bodyText:
Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no statewide rental registration or licensing fee and no rule letting you pass a government fee through to the tenant.

The one state-authorized fee aimed at rentals is a city or borough fee on the owner of residential property for excessive police responses, which the ordinance must let you avoid by prompt corrective action, including a notice to quit. Your tenant must not unreasonably cause that fee, and if the tenant's conduct does cause it you may recover your actual damages.

The library does not offer a clause making the tenant reimburse fees imposed on you: a lease promise to cover your legal liabilities or their costs is an indemnity, which an Alaska lease may not contain. Build expected local fees into the rent instead, and check your municipal code.

title: How Late Fees Work in Alaska
bodyText:
No Alaska statute sets or caps late fees on rent, but the court system's eviction materials describe how courts treat them.

A court will allow a late fee only if the lease provides for it, and usually not for any period after the tenant has moved out; after that you generally get interest instead, and interest on unpaid rent is generally not awarded if you also charged late fees.

A tenant cannot be evicted for unpaid late fees, so leave them out of the seven-day nonpayment notice and demand only rent.

If you accept rent knowing the tenant is in default, you give up the right to end the lease for that breach unless you and the tenant agree otherwise after the breach (put that agreement in writing).

After serving the seven-day notice you may accept a partial payment and extend the eviction date accordingly, but the court's booklet tells tenants that an accepted partial payment waives that nonpayment, so get the written agreement before you take it. A lease sentence saying in advance that acceptance is not a waiver does not meet that rule.

title: No Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations set no maximum late fee and no required grace period for residential rent; the amount and timing are whatever your lease states. The $5 late-fee cap you may see in Alaska law applies to rent-to-own agreements for goods, not to homes. Because a court will allow a late fee only if the lease provides for it, put the amount and the grace period in the lease. Keep the fee a reasonable estimate of what a late payment costs you, since courts may refuse to enforce a fee that works as a penalty, and charge it once for each late payment.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations do not require the same rent or terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies, and they do not cap the rent difference between them. Unless the lease fixes a definite term, a tenancy is week to week if rent is paid weekly and month to month otherwise. The notice to end a periodic tenancy is the same for both sides: at least 30 days' written notice before the rental due date for month to month, and at least 14 days' written notice for week to week while rent is current. Fair housing law still applies to how you set terms for different applicants.

title: No Rent Control
bodyText: Alaska has no statewide rent control or rent-increase cap, and no statewide rental registration, permit or inspection program. Alaska's former emergency rent regulation chapter has been repealed; old emergency rent review regulations are still printed in the administrative code, but they apply only in a governor-declared housing emergency under that repealed chapter. Alaska's statutes and regulations also contain no law that bars cities or boroughs from regulating rents, and home-rule cities and boroughs may exercise any legislative power not prohibited by law or charter, so check your local code. Whatever the local rules, you may not raise rent or cut services to retaliate against a tenant for complaining about conditions, enforcing rights or joining a tenants' union.

title: No Rent-Demand Bar
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule that bars you outright from demanding or collecting rent while a unit has code violations. Instead, rent is tied to your repair duties in several ways. No lease, assignment or security instrument may let anyone collect rent free of the duty to keep the unit fit. If you fail to deliver possession, rent abates until you do. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply heat, water, hot water, sanitary facilities or other essential services, the tenant may, after written notice, deduct the cost of supplying them or move to substitute housing and owe no rent for that period. In a nonpayment eviction or rent suit, the tenant may counterclaim, and the court may reduce the rent for the period of noncompliance or order rent paid into court.

title: No Rent Increase Notice Rule
bodyText:
Alaska's statutes contain no rent-increase notice period, no cap on increases and no limit on how often you raise rent.

During a fixed term you can raise rent only if the lease allows it. For a month-to-month tenancy, the only statutory period is the written notice to end the tenancy, at least 30 days before the rental due date named in the notice (14 days for week to week). The cautious course is to give the same written notice, effective on a rent due date, for any increase.

A 30-day notice rule printed in the emergency rent review regulations applies only during a housing emergency declared under a chapter that has been repealed.

You may not raise rent to retaliate against a tenant's protected complaint or activity, though cost, improvement and comparable-rent increases are allowed. No price-gouging law caps rent in an emergency.

title: No Duty to Give Rent Receipts
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations do not require you to give a tenant a receipt for rent, including rent paid in cash, and failing to give one is not a defense to eviction. Receipts still matter. In an eviction case a tenant may prove payment with receipts or canceled checks, so a cash payment without a receipt leaves you both without proof. Some tenants also need them: renters who are 65 or older, disabled veterans, and certain surviving spouses who apply for the state's property tax equivalency payment must send in rent receipts or other proof of the rent they paid. Give a dated written receipt for every cash payment and keep a copy.

title: Reporting Rent Payments to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations neither require nor limit a landlord's reporting of rent payments to a credit bureau. There is no state rent-reporting program, no duty to offer positive rent reporting in the lease, and no rule barring you from requiring a tenant to join a reporting service. If you report payment history, or use credit reports to screen applicants, federal consumer reporting law governs the accuracy, dispute and notice duties, so follow the reporting service's federal compliance rules.

title: Local Sales Tax on Rent
bodyText: Alaska has no state sales tax on residential rent. Cities and boroughs, however, may levy a local sales tax on sales, rents and services, and each decides by ordinance which sources to tax and what to exempt, so whether long-term residential rent is taxed, exempt, or taxed only for short stays depends on where the property is. Check your city and borough codes before you set rent, and if a local tax applies to your rentals, state in the lease whether the rent includes it. A 2026 state law also lets municipalities adopt optional property tax exemptions, including for a unit converted from short-term to long-term rental and for property rented to low-income families at no more than 30 percent of income; ask your assessor whether your municipality has adopted one.

title: No Required-Fee List Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations do not require the lease to list every fee with its purpose, and they set no notice period for adding a fee later. In practice the lease is still where fees belong. Alaska lets the lease include any terms the law does not prohibit, and a court will allow a late fee only if the lease provides for it. A new rule you adopt during the tenancy binds the tenant only after reasonable notice and only if it does not substantially change the rental agreement, so a new recurring charge added midterm is unlikely to bind a tenant under a fixed-term lease. List each required fee, its amount and when it is due in the lease, and add new fees only at renewal or by written agreement.

title: Bounced Rent Checks
bodyText:
A rent check that bounces leaves the rent unpaid: paying by an ordinary check only suspends the rent obligation until the check is dishonored.

Alaska's bad-check statute gives you an extra civil remedy when a check is dishonored for lack of funds, a closed or nonexistent account, or a stop-payment order issued without cause. First send a written demand, delivered in person or by first-class mail to the address on the check, explaining the penalties, at least 15 days before suing.

If the tenant does not pay the check amount plus a fee of up to $30 before you sue, you may recover $100 or three times the check, whichever is greater, but no more than $1,000 above the check amount. After you sue, the tenant may settle by paying the check plus your costs up to $150.

The remedy does not cover postdated checks. Keep any lease returned-payment fee at or below $30.

title: Government Shutdowns
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations give no special protection to tenants who are federal, state or tribal workers during a government shutdown: no delay of rent, no late-fee bar and no eviction defense. The ordinary rules apply, including the seven-day notice before a nonpayment termination. If a tenant's pay is interrupted, consider a written payment plan; after giving the nonpayment notice you may accept a partial payment and extend the eviction date, ideally confirming that agreement in writing.

title: Alaska's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Alaska sets these money limits for residential rentals, whatever the lease says. Security deposit plus prepaid rent (including last month's rent, but not the first month's): no more than two months' rent, except that the limit does not apply where rent exceeds $2,000 a month. Pet deposit: an extra amount up to one month's rent, never for a service animal. Wrongful deposit withholding: if you wilfully fail to account and refund on time, the tenant may recover up to twice the amount withheld. (The deposit statute, including the pet deposit and withholding rules, does not apply at all where rent exceeds $2,000 a month.) Holdover: up to one and one-half times actual damages for a wilful, bad-faith holdover. Interest on money past due: 10.5 percent a year, unless the lease sets a rate within the contract-rate limit; judgments carry their own rate. Storage of abandoned property on the premises: no more than the fair rental value. Late fees, application fees and rent increases: no statutory cap. Bounced checks: a separate statutory remedy applies. Attorney fees: the lease may not shift them; the court awards them to the prevailing party.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations have no special rule for reducing rent when part of a subsidized unit becomes uninhabitable, and nothing says how a reduction is split between the tenant's share and the subsidy. The general rules apply to every tenant. After a fire or other casualty that substantially impairs the unit, a tenant who may lawfully stay can vacate the unusable part, and the tenant's rent is reduced in proportion to the drop in the unit's fair rental value. In a nonpayment case the court may also reduce rent for a period when you failed to keep the unit fit. For a voucher or other subsidized tenancy, follow the program's contract and rules on abatement, which this library does not cover.

title: No Subsidy Late-Fee Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations have no rule on late fees for the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays, and no state cap on late fees generally. Charging a tenant a late fee because the housing agency paid its share late is not barred by Alaska law, but it is risky: the tenant did not cause the delay, and federal program rules and your housing assistance contract may limit or forbid it. The cautious course is to charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share of the rent, as stated in the lease.

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on a lease clause that passes real property tax increases to the tenant, and the library does not offer one. Your property tax is your own liability under the law, and an Alaska lease may not make the tenant indemnify you for such a liability or its costs, so a clause making the tenant pay your tax increase risks being unenforceable. Raise rent instead: at renewal, on a month-to-month tenancy, or during a fixed term only if the lease allows mid-term increases. A substantial property tax increase you became liable for at least four months earlier is a recognized reason for an increase that reasonably tracks it, even after a tenant complaint. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, you may not deduct a tax share from the deposit, which covers only unpaid rent and tenant damage.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText:
Alaska's legal interest rate on money after it is due is 10.5 percent a year. A contract, including a lease, may set its own rate, but no higher than the greater of 10 percent or five percentage points above the Federal Reserve rate on the day the lease is signed.

In court, judgments and prejudgment interest carry their own rate (three points above the Federal Reserve discount rate on January 2 of the judgment year) unless a written contract sets a lawful rate, which then carries into the judgment.

Under the statute's words, unless you and the tenant agreed otherwise, prejudgment interest runs from the date you serve the suit, or from an earlier written notice of a claim for personal injury, death or damage to property (such as damage to the unit).

The court system's booklet, however, tells landlords that prejudgment interest is due from the date each amount became due if they attach a computation sheet, so claim it that way and let the court decide.

The court system's booklet warns that interest is generally not awarded on rent for which you also charged a late fee, so do not stack the two.

title: Move-In Condition Statement
bodyText: Alaska does not require a move-in or move-out inspection, but it gives you a strong tool if you choose to use one. If you require it, you and the tenant include in, attach to, or incorporate into the lease a premises condition statement describing the condition of the unit and fixtures at the start of the tenancy, plus a contents inventory if the unit is furnished. The tenant must confirm its accuracy by signing, and once both of you sign it becomes part of the rental agreement. In a later dispute it is presumed to show the move-in condition and can be the basis for figuring damages unless the other side disproves its authenticity by clear and convincing evidence. A signed statement stays valid with a buyer of the property until a new one is made. Complete it at move-in, with dated photos.

title: Preset Cleaning or Repair Charges
bodyText:
Alaska's statutes and regulations do not let a lease preset cleaning, carpet or repair charges that you may keep from the deposit. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, you may apply the deposit only to unpaid rent and the damages you actually suffered from the tenant's breach of the tenant's duties, itemized in writing, and never to normal wear and tear.

A price list in the lease can tell the tenant what typical work costs, but deduct the actual, documented cost; the court system's guidance tells landlords to attach invoices and, for their own labor, to itemize the hourly rate and hours worked.

Carpets are a special case: if they were professionally cleaned right before the tenancy began, you may require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, and that rule needs no preset charge.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A deposit refund the tenant never claims is not yours to keep. First make a reasonable effort to deliver it if you know how to reach the tenant. Alaska's unclaimed property law lists security deposits and refunds as property a holder must turn over: a refund unclaimed for more than three years after it became payable is presumed abandoned. You then report it to the Department of Revenue before November 1 for property held on June 30, pay it over with the report, and keep the records. If the address you have is believed accurate and the amount is $100 or more, send the tenant written notice within 120 days before reporting. The reporting duty applies once your unclaimed property presumed abandoned that year, plus earlier unreported items, exceeds $750. Late reporting can bring interest and penalties. A lease clause forfeiting an unclaimed refund to you does not stop it from being presumed abandoned, and the library does not offer one.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations give tenants no right to pay a security deposit, pet deposit or prepaid rent in installments, and they neither require nor forbid an installment plan. You may agree to one in the lease. If you do, state each installment's amount and due date, remember that, where rent is $2,000 a month or less, the total of the security deposit and prepaid rent may not exceed two months' rent and each installment must go into the trust account as you receive it.

title: Last Month's Rent Paid in Advance
bodyText: In Alaska, last month's rent collected at move-in is prepaid rent: money you demand at the start of the tenancy to make sure rent will be paid. The first month's rent is not prepaid rent. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, prepaid rent is treated like the security deposit: together they may not exceed two months' rent, and you must deposit it in the trust account and account for it separately for each tenant. When the tenancy ends you may apply it to accrued rent, including the final month, and to damages the tenant caused, and you must include it in the itemized written notice and refund you mail within the 14- or 30-day deadline. Do not mix it with your operating funds or use it for another tenant.

title: Move-Out Notice and the Deposit
bodyText: You may not make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, a forwarding address or keys by a deadline; Alaska's deposit rules contain no such condition, and a lease cannot waive the tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant act. Notice does change your deadline. If either of you gave a proper written notice to end a periodic tenancy, mail the itemized notice and refund within 14 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant delivers possession, or within 30 days if you deduct for damage. If the tenant gave no proper notice, you have 30 days after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession, or you learn the unit is abandoned. Mail to the tenant's last known address; if you have no address but know how to reach the tenant, make a reasonable effort to deliver. These rules come from the deposit section, which does not apply where rent exceeds $2,000 a month; following them anyway is the cautious course.

title: No Domestic Violence Deposit Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no right for a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking to end a lease early, and no special rule on when the deposit is returned after such a move-out. The ordinary deposit rules and deadlines apply when the tenancy ends. Two related rules exist. A court's domestic violence protective order may remove and exclude the abuser from the victim's residence regardless of who owns it, so a co-tenant may lawfully be kept out. And a city fee for excessive police calls may not be charged for calls involving potential domestic violence or stalking. Consider agreeing in writing to an early termination when a tenant needs to leave for safety.

title: Returning the Deposit Early
bodyText: Alaska has no expedited security deposit procedure and no fee for handling a deposit early. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, your deadline is 14 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant delivers possession (30 days if you deduct for damage, or if the tenant gave no proper notice), and you may always return the deposit sooner. In those tenancies you may not deduct a processing, administrative or accounting fee: the deposit and prepaid rent may be applied only to accrued rent and to damages the tenant caused, itemized in your written notice.

title: No Deposit-Alternative Rules
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on fees in lieu of a security deposit, deposit insurance or surety bond programs, or credit reporting of damage claims under a no-deposit lease. Two cautions apply if you offer one. The deposit limit covers prepaid rent and security deposits however they are labeled, so money you collect and hold to secure rent or damage is a deposit, with the cap, trust account and refund rules where rent is $2,000 a month or less, even if you call it a fee. And a product that promises to pay you for a tenant's damage may be insurance, governed by insurance law this library does not cover. The library offers no deposit-alternative clause; if you use a vendor's program, make it optional and get advice.

title: Furnished Rentals
bodyText: Alaska has no higher deposit limit for a furnished unit and no separate furniture deposit; anything you hold as security for furniture is part of the security deposit and counts toward the two-month limit (where rent is $2,000 a month or less). What Alaska does provide is the contents inventory: if you require it, the lease includes or attaches an inventory itemizing the furnishings and other contents and the condition of each, which the tenant verifies by signing and which is presumed accurate in a later dispute. Where the deposit section applies, deductions may cover damage to the contents as well as the unit, but not normal wear and tear. Listing your furniture in the written lease also matters for entry: the right to enter to remove your own property does not reach items the written lease covers.

title: Holding Deposits
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on holding deposits or other money taken from an applicant before the lease is signed, and they do not say whether such money falls under the deposit statute. Treat it cautiously. Once the lease is signed, money you keep as security is a deposit however it is labeled, so a holding deposit you keep should be credited to the first month's rent or counted within the deposit limit and handled under the deposit rules (where rent is $2,000 a month or less; the deposit section does not apply above that). Put the terms in writing when you take it: the amount, how long you will hold the unit, whether it is credited or refunded if the lease is signed, and that you will refund it if you do not offer the lease. The Department of Law's landlord-tenant handbook says it is not lawful to take money that becomes the security deposit if the applicant moves in but is forfeited if the applicant decides not to rent; the statute does not say so in terms, so the cautious course is not to make such money forfeitable. A real estate broker managing the property must place it in the broker's trust account.

title: No Inspection Notice Penalty
bodyText: Alaska does not require you to offer a move-in or move-out inspection or to tell the tenant about inspection rights, so there is no penalty, such as losing the right to deduct for damage, for skipping one. The move-in premises condition statement is optional, though it is strong evidence if you use it. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, Alaska's deposit penalty attaches instead to the itemized accounting and refund: if you wilfully fail to apply the deposit only to proper charges, itemize them in a written notice and mail it with any refund on time, the tenant may recover up to twice the amount withheld.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits
bodyText:
Alaska law has no category of nonrefundable deposit and no notice rule for one.

Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, any money you hold as prepaid rent or a security deposit, however you label it, may be applied when the tenancy ends only to accrued rent and to damage the tenant caused, and the rest must be refunded with an itemized written notice. So do not describe any part of a deposit as nonrefundable.

Alaska's statutes do not regulate a separately stated one-time fee, such as a move-in or administrative fee, but a fee that in substance secures rent or damage risks being treated as a deposit, counted toward the limit and refundable. If you charge a fee, state its amount and the service it pays for in the lease, and keep it separate from the deposit.

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Alaska has no rule requiring a separate written notice, when you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, that is because no part of an Alaska security deposit or prepaid rent can be made nonrefundable: when the tenancy ends you may apply it only to accrued rent and to damage the tenant caused, and refund the rest with an itemized written notice. What Alaska does require in those tenancies when you take a deposit is that you give the tenant the terms and conditions under which you may withhold it and deposit it in a trust account.

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText:
For a unit renting for $2,000 a month or less, the security deposit and any prepaid rent together may not exceed two months' rent, whatever you call them. Prepaid rent includes last month's rent collected in advance but not the first month's rent.

If the tenant has a pet that is not a service animal, you may also take a pet deposit of up to one month's rent; account for it separately and use it only for damage the pet causes. The extra pet deposit may not be charged for a service animal.

Where the rent exceeds $2,000 a month, the deposit section, including the limit, does not apply at all. Alaska has no separate furniture deposit and no limit that changes with the tenancy's length; if you raise the rent, keep any deposit increase within the limit at the new rent.

title: Holding Deposits in Trust
bodyText:
Deposit every security deposit and all prepaid rent promptly, wherever practicable, in a trust account at a bank, savings and loan association, or licensed escrow agent.

You may keep all tenants' deposits and prepaid rent together in one trust account, but you must keep a separate accounting for each tenant, and you may not mix that money with your own or other funds. Never use one tenant's money to refund another tenant's deposit or to cover another tenant's rent or damage.

Give the tenant the terms and conditions under which you may withhold any part of the deposit; the lease is the place to do it. Alaska does not require you to tell the tenant where the account is or to pay interest.

These statutory deposit rules apply to units renting for $2,000 a month or less; the deposit section does not apply where the rent is higher, though keeping the same practice is the cautious course. If a licensed real estate licensee manages the property, failing to trust-account deposits is treated as fraudulent or dishonest conduct for licensing purposes.

title: No Interest on Deposits
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations do not require you to pay the tenant interest on a security deposit, pet deposit or prepaid rent, and they do not say who keeps any interest the trust account earns. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, you must still hold the money in a trust account and account for each tenant separately. If you want to pay interest, or to keep it, say so in the lease so there is no dispute at move-out.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease may not make the tenant give up any right or remedy under Alaska's landlord-tenant act, including the deposit rules: the two-month limit, the trust account, deductions only for unpaid rent and tenant damage, the itemized notice and refund deadlines, and the right to recover up to twice the amount wrongfully withheld. A lease term that tries to waive them is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing a prohibited term, the tenant may recover actual damages. One limit on this protection: the deposit section itself does not apply where the rent exceeds $2,000 a month, so those deposit rules are not statutory rights for such units, though the act's other protections still are.

title: Deposits When You Sell
bodyText: When you sell a rental in good faith to a genuine buyer, you are released from liability under the lease and the landlord-tenant act for events after you give the tenant written notice of the sale. The deposit is the exception: you stay liable to the tenant for the deposit and prepaid rent unless that money is specifically assigned to the buyer and the buyer accepts it. Transfer the funds and get the buyer's written acceptance at closing, then tell the tenant. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules, so a buyer who takes over must handle the refund. A signed move-in condition statement and contents inventory stay valid between the buyer and the tenant until they make new ones. The law lets the parties agree otherwise; the library offers no clause, since the default already protects a selling landlord who gives notice.

title: Penalty for Mishandling a Deposit
bodyText:
Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, if you wilfully fail to follow the deposit accounting rule, by keeping money for something other than unpaid rent and tenant-caused damage, by not itemizing deductions in a written notice mailed to the tenant's last known address, or by missing the 14- or 30-day deadline, the tenant may recover up to twice the amount you withheld.

That is a ceiling set by the court, not an automatic forfeiture of your right to deduct, and it applies to the amount withheld rather than the whole deposit. Either side may still recover other damages the act allows, and the court awards attorney fees to whoever prevails.

Alaska has no separate forfeiture for trust-account mistakes, but a licensed property manager who fails to trust-account deposits faces license discipline.

title: Deposit Return Deadlines
bodyText:
When the tenancy ends, mail the tenant a written notice itemizing any unpaid rent and damages you are keeping, together with the balance, to the tenant's last known address.

If either of you gave a proper written notice ending a periodic tenancy, the deadline is 14 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant delivers possession, or 30 days if you deduct for damage. Otherwise it is 30 days after the tenancy ends, the tenant delivers possession, or you learn the unit was abandoned.

If you have no mailing address but know how to reach the tenant, make a reasonable effort to deliver the notice and refund. Account for a pet deposit separately and use it only for pet damage.

No demand by the tenant is needed, and the lease cannot lengthen these deadlines. If the tenant ends the lease because of your breach, return what is owed the same way.

These statutory deadlines apply to units renting for $2,000 a month or less; the deposit section does not apply where the rent is higher, though following them is still the cautious course.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: Alaska does not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits. Two limits still apply. Every deposit plus prepaid rent is capped at two months' rent where the rent is $2,000 a month or less. And Alaska's fair housing law makes it unlawful to treat a person differently in the terms of a rental because of sex, marital status, pregnancy, race, religion, disability, color or national origin, so base any difference on documented, neutral criteria such as credit history.

title: What the Deposit May Cover
bodyText:
In Alaska, where rent is $2,000 a month or less, the deposit and prepaid rent are applied when the tenancy ends, and only to two things: rent that has accrued and is unpaid, and damages you suffered because the tenant broke the tenant's statutory duties, such as damaging the unit or not leaving it in substantially the same condition as at move-in.

Damages means deterioration of the unit and any furnishings. It does not include normal wear and tear, meaning deterioration from intended use without negligence, carelessness, accident, misuse or abuse by the tenant, household members or guests.

Nor does it include deterioration caused by your own failure to prepare for expected conditions, such as freezing weather, or to meet your repair duties.

A pet deposit may cover only damage the pet caused. Use the signed move-in condition statement to show what changed.

title: No Separate Utility Deposit
bodyText: Alaska has no separate category of landlord-held utility deposit and no special refund rule for one. Money you collect in advance to secure utility charges the tenant will owe you is a security deposit, however it is labeled: where rent is $2,000 a month or less, it counts toward the two-month limit and follows the trust-account, itemization and refund rules. Be careful about using it for utilities. In those tenancies the statute lets you apply a deposit only to accrued rent and to damages from the tenant's breach of the tenant's statutory duties, so unpaid utility charges that are not part of the rent may not be deductible; recover them as damages for breach of the lease instead. Deposits a utility company itself takes from the tenant are governed by that utility's tariff and state utility regulations, not by your lease.

title: No Alaska Bed Bug or Pest Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on bed bugs or other pests in rental housing: nothing assigns treatment costs, sets inspection or treatment deadlines, or lists tenant preparation duties. The general rules decide it. You must make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises fit and habitable, and keep common areas clean and safe. The tenant must keep the part of the premises the tenant uses as clean and safe as its condition permits and may not deliberately or negligently damage the premises. The tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to inspect or to supply necessary services, and except in an emergency you must give at least 24 hours' notice and enter at reasonable times. Preparation steps, such as laundering bedding or moving furniture before treatment, can be set as reasonable written rules adopted under the rules statute. Municipal codes may add requirements.

title: No Alaska Cold-Weather Vacancy Notice Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no cold-weather rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving a unit empty in winter, and none addresses frozen pipes. You get similar protection another way. Alaska requires every rental agreement to make the tenant notify you of an anticipated absence of more than seven days, given as soon as reasonably possible after the tenant knows the absence will exceed seven days; the library's Alaska Extended Absence clause does this. A tenant who wilfully fails to give that notice owes up to one and one-half times your actual damages, such as freeze damage. During an absence of more than seven days you may enter at times reasonably necessary, for example to check the heat, following the access statute: give at least 24 hours' notice unless there is an emergency or notice is impracticable. The tenant must also use the heating and plumbing in a reasonable manner and may not negligently damage the premises.

title: No Alaska Common-Area Lighting Standard
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations set no lighting standard for the halls, stairways or entrances of rental buildings, and have no rule on making a tenant pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's electric service. Your general duties apply instead: you must keep all common areas of the premises clean and safe, and keep the electrical facilities you supply in good and safe working order. A dark stairway or entrance that makes a common area unsafe can breach those duties. Lighting may also be required by the building code your municipality enforces or by local housing ordinances. If a common-area light runs through a tenant's meter, say so plainly in the lease so the tenant agrees to the cost before signing.

title: Mechanics' Liens for Tenant Work in Alaska
bodyText: In Alaska, work a tenant orders can become a lien on your property. The mechanics' lien law treats a building or improvement made with the owner's knowledge as made at the owner's instance, so your interest is subject to a recorded lien unless you act within three days after learning of the construction, alteration or repair: post a written notice in a conspicuous place on the land or building saying you will not be responsible for it, signed before two attesting witnesses or acknowledged before a notary, with the posting attested by a witness, and record an attested or notarized copy with the recorder within three days after posting. Alaska's statutes contain no rule letting the lease itself keep your interest free of liens. If you approve tenant alterations, require the tenant to tell you before work starts and to pay contractors in full, and post and record a notice of nonresponsibility for work you are not paying for.

title: Why the Alaska Move-In Condition Statement Matters
bodyText:
Alaska gives a signed move-in condition record real legal weight.

If you require one, the premises condition statement (the condition of the premises, including fixtures) and, if applicable, a contents inventory (each furnishing and its condition) must describe the premises at the start of the term and be included in, incorporated by reference in, or attached to the rental agreement; once you and the tenant sign them, they become part of the rental agreement.

The tenant must acknowledge or verify their accuracy by signature.

In a later action for damages under the landlord-tenant act, the signed statement and inventory are presumptive evidence of the move-in condition, and unless the other side rebuts their authenticity by clear and convincing evidence, either of you may use them, without other evidence, to compute damages, including deposit deductions.

If you sell, they stay valid between the buyer and the tenant until the two sign new ones.

title: Extended Absence: Penalty, Entry and Abandonment in Alaska
bodyText:
Alaska requires every rental agreement to make the tenant notify you of an anticipated absence of more than seven days, given as soon as reasonably possible after the tenant knows the absence will exceed seven days; the library's Alaska Extended Absence clause does this.

The rule has consequences. If the tenant wilfully fails to give the notice, you may recover up to one and one-half times your actual damages.

During any absence of more than seven days you may enter at times reasonably necessary, as the access statute provides (give at least 24 hours' notice unless there is an emergency or notice is impracticable).

Absence also defines abandonment: a tenant who has left belongings in the unit, stayed away seven days or longer without giving the notice, and defaulted in rent has abandoned it, and with evidence of abandonment you may terminate the rental agreement, but you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at fair rental value. The law lets a lease restrict that termination right; the library does not offer this, because it only limits your remedies.

title: No Alaska Family Child Care Rental Rule
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant law gives a tenant no right to run a family child care home in a rental and sets no lease conditions for one. Unless the lease says otherwise, a tenant must use the unit only as a dwelling unit, so caring for other families' children for pay is allowed only if you agree. If you allow it, you may require the tenant to hold any child care license state law requires and to carry insurance, but the lease may not make the tenant indemnify you or limit your own liability. Two other rules matter. Alaska's smoke-free law bars smoking, including e-cigarettes and lighted plant products such as marijuana, in an enclosed area of a building or residence used to provide paid child care, whether or not children are present (the ban does not reach a different private residence in the same building). And proposed commercial activity is a lawful ground for refusing a sublease or assignment. Local zoning may also limit home child care.

title: No Alaska Home Business Right for Tenants
bodyText:
Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule making a home-based business a permitted use of a rental home or limiting a lease restriction on one.

Unless the lease says otherwise, a tenant must use the unit only as a dwelling unit, so the lease decides: you may bar business use, or allow quiet home-office work while barring customer traffic, employees, signs or stored inventory.

Business use that materially breaches the lease can be addressed with a written notice to quit, served as AS 09.45.100 requires, that names the breach and a termination date at least 10 days after service (if you serve it by registered or certified mail, the only mail method allowed for a notice to quit, add three days); if the tenant cures before that date, the lease does not end.

Using the unit for other than living purposes in violation of the rental agreement is also one of the grounds on which you may still seek possession after a tenant has complained or asserted rights. Proposed commercial activity is a lawful ground for refusing a sublease or assignment. Municipal zoning regulates home occupations separately.

title: Municipal Utility Liens in Alaska
bodyText:
Alaska leaves it to each municipality whether past-due utility fees become a lien on your property.

State law gives every municipality power to provide by ordinance for the creation, recording and notice of a lien on real or personal property to secure payment of past due utility fees, costs of abating an unsafe or dangerous building, and other fees and charges set by ordinance. Once recorded, such a lien outranks all other liens except property taxes, special assessments and sales and use taxes, liens perfected earlier, liens state law makes paramount, and mechanics' liens already of record.

No Alaska statute or regulation exempts you when the unpaid bill is your tenant's, or lets a lease or affidavit keep the lien off; that depends on your municipality's ordinance. Before letting a tenant hold a municipal water, sewer or refuse account, check the local rules, and ask the tenant for proof of payment.

title: Occupancy Limits in Alaska Rentals
bodyText:
Alaska makes your lease's occupancy limit a statutory tenant duty: a tenant may not allow the number of individuals occupying the premises to exceed the number allowed by applicable law, by a covenant limiting your use of the premises, or by the rental agreement.

A breach can be handled with the 10-day notice for material noncompliance.

Alaska has no statewide persons-per-bedroom or floor-area standard for private rentals; overcrowding is one condition a municipal unfit-dwelling ordinance may treat as making a dwelling unfit, and local housing codes may set limits.

Keep any limit reasonable. Alaska fair housing law bars discrimination because of marital status or pregnancy, and if your rental is financed by the Alaska Housing Finance Corporation, your loan bars discrimination because of parenthood; federal law also protects families with children. The sublease statute lets you refuse a subtenant because of household size, but its under-18 ground may conflict with that federal protection.

title: Nuisance Abatement Ends the Lease in Alaska
bodyText:
An Alaska court order abating a nuisance ends the lease.

A building or place used for prostitution, or for illegal activity involving alcoholic beverages, controlled substances, imitation controlled substances or gambling, is a nuisance, and anyone who owns or leases it can be guilty of maintaining one. The attorney general, a citizen or a home rule municipality may sue to enjoin it, naming the owner and lessee.

If the court finds a nuisance, its order must direct termination of the lease if the tenant had notice of the proceedings, removal and sale of the movable property used in the nuisance, and closing of the place against any use for one year unless released sooner; the landlord-tenant act confirms the order terminates the rental agreement.

The court may release the premises to you if you were not in contempt, pay the costs and post a bond, but the lease stays terminated.

You need not wait for a lawsuit: the same activities let you serve a notice to quit ending the tenancy in 24 hours to five days (a notice to quit may be mailed only by registered or certified mail, and mailing adds three days before you may file).

title: Smoking, Vaping and Marijuana Rules in Alaska Rentals
bodyText:
You may ban smoking, vaping and marijuana use in an Alaska rental, and some smoking is already illegal by statute.

Alaska's smoke-free law bars smoking in an enclosed common area of an apartment building or multiple-family dwelling, and in a building or residence used to provide paid child care or fee-for-service adult care. It also bars smoking within 20 feet of an entrance, open window or air intake vent of an enclosed area where smoking is prohibited.

Smoking includes e-cigarettes and lighted or heated plant products such as marijuana. The marijuana law lets whoever owns or controls private property prohibit or regulate marijuana possession, use and growing there, so a lease may ban or limit it.

Alaska has no statute on smoke drifting between units and no required lease disclosure form. A no-smoking rule adopted after the lease is signed binds only if you give reasonable notice and it does not substantially modify the lease; a signed amendment is safer.

title: Alaska Sublease Consent: 14 Days and Fixed Grounds
bodyText:
Alaska sharply limits how you control subletting, and a lease cannot add restrictions. Unless otherwise agreed in writing, a tenant needs your consent to sublet or assign, but you may withhold consent only on the statutory grounds; no further restrictions are enforceable.

Each prospective occupant must give you a signed written offer with listed information.

Within 14 days after the offer is delivered, you may refuse by a signed written rejection stating one or more grounds: insufficient credit or financial responsibility, household size, number of persons under 18, unwillingness to assume the same lease terms, proposed pets, proposed commercial activity, or a previous landlord's signed written report of abuses, attached.

If your rejection states no permitted ground, the tenant may treat consent as given or end the lease on 30 days' written notice. If you send no signed rejection within 14 days, consent is conclusively presumed.

A lease could allow subletting without consent; the library does not.

title: No Alaska Rule on Claims Against a Tenant's Insurance
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on requiring a tenant to file a claim on the tenant's renters insurance, or on your filing a claim against the tenant's policy. Other limits apply. A lease may not make the tenant indemnify you or limit your liability, so you cannot use the tenant's policy to shift repairs or liability Alaska places on you, such as keeping the premises fit and habitable; knowingly using a lease with a prohibited term lets the tenant recover actual damages. What you can do is recover from the tenant the actual damages the tenant causes by breaching the lease or the tenant's statutory duties, and the tenant may choose to pay them through the tenant's insurer. Treat a claim on the tenant's policy as the tenant's decision, and get the tenant's written permission before you contact the insurer.

title: Wells and Septic Systems in Alaska Rentals
bodyText: In Alaska a private well or septic system stays your responsibility unless a valid agreement shifts a task. You must keep the plumbing and sanitary facilities you supply in good and safe working order, and supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, insofar as energy conditions permit. Two exceptions matter. A landlord of a single family residence in an undeveloped rural area, or where public sewer or water service has never been connected, is not liable for those duties if the unit had no running water, hot water, sewage or sanitary facilities from a private system when the rental began. And where the premises have no well or public water connection, the rental agreement may waive your duty to supply running or hot water. Otherwise, a tenant may take on specified tasks, such as watching a septic alarm, by written agreement in a single family residence or by a separate signed writing for consideration elsewhere; in a one- or two-family residence the tenant may also agree in writing to take over your duty to supply running water, hot water and heat (and the waste, lock and detector duties), but taking over maintenance of the plumbing and sanitary facilities themselves requires rent over $2,000 a month. Any such agreement must be made in good faith, not to evade your obligations.

title: Tenant Repair and Chore Agreements in Alaska
bodyText:
Alaska lets a tenant take on repairs and chores only through the right kind of agreement.

For a one- or two-family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant performs specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling, and some of your listed duties; a tenant may never agree to maintain elevators.

For any dwelling unit other than a single family residence, the agreement must be a separate writing signed by both of you and supported by adequate consideration, and it may not reduce your duties to other tenants. Because both rules reach a two-family residence, use the separate writing there too.

Every such agreement must be made in good faith and not to evade your obligations, and you may not make the tenant's performance of a separate agreement a condition of the lease. A lease term that shifts these duties any other way is an unenforceable waiver of the tenant's rights.

title: Statutory Tenant Duties in Alaska
When the Tenant Holds the Utility Account in Alaska
bodyText:
When your tenant holds an Alaska electric account, state utility rules protect you as owner.

A regulated electric utility that knows of a landlord-tenant relationship must notify you in writing at least 15 days before disconnecting a tenant-customer, offering you the option to take the service in your name, and it may not try to collect the tenant's unpaid bill from you or condition your service on it, unless you owe your own past balance at that address. Nor may it disconnect a customer for a prior customer's unpaid bill at the premises unless that person still lives there.

If a public utility shuts off a tenant's electricity, natural gas or water for nonpayment, you may serve a notice to quit ending the tenancy five days after service (if you serve it by registered or certified mail, the only mail method allowed for a notice to quit, add three days); it does not end if, within three days, the tenant restores service and repays any reinstatement costs you paid, and no damage resulted.

If the tenant, in the absence of due care, repeats substantially the same shutoff within six months after a notice, you may end the tenancy on at least three days' written notice. Municipal utilities exempt from state regulation follow their own rules.

title: No Utility Shutoffs by Alaska Landlords, Even When Submetered
bodyText:
Alaska gives a landlord no right to interrupt electricity or other utilities a tenant has not paid, even if you submeter or bill them yourself, and Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no submetering billing regime.

You may not recover possession by interrupting, or causing the interruption of, electricity, gas, water, sanitary or other essential services, except in case of abandonment, surrender, or energy conditions beyond your control. If you wilfully cut off an essential service, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to one and one-half times actual damages.

Treat unpaid utility charges you bill as a lease debt. They are probably not rent, which the act defines as the uniform periodic payment, so the cautious course is the 10-day notice for material noncompliance, or a suit for the amount.

Reselling electricity or water to tenants may also raise state utility-regulation questions; get advice first.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors in Alaska Rentals
bodyText: Alaska requires smoke detectors in every dwelling unit and carbon monoxide detectors in every qualifying unit: one that contains or is served by a carbon-fueled appliance or device, has an attached garage or carport, or is next to a parking space. At the start of each occupancy you must provide working devices, and after the tenant reports a deficiency you must repair or replace them. The tenant must keep them working by keeping batteries charged, testing them periodically and not permanently disabling them. Smoke detectors must be a type and installation the state fire marshal approves: single-station devices must meet NFPA 72 and the building code's placement rules, and may run on batteries alone only in buildings built before January 1, 1989 or without commercial power. CO detectors need an alarm and follow the manufacturer's recommendations. If you did not know of and were not told about a needed repair, failing to make it is not evidence of negligence. Violations are a misdemeanor; CO violations are a lesser offense.

title: Substitute Housing Remedies in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska does not require you to house a tenant elsewhere during repairs, after a fire, or when a unit is ordered closed, and sets no relocation payment for private landlords. Tenants have remedies that can cost you instead. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat, sanitary facilities or other essential services, the tenant may, after written notice, procure reasonable substitute housing while your noncompliance lasts, owe no rent for that period, and recover the amount by which its actual and reasonable cost exceeds the rent. When you sue for possession or rent and the tenant counterclaims, a court may order the tenant to vacate during repairs that cannot otherwise be made, with reinstatement afterward. If fire or casualty substantially impairs the unit, the tenant may vacate and end the lease, or vacate the unusable part and pay reduced rent. State relocation assistance covers people displaced by state-agency projects, not private repairs.

title: Excluding Appliances in Alaska Leases
bodyText:
Alaska has no rule presuming that appliances in a unit are yours to maintain, and no rule on excluding them in the lease.

Your repair duty covers the electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning, kitchen and other facilities and appliances supplied or required to be supplied by you, so the lease should say which appliances you supply (the Appliances Included list) and which belong to the tenant. Appliances a tenant brings in are the tenant's to maintain, and the tenant must use your facilities reasonably.

Be careful with items a former tenant left behind: if they stay in place for the new tenant's use without a clear statement, the tenant may argue you supplied them.

Excluding an appliance cannot remove a duty the law imposes, such as supplying heat and hot water, and a lease term limiting your liability for items you supply is unenforceable.

title: Condemned or Closed Units: No Express Alaska Rent Bar
bodyText: Alaska's statutes contain no express bar on collecting rent once a unit is condemned or ordered vacated. Other rules lead to a similar place. Where a municipality has adopted an unfit-dwelling ordinance, the Alaska Housing Finance Corporation may, after a complaint and hearing, find a dwelling unfit for human habitation and order you to repair it or to vacate and close it, or to remove or demolish it if repair would cost too much; if you do not comply, it may do the work and its costs become a lien on the property. A unit that cannot lawfully be lived in is not fit and habitable, so the tenant's remedies apply: ending the lease after an unremedied material breach, rent reduction or rent paid into court on a counterclaim, and substitute housing for lost essential services. If code-required work would deprive the tenant of the unit, you may recover possession after a notice to quit even after a tenant complaint, but the tenant does not unlawfully hold until at least 30 days after that notice (or any longer period the lease sets). Local codes may add rent rules.

title: Habitability Rules Other States Have That Alaska Lacks
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no Alaska counterpart. (1) No list of imminently dangerous conditions, no mold rule and no numeric heat standard: the general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable governs. (2) No statutory presumption that you breached a habitability duty; the act's one presumption concerns the signed move-in condition statement. (3) No rent escrow outside court: a tenant may pay rent into court only when you sue for possession for nonpayment, or for rent while the tenant is in possession, and the tenant counterclaims and the court orders it. (4) No small-landlord exemption from tenant remedies; the exemptions turn on the property, not the landlord's size: the heat and hot-water exception for a tenant-controlled installation on a direct utility connection, the water waiver where there is no well or utility water, and the exemption for a single family residence in an undeveloped rural area, or never connected to public water or sewer, that had no water or sanitary facilities from a private system at the start. (5) No rule on oral repair requests; the termination and essential-services remedies require written notice. (6) No rule making air conditioning an essential service, though you must maintain any you supply. The duties themselves cannot be waived, and rent cannot be collected free of them.

title: No Alaska Rule Naming Who Does Tenant Self-Help Work
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations neither allow nor forbid a lease clause naming the person or firm who must do work a tenant arranges at your expense. Alaska's self-help remedy is narrow: it reaches only essential services. If, contrary to the lease or your duties, you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat, sanitary facilities or other essential services, the tenant may, after written notice, procure reasonable amounts of them while your noncompliance lasts and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from the rent. There is no general repair-and-deduct right for other repairs. Because a lease may not waive or limit a tenant's remedies under the act, a clause restricting who may supply those services could be unenforceable if it delays or blocks the remedy, so the library does not offer one. Instead, give the tenant a preferred contractor and an emergency number to call you first.

title: Disability Accommodations Under Alaska Fair Housing Law
bodyText:
Alaska fair housing law makes it unlawful for an owner, lessee, manager or anyone else with the right to rent to refuse to rent, or to discriminate in a term, condition or privilege of a rental, because of physical or mental disability.

The statute does not spell out reasonable accommodations or modifications. The Human Rights Commission must adopt regulations on when accommodations are needed, and so far its rules for rentals cover only service animals: the public-accommodation service-animal rules, including no surcharge, also apply to landlords, except for a room in a home the owner lives in with shared living areas. Disability includes a condition that may require a service animal.

The federal Fair Housing Act separately requires reasonable accommodations in rules and policies and lets a tenant make reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense. Answer requests promptly and in writing, and ask only what you need to evaluate them.

title: No Alaska Statute on Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations do not address renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, and set no special remedy for it. The general possession rules cover it. At the start of the term you must deliver possession of the premises in compliance with the rental agreement. If you do not, rent abates until possession is delivered, and the tenant may either end the lease on at least 10 days' written notice and get back all prepaid rent and security deposits, or demand performance, sue for possession against you and anyone wrongfully in possession, and recover damages. If your failure to deliver possession is wilful and not in good faith, the tenant may recover up to one and one-half times actual damages. You may also serve a notice to quit on a person wrongfully in possession and sue for possession.

title: No Alaska Background-Check Rule for Apartment Staff
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no requirement to run background checks on apartment employees, maintenance staff or managers who enter tenants' units, and none forbidding it. Your staff's entries still count as yours. Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, you must give at least 24 hours' notice of intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times and with the tenant's consent, and you may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass. An unlawful entry, a lawful entry made unreasonably, or repeated harassing demands for entry let the tenant seek an injunction or end the lease, and recover up to the greater of actual damages or one month's rent, plus court costs and reasonable attorney fees. If you do screen staff through a consumer reporting agency, follow federal consumer-reporting law.

title: How Serious a Defect Must Be for Each Alaska Tenant Remedy
bodyText: Alaska ties the tenant's strongest remedies to how serious the problem is. To end the lease, the tenant needs a material noncompliance by you with the rental agreement, or a noncompliance with your statutory maintenance duties materially affecting health and safety. The tenant's written notice must specify the breach and a termination date at least 20 days after you receive it, and the lease does not end if you remedy the breach within 10 days. If substantially the same breach recurs within six months without due care on your part, the tenant may terminate on 10 days' written notice. The essential-services remedies (buying the service and deducting its cost, damages for reduced rental value, or substitute housing) apply when you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat, sanitary facilities or other essential services. For any noncompliance, material or not, the tenant may sue for damages or an injunction. None of these remedies covers a condition the tenant, family or guests caused.

title: Which Alaska Habitability Duties a Lease Can Change
bodyText:
Most of your Alaska habitability duties cannot be changed by the lease: a term waiving the tenant's rights or remedies is unenforceable, and no lease, assignment, deed or security instrument may let anyone collect rent free of the duty to keep the premises fit.

The statute builds in a few exceptions. The heat and hot-water duty does not apply where heat or hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control supplied by a direct public utility connection. Where the premises have no well and no public water connection, the rental agreement may waive your duty to supply running or hot water if it specifically says so. A single family residence in an undeveloped rural area, or never connected to public water or sewer, is exempt from the facilities and water duties if it had no water or sanitary facilities from a private system at the start. Heat and water are owed only insofar as energy conditions permit.

Shifting tasks to the tenant needs the agreements described in the Alaska tenant repair agreement row.

title: No Alaska Presumption of Habitability Breach
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations create no presumption that you breached your repair or habitability duties because a unit violates a code or lacks a facility, none that you had notice, and none about how long a repair may take. The tenant proves the condition and gives the written notice each remedy requires. The landlord-tenant act's one presumption concerns condition at move-in: a signed premises condition statement and contents inventory are presumptive evidence of the condition at the start of the term, and either side may use them to compute damages unless their authenticity is rebutted by clear and convincing evidence. That presumption helps you prove tenant-caused damage at move-out, and helps the tenant prove a defect existed from the start. The act sets no repair deadline other than the 10-day cure period in a tenant's termination notice.

title: No Required Alaska Lease Statement on Habitability
bodyText: Alaska does not require your lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation. The duties apply whether or not the lease mentions them: at the start of the term you must deliver possession in compliance with the rental agreement and your maintenance duties, and you must make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises fit and habitable. The statements Alaska does require in or with a residential lease are narrower: the extended-absence notice term, the specific water-waiver statement if you use that waiver, the scope of any mediation or arbitration agreement, a signed condition statement if you require one, and the terms and conditions under which you may withhold the deposit (where the deposit section applies); the manager's and owner's names and addresses must be disclosed in writing at or before move-in. A habitability promise in the lease adds a contract claim but cannot narrow the statute.

title: No Alaska Health-District Rental Rules
bodyText: Alaska has no health-district rental regulations and no statute requiring you to give tenants health or housing regulations on request or to refer them to a health agency. State law sets up local boards of health in health units, under the health commissioner's supervision, and lets the health department combine contiguous units into a health district, but gives them no rental-housing rules. Rental housing standards come instead from the landlord-tenant act, the state fire and life-safety regulations for residential buildings of four or more units, and municipal codes adopted under the power to set minimum standards for the use and occupancy of dwellings. If a tenant asks which codes apply, point the tenant to your municipality's building or code enforcement office.

title: Heat in Alaska Rentals
bodyText: Alaska requires you to supply heat, running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, insofar as energy conditions permit, and to keep heating facilities you supply in good and safe working order. There is no numeric temperature standard. The heat duty does not apply where heat is generated by an installation in the tenant's exclusive control and supplied by a direct public utility connection, such as a tenant-metered gas furnace. In a one- or two-family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant supplies heat, for example by buying heating oil; in other dwellings the duty stays with you. If you deliberately or negligently fail to supply heat, the tenant may, after written notice, buy reasonable heat and deduct its actual and reasonable cost from rent, recover damages for reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing and owe no rent meanwhile. You may never cut heat to force a tenant out, except where energy conditions beyond your control cause the interruption.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach in Alaska
bodyText: When you breach the lease or your Alaska duties, the tenant has statutory remedies the lease cannot take away. For a material breach of the lease, or a breach of your maintenance duties materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may give written notice ending the lease at least 20 days after you receive it unless you remedy within 10 days. For any breach of the lease or your maintenance duties, an unlawful ouster or a utility cutoff, the tenant may recover damages and an injunction. If you fail to deliver possession, rent abates and the tenant may end the lease on 10 days' notice. If you unlawfully remove or exclude the tenant or wilfully interrupt essential services, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease, and recover up to one and one-half times actual damages. Unlawful or harassing entry lets the tenant seek an injunction or end the lease on 10 days' written notice, and recover up to the greater of actual damages or one month's rent, plus court costs and reasonable attorney fees. Retaliation brings the ouster remedies and a defense to eviction.

title: Alaska Repair and Maintenance Duties
Which Alaska Landlord Duties Can Move to the Tenant
bodyText:
In Alaska only some of your listed duties can move to the tenant, and only in small residences.

In a one- or two-family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant takes over providing waste receptacles and arranging removal; supplying running water, hot water and heat; and providing locks and keys.

A tenant may also take over maintaining the electrical, plumbing, heating, kitchen and other facilities and appliances, but only where rent exceeds $2,000 a month, and never elevators.

The detector duty is listed too, but a separate statute still makes you provide working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors at each occupancy.

In any other dwelling unit none of these duties can shift; only specified repairs and maintenance tasks can, by a separate signed writing supported by consideration.

Every such agreement must be made in good faith and not to evade your duties. The library's optional Tenant-Assumed Duties clause covers a single family residence.

For a two-family residence, do not use that clause: put the agreement in a separate writing signed by you and the tenant and supported by adequate consideration.

title: Specific Facilities Alaska Requires You to Provide
bodyText: Beyond the general repair duty, Alaska names specific facilities and services you must provide. You must provide and maintain appropriate receptacles and conveniences for removing ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste, and arrange for their removal. If the tenant asks, you must provide and maintain locks and furnish keys reasonably adequate to ensure the safety of the tenant and the tenant's property. You must provide smoke and carbon monoxide detectors as the detector statute requires. And you must keep elevators, air conditioning and the other facilities and appliances you supply in good and safe working order. Alaska's statutes and regulations set no mailbox, telephone-jack, window-screen or window-latch requirement for rentals; municipal housing and building codes may. In a one- or two-family residence the waste and lock duties may be shifted to the tenant by written agreement, but you must still supply working detectors at each occupancy.

title: Promises to Repair: No Alaska Writing Rule, but Oral Promises Count
bodyText: Alaska has no rule that your promises to clean, repair or improve a unit be in writing, carry a completion date, or be made before the lease is signed. Promises you make still bind you. Alaska treats all agreements, written or oral, embodying the terms of use and occupancy as part of the rental agreement. A material noncompliance with the rental agreement lets the tenant give written notice ending the lease unless you remedy the breach within 10 days, and any noncompliance supports a claim for damages or an injunction. The tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry to make agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements. To avoid disputes, put any promised work in the lease or a signed addendum with a target date, and note the condition before the work on the move-in condition statement.

title: Quiet Possession: No Alaska Lease Covenant Statute, but Possession Is Protected
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant act does not write out a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment; the only statutory quiet-possession covenant is in the warranty-deed form for sales of land. The act protects the same interest directly. You may not recover possession by action or otherwise except as the act permits, including by cutting essential services, and an unlawful removal, exclusion or wilful service interruption lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease and recover up to one and one-half times actual damages. You may enter only with notice and at reasonable times, and may not abuse access or harass; abuse lets the tenant seek an injunction or end the lease, and recover up to the greater of actual damages or one month's rent, plus court costs and reasonable attorney fees. The tenant, for the other side, may not unreasonably disturb neighbors' peaceful enjoyment. Whether Alaska courts imply a covenant of quiet enjoyment in leases is case law not searched here; act as though one exists.

title: Rent Cannot Be Collected Free of the Repair Duty in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska forbids splitting the right to collect rent from the duty to keep the unit fit.
