No rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed or security instrument may let anyone receive rent free of the obligation to comply with your maintenance duties, so an assignment of rents to a lender or a master lease cannot carve out the repair duty. A manager who fails to make the required name-and-address disclosure counts as a landlord and becomes your agent for performing your duties, and must make the rent collected available for that purpose. If you sell in a good-faith sale, you are relieved of later obligations only after written notice of the sale to the tenant, and you stay liable for deposits unless the buyer specifically accepts them. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit rules.

title: Rental Inspections in Alaska: No Statewide Program
bodyText: Alaska has no statewide rental registration, licensing or periodic inspection program. Inspections come from two other sources. The state Department of Public Safety may enter a residential building of four or more dwelling units subject to its fire and life-safety regulations, during reasonable hours, solely to inspect or abate a fire hazard. And a municipality that adopts an unfit-dwelling ordinance may authorize entry to examine premises, made in the way least inconvenient to the person in possession, or by court order if entry is denied. The landlord-tenant act lets you enter only for its listed purposes, by court order, during a tenant absence of more than seven days (at times reasonably necessary, as provided in the access section, so give the usual notice where practicable), or after abandonment or surrender, and a lease cannot add an inspector's right of access. You may enter to inspect on 24 hours' notice; for an inspector's own inspection, get the tenant's consent or rely on the inspector's authority. Municipal rental programs may exist.

title: No Alaska Small-Landlord Opt-Out From Tenant Remedies
bodyText: Alaska has no notice or other procedure that lets a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' repair remedies. The termination remedy, the essential-services remedies, rent reduction or rent paid into court on a counterclaim, and the fire and casualty rights apply however few units you own, and a lease may not waive them. The exemptions in Alaska's landlord-tenant law turn on the property, not the size of your business: a single family residence in an undeveloped rural area, or never connected to public water or sewer, is exempt from the facilities and water duties if it had no water or sanitary facilities from a private system at the start; and the security-deposit limits do not apply where rent exceeds $2,000 a month.

title: Repair Notices in Alaska: When Writing Matters
bodyText: Alaska ties the tenant's main repair remedies to written notice. To end the lease for your breach, the tenant must deliver a written notice specifying the acts and omissions constituting it; the essential-services remedies arise only after the tenant gives you written notice; and you must repair or replace a smoke or carbon monoxide detector after the tenant tells you of a deficiency. A lease may ask for repair requests in writing, but it cannot narrow rights that do not depend on written notice. A tenant who complains to you about a maintenance violation is protected from retaliation however the complaint is made, and when you sue for rent or possession the tenant may counterclaim for any amount recoverable, with rent reduced for the period of noncompliance. Because a lease may not waive either side's rights under the act, a term making oral notice enough probably does not displace the written-notice rules. Treat any report you receive as notice and act promptly.

title: Locks and Security Devices in Alaska Rentals
bodyText:
Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no requirement for deadbolts, door viewers, window latches or rekeying between tenants.

Your duty arises on request: if the tenant asks, you must provide and maintain locks and furnish keys reasonably adequate to ensure the safety of the tenant and the tenant's property. In a one- or two-family residence that duty may be shifted to the tenant by written agreement.

The tenant may not change the locks without your written agreement, except in an emergency when you cannot be reached after reasonable effort, and must then give you keys to the changed locks, immediately after an agreed change or within five days with written notice after an emergency change.

Rekeying at turnover is not required by statute but is a sensible way to meet the on-request duty before it is invoked. Municipal building codes may require specific hardware.

title: No Alaska Work-Card Rule for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: Alaska has no work-card, licensing or background-check requirement for maintenance or management staff in housing for older persons, or in any other private rental housing. Alaska's fair housing statute does not list age among the grounds on which refusing to rent is unlawful, though it bars age-based discrimination in real estate listings and in representing that property is unavailable; federal law governs housing for older persons. Your staff's entries into units count as yours and must follow the 24-hour notice, reasonable-time and consent rules, except in an emergency. An older Alaskan with a complaint about a landlord or senior citizen housing may take it to the state long-term care ombudsman.

title: No Alaska Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText:
Alaska's statutes and regulations do not require you to supply a stove, range, oven or refrigerator.

If you do supply them, they are kitchen appliances you must keep in good and safe working order, and in a one- or two-family residence a tenant may take over that maintenance only where rent exceeds $2,000 a month. Appliances the tenant brings in are the tenant's to maintain, and the tenant must use yours in a reasonable manner.

List the appliances you supply in the lease so the duty is clear, and record their condition on the move-in condition statement or contents inventory. Municipal housing codes may require cooking or refrigeration facilities.

title: No Alaska Housing Receivership; Unfit-Dwelling Orders Instead
bodyText: Alaska has no tenant receivership or court-appointed receiver for substandard rental housing. Code enforcement runs through other tools. Where a municipality adopts an unfit-dwelling ordinance, a public officer must investigate when at least five residents petition or the officer finds a dwelling unfit, serve a complaint on the owner, mortgagees and those in possession, and set a hearing 10 to 30 days later. The Alaska Housing Finance Corporation may then order repair, vacating and closing, or demolition, do the work itself if you do not comply, and recover the costs, including attorney fees, as a lien on the property. Municipalities may also set minimum standards for using and occupying dwellings, and their recorded liens for abating unsafe buildings outrank most other liens. Tenants' own route is the landlord-tenant act: termination, essential-services self-help, and rent paid into court on a counterclaim.

title: No Alaska Rule on Cable, Satellite or Internet Access in Rentals
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule giving tenants a right to cable television, satellite, broadband or other telecommunications access in a rental building, requiring you to let a provider wire your building, barring exclusive provider arrangements, or barring different rent for cable subscribers. Cable television utilities are largely exempt from state utility regulation, and nothing in the landlord-tenant act addresses telecommunications. Federal rules limit lease restrictions on satellite dishes and antennas a tenant installs in an area under the tenant's exclusive use, such as a balcony. Your lease terms on alterations govern wiring and mounting, and any building rule on equipment must meet Alaska's test for enforceable rules: a proper purpose, reasonably related to it, applied fairly to all tenants and explicit enough to follow.

title: Alaska Tenant Self-Help and Rent-Into-Court Remedies
bodyText: Alaska's tenant self-help remedies are narrower than many states'. There is no general repair-and-deduct right and no rent withholding outside court. If, contrary to the lease or your duties, you deliberately or negligently fail to supply running water, hot water, heat, sanitary facilities or other essential services, the tenant may give you written notice and immediately buy reasonable amounts of them and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent, recover damages for the reduced rental value, or move to substitute housing, owing no rent meanwhile and recovering any excess cost. A tenant who uses this remedy may not also terminate under the general remedy for the same breach. When you sue for possession for nonpayment, or for rent while the tenant stays, the tenant may counterclaim; the court may reduce rent, continue the case so you can cure, or order rent paid into court, and if the violations are not cured within six months it enters judgment for the tenant. None of this applies to tenant-caused conditions.

title: No Alaska Rule on Utility Allowances
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation on utility allowance plans, in which you pay a utility up to a set monthly amount and the tenant reimburses the excess, and none on passing master-metered costs to tenants through rent. Such a plan is a matter of contract, with three cautions. Your duty to supply heat and hot water cannot be shifted except under the narrow statutory exceptions or, in a one- or two-family residence, by written agreement, so an allowance may limit what the tenant pays but not whether the service is supplied. Overage charges are probably not rent, which the act defines as the uniform periodic payment, so collect them as a separate lease debt rather than through the seven-day nonpayment notice. And you may never cut off the service to collect. Reselling metered service to tenants may also raise state utility-regulation questions.

title: Splitting Shared Utility Bills in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation on splitting a shared utility bill among tenants by ratio, floor area or occupancy, and no rule making such a term unenforceable. If you divide a master-metered bill, it is a contract term: before the tenant signs, state the method, the utilities covered and how the tenant can see the underlying bills. Keep three limits in mind. Heat and hot water remain your duty except under the statutory exceptions or a written one- or two-family agreement, so a share of a building heating bill is a charge, not a shift of the duty. Variable shares are probably not rent, so the seven-day nonpayment notice may not reach them. And you may not cut a tenant's service for nonpayment. On the utility side, a regulated electric utility bills each meter separately and must give each tenant on a master meter notice before disconnecting your account.

title: Getting Notice of a Tenant's Pending Electric Shutoff in Alaska
bodyText:
Alaska has no procedure for an owner, by a separate document, to authorize a utility to warn the owner of a tenant's pending disconnection.

Two electric-utility rules cover much of the ground. When a regulated electric utility knows a landlord-tenant relationship exists and the tenant is the customer, it must notify you in writing at least 15 days before disconnecting the tenant, offering you the service in your name, and it may not charge the tenant's debt to you.

And every applicant for electric service is asked for the name and address of any third party to be copied on termination notices; the utility must send that copy at the same time as the customer's notice. You can ask your tenant to name you as that third party.

Gas, water and municipal utilities follow their own tariffs, which this summary does not cover.

title: When the Utility Account Is in Your Name in Alaska
bodyText:
When the utility account is in your name, Alaska's electric-utility rules protect your tenants.

For an individually metered unit, a regulated electric utility must notify the tenant in writing at least 15 days before disconnecting your account, offering service in the tenant's own name, and it may not collect your unpaid bill from the tenant or condition the tenant's service on it, unless the tenant owes an old balance at that address.

For a master-metered building, the utility must either, after the usual notice period has run, give each tenant on the master meter individual notice at least 14 days before disconnection, or give each such tenant notice at least 15 days before the scheduled disconnection.

Under the landlord-tenant act, if you deliberately or negligently fail to supply an essential service you owe, the tenant, after giving you written notice, may buy it and deduct the cost from rent, recover damages, or move to substitute housing, and a wilful interruption brings up to one and one-half times actual damages. Alaska has no rent receivership for unpaid utilities.

title: Electric Disconnection Rules in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska's disconnection protections come from the Regulatory Commission of Alaska's rules for regulated electric utilities, not from a statute. A utility may begin disconnection when a bill is unpaid 40 days after it was rendered, unless the customer has a deferred payment agreement, and must mail or deliver written notice at least 15 days before the disconnection date, or 30 days if it knows the home has a seriously ill, elderly or disabled resident or one dependent on life support. It must then attempt personal contact at least three working days before. It may disconnect only between 8 a.m. Monday and 5 p.m. Thursday, never on a Friday or the day before a holiday, and must offer a deferred payment plan to a residential customer showing economic hardship. Alaska has no winter moratorium or temperature ban. Municipal utilities exempt from state regulation, and gas and water utilities, follow their own rules. The landlord and tenant notice rules appear in the related rows.

title: No Alaska Submetering Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation requiring a lease disclosure when you submeter utilities or bill tenants for them, and no prescribed form, type-size rule, billing limit or regulator authorization for landlord billing. The lease is the only disclosure, so state which utilities you bill, how you measure or allocate them, when bills are due, and how the tenant can see the readings or source bills. A few rules still bear on it. You may not cut off service to collect. Billed utility charges are probably not rent, so the seven-day nonpayment notice may not reach them. A charge added after the lease is signed binds only by agreement or a valid rule that does not substantially modify the lease. And if you furnish electricity or water to tenants for compensation, you may come within the state's public-utility definitions; one water-utility exemption, for example, is lost if the system sub-meters water. Get advice before reselling metered service.

title: No Utility Cutoff When an Alaska Tenant Fails to Transfer Service
bodyText: Alaska has no rule letting you shut off utilities still in your name because a tenant did not move the account into the tenant's name, and no opt-in lease procedure for it. You may not recover possession by interrupting, or causing the interruption of, electricity, gas, water, sanitary or other essential services, and a wilful interruption lets the tenant recover possession or end the lease with up to one and one-half times actual damages; a lease term permitting a cutoff would be an unenforceable waiver. A lease may require the tenant to put specified utilities in the tenant's name by a set date, and failing to do so is a breach you can address by a notice to cure or by charging the tenant, under the lease, for service used. If you stop paying your own account, the electric utility must first offer the tenant service in the tenant's own name, at least 15 days before disconnecting an individually metered unit.

title: Alaska Landlord Entry Rules
bodyText:
You may enter to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, remove your own property not covered by a written rental agreement, or show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, lenders, tenants, workers or contractors, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent.

Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, give at least 24 hours' notice, enter only at reasonable times, and enter with the tenant's consent. In an emergency you may enter without consent.

Otherwise you have no right of entry except by court order, during an absence of more than seven days (at times reasonably necessary, still following the notice rules above), or after abandonment or surrender, and you may not use access to harass.

If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may get a court order or end the lease on 10 days' written notice, and recover up to the greater of your actual damages or one month's rent.

If you enter unlawfully or unreasonably, or harass with repeated demands, the tenant has the same remedies plus court costs and reasonable attorney fees; the court's answer form invites a claim for each unlawful entry. A lease cannot remove the notice or consent requirement.

title: No Alaska No-Notice Service Entry
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule letting you enter for regularly scheduled services, such as filter changes, smoke alarm checks or pest treatment, without notice or without the tenant's consent, even if the lease says so conspicuously. The ordinary entry rule governs every visit: except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, give at least 24 hours' notice, enter only at reasonable times, and enter with the tenant's consent. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to an entry to supply necessary or agreed services. A lease term that dispensed with the notice or the consent would waive a right under the landlord-tenant act and would be unenforceable. A workable practice is to give the tenant a written service schedule at move-in, then a reminder at least 24 hours before each visit, and to note the tenant's agreement to the time.

title: No Alaska Showing-Notice Waiver
bodyText: Alaska law has no procedure letting a tenant waive or shorten the 24-hour entry notice for showings, whether in the lease or in a separate signed document. You may show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, lenders or tenants, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent, but except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable you must give at least 24 hours' notice and enter at reasonable times with the tenant's consent. A rental agreement may not make the tenant waive rights under the landlord-tenant act, so a lease waiver of the notice is unenforceable, and wilfully using a lease you know contains a prohibited term lets the tenant recover actual damages. A tenant can still agree to a particular showing time on shorter notice; record that agreement for each showing rather than relying on a standing waiver. Repeated showing demands that unreasonably harass the tenant expose you to the access-abuse remedies.

title: No Alaska Smart-Lock Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on smart locks, keypads, app-based or biometric entry systems in rentals: nothing requires an alternative physical key, a privacy policy, or limits on the entry data you collect. The general rules apply whatever the technology. If the tenant asks, you must provide and maintain locks and furnish keys reasonably adequate to ensure the safety of the tenant and the tenant's property; the law does not say whether a code or phone credential counts as a key, so offering a physical key or fob that needs no app is the cautious course. Remote unlocking does not change the entry rule: except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable, give at least 24 hours' notice and enter at reasonable times with the tenant's consent. The tenant may not change the locks without your written agreement except in an emergency. Tell tenants in writing what entry data the system records and who can see it.

title: No Alaska DV Lock-Change Statute
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule letting a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking require you to change the locks, and set no deadline or cost rule for a lock change. Two rules bear on a request. A tenant may not change the locks without your written agreement, except in an emergency when you cannot be reached after reasonable effort; after an emergency change the tenant must give you keys and written notice within five days. And a court's domestic violence protective order may remove and exclude the abuser from the victim's residence regardless of who owns it; a person who stays in violation of that order is there unlawfully. If a tenant shows you a protective order excluding a co-tenant or occupant and asks for new locks, changing them promptly is the cautious course; keep a copy of the order and give keys only to the protected tenant and other lawful occupants. Federal rules for assisted housing may add duties.

title: Alaska Abandoned Property Rules
bodyText:
When a tenancy ends, including by expiration, surrender or abandonment, and the tenant leaves belongings you reasonably believe are abandoned, Alaska gives you a procedure.

Give the tenant written notice demanding removal by a date at least 15 days after you deliver or mail it, stating that property not removed may be sold. If it is not removed, you may sell it at a public sale run under the execution-sale rules (posted notice in three public places at least 10 days before the sale) and dispose of anything that draws no bid.

Property you reasonably judge worthless, or worth less than storing and selling it would cost, may be destroyed or disposed of after the same 15-day notice, which must say which items you will sell and which you will dispose of. Perishables may be disposed of in any manner.

Meanwhile store the property with reasonable care; storage on the premises may not cost more than the fair rental value. A tenant who removes the property owes the storage cost.

Deliberate or negligent violations make you liable for actual damages plus penal damages up to the same amount.

title: Alaska Abandonment and Re-Renting
bodyText:
Alaska defines abandonment narrowly: the tenant has left the unit with belongings in it, stayed away for seven days or longer in a row without giving the required absence notice, and defaulted in rent. A tenant who moves out with rent paid has not abandoned in this sense, though the tenant may have surrendered or breached the lease.

With evidence of abandonment you may terminate the lease. You must then make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental value. If you re-rent for a term starting before the old lease would have ended, the old lease ends when the new tenancy begins, so the departed tenant's rent liability runs until then.

If you do not make reasonable efforts, or you accept the abandonment as a surrender, the lease is treated as ended on the date you had notice of the abandonment. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy the term is treated as one month or one week.

After termination you may claim possession, rent, and separately actual damages for breach, and every aggrieved party must mitigate damages. Keep records of your advertising and showings.

title: Alaska Attorney Fee Rules
bodyText: In Alaska attorney fees come from statute and court rule, not from the lease. A rental agreement may not say the tenant will pay your attorney fees; that term is unenforceable, and wilfully using a lease you know contains a prohibited term lets the tenant recover actual damages. A mutual prevailing-party clause adds nothing, so leave fee language out. Instead, the landlord-tenant act says attorney fees shall be allowed to the prevailing party, landlord or tenant, in any proceeding arising out of the act or a rental agreement. Civil Rule 82 supplies the usual measure: for a money judgment, a percentage schedule (for the first $25,000, 20% after a contested trial, 18% if contested without trial, 10% if uncontested); with no money judgment, 30% of reasonable actual fees after trial or 20% without one; on a default judgment, the schedule amount or your reasonable actual fees, whichever is less. Whether the act's rule allows more than Rule 82 is a question of case law. A tenant who proves unlawful or harassing entry recovers reasonable attorney fees under the access statute.

title: Alaska Fire and Casualty Rules
bodyText: If fire or another casualty damages the unit or premises so that enjoyment of the unit is substantially impaired, the tenant chooses what happens. The tenant may immediately vacate and notify you of the intention to terminate, and the lease ends on the date the tenant vacates. Or, if continued occupancy is lawful, the tenant may vacate only the part made unusable and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost fair rental value. Either way, rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty, and if the lease ends you must return the prepaid rent and deposit the tenant is entitled to under the deposit rules. The statute has no exception for a casualty the tenant caused; your remedy then is actual damages for the tenant's breach. The statute gives you no termination right of your own, and this library offers no landlord casualty-termination clause, because it could cut off the tenant's statutory choice to stay in the usable part. If you must substantially rebuild or demolish, see the optional Alaska owner-recovery clause, which uses the statutory good-faith ground with at least 30 days' notice.

title: Alaska Condominium Conversion Notice
bodyText: If you convert a rental building into a condominium, cooperative or other common interest community, Alaska requires the declarant, and any dealer offering units, to give each residential tenant and subtenant in possession notice of the conversion and the public offering statement at least 180 days before they must move out (one year in a mobile home park). Deliver the notice by hand or by certified mail, return receipt requested, and describe the tenants' rights. During the notice period you may not change the tenancy terms, and failing to give the notice is a defense to an eviction. Shorter notice is allowed only for rent default, a continuing harmful law violation after conviction, or violating an enforceable lease term or rule. For 90 days after the notice you must offer to sell each occupied unit to its tenant; after that, the tenant keeps a right of first refusal against better terms offered to others. A conversion notice that states a vacate date and meets the eviction-notice rules also serves as the notice to quit. The law does not let you end a lease early in violation of its terms.

title: Alaska Illegal Activity Rules
bodyText:
Alaska forbids a tenant to knowingly engage at the premises in, or knowingly permit others in the premises to engage in, prostitution, illegal activity involving a place of prostitution, illegal alcohol delivery in a local-option dry area, illegal gambling (not social games), or illegal activity involving controlled or imitation controlled substances, each defined by specific criminal statutes.

These breaches allow a notice to quit with no right to cure, ending the tenancy not less than 24 hours or more than five days after service.

Other crimes, such as assault, are not on the list; treat them as a material lease breach on the 10-day notice, or, if the tenant is using the unit for an illegal purpose, get advice on the five-day track.

No statute requires you to evict, and Alaska has no crime-free addendum statute. But knowingly keeping a dwelling used for keeping or distributing controlled substances in violation of a felony drug law is a crime, and an owner or lessor of a place used for the listed activities can face a nuisance action that ends the lease and can close the building for a year. You may also prohibit possession, use and growing of marijuana on your property.

title: Alaska Tenant Cure Periods
bodyText:
Alaska sets fixed cure tracks for a tenant's breach.
- For a material breach of the lease, or a breach of the tenant's statutory duties that materially affects health and safety, your notice to quit must give at least 10 days; if the breach can be fixed by repairs, paying damages or otherwise and the tenant fixes it in time, the lease continues.
- If substantially the same breach recurs within six months without due care, you may end the lease on at least five days' written notice, with no second cure.
- If a utility cuts off electricity, gas or water for the tenant's nonpayment, your notice ends the tenancy in five days unless, within three days, the tenant restores service, repays what you paid, and no damage resulted; if, in the absence of due care, substantially the same shutoff recurs within six months after a notice, you may end the tenancy on at least three days' written notice.
- Rent: the tenant has seven days to pay in full.
- Deliberate damage over $400 and the listed illegal activities have no cure: the notice ends the tenancy not less than 24 hours or more than five days after service.

If you serve the notice by registered or certified mail (the only mail method allowed for a notice to quit), add three days to the period.

The notice must state the breach, what the tenant must do to fix it, and the date and time to fix it and to move out.

title: No Alaska Disaster Tenancy Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule that a declared disaster ends a tenancy or suspends rent, and set no landlord cleanup, testing or notice duties after a disaster. The ordinary rules apply. If fire or another casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may vacate and end the lease as of the date of vacating, or, where continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost fair rental value; rent is accounted for as of the date of the casualty. Your duty to make repairs and keep the premises fit and habitable continues, and your heat and water duties apply insofar as energy conditions permit. State disaster programs may place victims in temporary housing; those arrangements do not change your lease. Municipal emergency orders may add rules.

title: Alaska Drug-Free Addendum Note
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring, permitting or regulating a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum. The tenant's core duty is already statutory: a tenant may not knowingly engage in, or knowingly permit others in the premises to engage in, illegal activity involving controlled substances or imitation controlled substances at the premises, and that breach allows a notice to quit ending the tenancy 24 hours to five days after service, with no right to cure. The library's optional Alaska illegal-activity clause covers it. A broader addendum, for example one reaching drug activity away from the premises or by guests without the tenant's knowledge, is an ordinary lease term: you could enforce it only as a material breach, on at least 10 days' notice with a chance to cure where the breach is remediable, not on the 24-hour-to-five-day track; where the tenant has used or allowed the unit to be used for an illegal purpose, the separate five-day illegal-use track may also apply (get advice). You may prohibit marijuana possession, use and growing on your property. Federally assisted housing has its own federal addendum rules.

title: No Alaska DV Eviction Protection
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule barring you from evicting, refusing to renew, or penalizing a tenant because the tenant or a household member is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, or because of calls for police help. Related rules matter. A city may charge an owner a fee for excessive police responses, but never for calls involving potential domestic violence, child neglect or stalking, so those calls cannot breach the tenant's duty not to cause such fees. A court's protective order may remove and exclude the abuser from the victim's residence regardless of ownership. Alaska's fair housing law forbids sex discrimination in the terms of a rental, and federal law protects tenants in federally assisted housing. The cautious course is to treat violence against a tenant as the abuser's conduct, not the victim's breach, and to act against the abuser where the lease and the eviction rules allow.

title: No Alaska DV Lease Termination
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations give a tenant who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking no right to end a lease early, and say nothing about whether one tenant's departure ends the lease for the other tenants. Ordinary rules apply. A tenant who leaves before the term ends remains liable for rent, but you must mitigate: if the unit is abandoned you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent it at a fair rental value. A court's protective order may exclude the abuser from the home regardless of whose name is on the lease. Because there is no statutory release, the cautious course when a tenant must leave for safety is a written early-termination agreement that releases the departing tenant and says what happens to the deposit and any remaining co-tenants. Federally assisted housing has its own federal rules.

title: No Alaska DV Document Rule
bodyText: Because Alaska has no domestic violence tenancy statute, it has no list of documents a tenant must give you to prove victim status, and no rule on keeping such documents confidential. The document you are most likely to see is a court protective order, which may exclude the abuser from the victim's home regardless of who owns or leases it and is entered in a statewide registry for law enforcement. If a tenant asks you to keep an abuser out, change locks, or agree to an early termination, it is reasonable to ask for a copy of the order, but you may also act on other reliable information. Keep anything you receive private, share it only as needed to act on the request, and store it separately from the lease file. Federally assisted housing has its own federal certification rules.

title: Alaska Early Termination Rules
bodyText:
Alaska has no statute on early-termination fees or lease-break options in residential leases: nothing caps a fee or requires a separate addendum.

An option the tenant may choose, such as notice plus a set buyout, is a lease term the parties may agree to; a charge imposed as a penalty for breach may be unenforceable under general contract law if it is not a reasonable estimate of your loss.

Without an agreed option, a tenant who leaves early stays liable for rent, subject to your duty to mitigate: if the unit is abandoned you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental value, and the lease ends when the new tenancy begins. A tenant who moves out with rent paid has not abandoned under Alaska's definition, which requires a rent default and seven days' absence without the required notice.

Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, you may apply the security deposit only to accrued rent and to damage from the tenant's breach of the statutory tenant duties, so do not withhold a buyout fee from the deposit unless the tenant agrees in writing at the time.

title: No Alaska Condemnation Lease Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on what happens to a residential lease or the rent when the property is taken by eminent domain, and none letting the court in the condemnation case cancel the lease. The taking itself, compensation, and whether a tenant's leasehold shares in the award are handled in the condemnation proceeding under separate statutes and case law, not reviewed here. Between you and the tenant, ordinary rules apply: rent is owed while the tenant has possession, and a periodic tenancy can be ended on the usual written notice. Many leases say the lease ends on a taking and the award belongs to the owner; Alaska law neither requires nor forbids that, and this library does not offer such a clause. If you receive notice of a taking, tell your tenants promptly and get advice on the award.

title: Alaska Entity Landlords in Court
bodyText: In Alaska a corporation must appear in court through an attorney unless a law explicitly makes an exception, so a corporate owner needs a lawyer to file and pursue an eviction. The court's eviction booklet says the same for a property manager or anyone acting for the owner under a power of attorney, because representing someone else in court is the practice of law; the complaint form lets a manager sue only with the owner's written authority and an attorney. The one statutory exception: a nonprofit housing corporation may designate an officer or employee who is not an attorney to bring and maintain an eviction for it, and that person is its sole representative in the case. An individual owner may represent himself or herself. The statute does not say whether a limited liability company counts as a corporation for this rule; the cautious course is to use an attorney. Plan for this before serving a notice to quit, because the hearing comes quickly.

title: No Alaska Environmental-Event Termination
bodyText: Alaska gives neither you nor the tenant a statutory right to end a lease because of a sudden environmental or public health event, or a government order that makes occupancy impossible or unlawful, so there is no opt-in landlord right to preserve in the lease. Related rules decide most cases. If fire or another casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may vacate and end the lease. A tenant may end the lease for your material breach, or a habitability breach materially affecting health and safety, if you do not fix it within 10 days of written notice. A court nuisance-abatement order ends the lease. You may end a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' written notice. If you must take the unit out of residential use for at least six months, see the optional Alaska owner-recovery clause, which uses that statutory ground with at least 30 days' notice.

title: No Alaska Eviction Hardship Stay
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and court rules contain no hardship stay of an eviction: nothing lets a judge delay the move-out because the tenant cannot find housing, is ill, or has children in school. The process is fast. The eviction hearing is set no more than 15 days after you file, and a continuance needs good cause; one longer than two days requires the tenant to post an undertaking with sureties for the rent that may accrue. The judge sets the move-out date and time in the judgment for possession. A tenant who appeals may ask the court to stay the eviction until the appeal is decided, and the court may require a bond. The court's free Eviction Diversion Program offers mediation before or after you file, which can produce an agreed move-out date or payment plan; an agreement you choose to make is often faster than contested litigation.

title: Alaska Eviction Process
bodyText: An Alaska eviction follows set steps. Serve a written notice to quit stating the breach, any cure and its deadline, and the date and time the tenancy ends, by hand delivery, by leaving it at the premises if the tenant is absent, or by registered or certified mail (mailing adds three days). If the tenant neither cures nor leaves, file in the district court where the property is located (rent and damage claims up to $100,000), using the complaint form with the notice attached, the federal 30-day-notice affidavit, and the court's confidential tenant contact sheet. Name everyone on the lease and all other adults in the home. A process server or peace officer serves the summons at least two days before the hearing, which is set within 15 days of filing. At the hearing the judge decides only possession and sets a move-out date; a writ of assistance lets a peace officer remove anyone who stays. The tenant has 20 days to answer money claims, then trial or default follows. A case with nothing scheduled may be dismissed after 180 days. A tenant sued for nonpayment may counterclaim, and the court may order rent paid into court.

title: No Alaska Eviction Record Sealing
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and court rules contain no eviction-specific procedure to seal, expunge or remove eviction case records, and no automatic removal of dismissed cases or old judgments. The general court-records rules still apply: on request of an affected person, a judge may seal or make confidential a case file or parts of it while the case is open or within 90 days after it closes, if the public interest in disclosure is outweighed by a legitimate interest in confidentiality, and a presiding judge may keep a party's name off the public index in narrow circumstances. The only confidential eviction filing is the information sheet giving the tenants' phone, email and other contact details, which the court keeps confidential and uses to offer its Eviction Diversion Program. The court's default form even tells landlords to search the court's online case index for a defendant's other cases. Criminal-record sealing rules apply to criminal justice information, not to civil eviction cases. Because eviction filings stay visible, consider the free mediation program or a negotiated move-out before filing when a tenant would cooperate. When you screen applicants, tenant screening reports are governed by the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, and you should treat a dismissed case differently from a judgment against the tenant.

title: No Alaska Tenant Service Agent Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no rule letting a lease name a person to accept a tenant's eviction papers, and this library offers no such clause. Eviction papers are served under Civil Rule 85 and the general service rule: a process server or peace officer delivers the summons and complaint to each defendant personally, leaves them at the defendant's home with a resident of suitable age and discretion, or delivers them to an agent authorized by appointment or by law to receive service, at least two days before the hearing. Whether a lease clause counts as such an appointment is not settled. The court's booklet tells you to name everyone on the lease and all other adults living in the home, and to serve each one. Later papers may not be mailed to the address the tenant was evicted from unless the tenant's current address and whereabouts are not readily ascertainable. You must disclose to the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the person authorized to receive notices and process for you; the lease is the usual place.

title: Alaska Fast-Track Eviction
bodyText:
For two kinds of breach Alaska allows a fast eviction with no right to cure: the tenant, or someone in the tenant's control, deliberately damages the premises by more than $400, or the tenant engages in or knowingly permits prostitution or another listed illegal activity at the premises.

Serve a written notice to quit that describes the act and sets a termination date at least 24 hours and no more than five days after service; the court's forms CIV-728 (damage) and CIV-729 (illegal activity) follow this.

For illegal activity the eviction statute treats the tenant as unlawfully holding only after five days, so set a five-day date. Add three days if you mail the notice. Serve by handing it to the tenant, leaving it at the premises if the tenant is absent, or registered or certified mail.

If the tenant stays, file an ordinary eviction case; there is no separate expedited court track, but the hearing is set within 15 days of filing.

title: No Alaska Just-Cause Rule
bodyText:
Alaska has no general just-cause eviction rule. You may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before the rental due date named in the notice, or a week-to-week tenancy by written notice at least 14 days before the termination date while rent is current, without giving a reason, and a fixed-term lease ends when its term expires.

Limits remain. You may not end a tenancy, or threaten to, in retaliation for a complaint or the exercise of the tenant's rights unless a statutory exception applies; you may not discriminate on grounds Alaska's fair housing law protects; a condominium conversion needs 180 days' notice; and mobile home park tenants, outside this library, can be evicted only for listed causes.

Even after a tenancy ends, serve a notice to quit before filing.

During a fixed term you need a statutory ground: nonpayment, material breach, deliberate damage, illegal activity, a utility shutoff, or, if the lease gives you that right, one of the good-faith owner grounds on at least 30 days' notice; whether those owner grounds end a fixed term when the lease is silent is unsettled.

title: Alaska Foreclosure and Tenants
bodyText: Alaska's foreclosure statutes give residential tenants little protection of their own. In a nonjudicial trustee's sale, the trustee must mail the notice of default within 10 days after recording it to, among others, anyone actually in physical possession of the property, so tenants usually learn of the foreclosure. After the trustee's deed, the buyer is entitled to possession against the borrower and anyone claiming through the borrower after the deed of trust was recorded, which can include a tenant whose lease came later; a recorded lease shares in surplus sale proceeds only as a subordinate interest. A lender may not take possession on the strength of the mortgage alone, without foreclosure and sale. Alaska has no rule of its own requiring notice to tenants of the sale date, keeping leases in force, or delaying the new owner's eviction. If your rental is in default, tell your tenants promptly.

title: Alaska Pre-Judgment Redemption
bodyText: An older Alaska statute outside the landlord-tenant act says that, unless the lease provides otherwise, a landlord may re-enter when rent is unpaid and sue for possession, and that a tenant who pays the rent in arrears with interest and the costs of the action, and performs the other covenants, at any time before judgment may continue in possession. Whether that statute applies to residential tenancies governed by the landlord-tenant act is unsettled. The act's own rule is stricter for tenants: if rent is not paid in full within seven days after your written notice, the tenancy terminates unless you agree to let the tenant stay, and the general recovery statute sends recovery from a tenant to the eviction statutes. Cautious course: if a tenant tenders all arrears, interest and court costs before judgment, get advice before refusing it. The older statute lets a lease opt out, but this library does not offer that clause, because the statute's reach is uncertain and the clause would mainly add a dispute.

title: No Alaska Lease Guarantor Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on lease guarantors or cosigners: nothing limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a stated maximum amount or end date, or says whether a guaranty covers renewals. General contract and guaranty law decides these questions. Two statutes matter. A promise to answer for another person's debt is unenforceable unless it is in writing and signed by the guarantor. And the deposit cap bars you from demanding or receiving prepaid rent or a security deposit, however named, above two months' rent (for units renting at $2,000 a month or less); because it does not say only from the tenant, count any deposit taken from a guarantor toward the cap. Use a separate written guaranty, signed by the guarantor, that states whether it covers renewals, extensions and any month-to-month continuation, and any maximum amount.

title: Alaska Holdover Rules
bodyText:
If a tenant stays without your consent after the lease term expires, or after a periodic tenancy ends on proper notice, you must still serve a notice to quit before suing for possession; then you may bring an eviction case.

If the holdover is wilful and not in good faith, you may also recover up to one and one-half times your actual damages, such as the rental value of the holdover period.

If you consent to the tenant staying, for example by accepting rent for a new period, the general lease rules apply: without a new definite term the tenancy becomes month to month (week to week if rent is paid weekly) on the existing terms, and you would end it with the periodic notice.

Alaska has no separate double-rent holdover statute. Decide quickly whether you want the tenant to stay, and do not accept rent for a period after the end date unless you do.

title: Alaska Holdover Rate Not Offered
bodyText: Alaska has no statute authorizing or capping a lease-set holdover rate, such as a premium daily rent for each day a tenant stays past the end of the term. The landlord-tenant act already sets the measure for an unconsented holdover: you may sue for possession after a notice to quit and, if the holdover is wilful and not in good faith, recover up to one and one-half times your actual damages. A fixed premium rate is lawful only to the extent general contract law allows agreed damages. It could be attacked as a penalty or as a way around the statutory measure, and collecting it as rent could be treated as consent to a new month-to-month tenancy. For those reasons this library does not offer a holdover-rate clause for Alaska. The Alaska lease instead recovers your actual damages, including the reasonable rental value, for any holdover period.

title: Alaska Exemption Waivers Void
bodyText: A lease cannot effectively waive a tenant's Alaska exemptions from collection. A waiver of exemption given to an unsecured creditor before a levy is unenforceable, and a landlord collecting rent or damages is ordinarily an unsecured creditor; a valid security interest may still be given in exempt property, but a landlord's lien or security interest in the tenant's household goods is unenforceable. The exemptions include a homestead exemption of up to $54,000 in the principal residence, plus other property exemptions in the exemptions chapter, which the tenant claims when you try to collect a judgment. One rule helps you: a judgment for unpaid rent or damage owed by a former tenant is not limited by the usual 20% exemption of the permanent fund dividend, so you may levy on the dividend to collect it. Leave exemption-waiver language out of the lease; it adds nothing you can enforce.

title: No Alaska Medical Termination Right
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations give a tenant no right to end a lease early because of age, illness, disability, or a move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility, and give a tenant's representative no such right either. Ordinary rules apply. A tenant who must leave stays liable for rent, but you must mitigate: if the unit is left, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at a fair rental value, and the lease ends when a new tenancy begins. Alaska's fair housing law bars disability discrimination in rentals, and a request to end a lease or transfer units because of a disability may raise a reasonable-accommodation question under federal law. The long-term care ombudsman may take older Alaskans' complaints about landlords. A written early-termination agreement, with a short notice period, is often the practical answer.

title: No Alaska Landlord Lien
bodyText: Alaska abolished a residential landlord's remedies against the tenant's belongings. A lien or security interest for you in the tenant's household goods is unenforceable unless it was perfected before March 19, 1974, and distraint, seizing goods for unpaid rent, is abolished. The commercial-code rules on security interests do not apply to a landlord's lien. So a lease may not give you a lien on the tenant's property or a right to hold or sell it for unpaid rent, and a waiver of the tenant's collection exemptions in the lease is unenforceable. To collect, sue for rent and damages and enforce the judgment through the court; a judgment for unpaid rent or damage against a former tenant can be collected from the tenant's permanent fund dividend without the usual exemption. Property left after the tenancy ends follows the abandoned-property procedure: if the tenant reclaims it you may recover the storage cost, but the statute does not let you keep it until rent is paid.

title: Alaska Landlord Remedies After Termination
bodyText: When the rental agreement ends, you may claim possession and rent, and separately your actual damages for the tenant's breach. Apart from termination, you may recover actual damages and get an injunction for any breach of the lease or the statutory tenant duties. You must mitigate your damages. In the eviction case the judge decides only possession at the first hearing. Rent and damage claims come later: the tenant has 20 days after service to answer, then the claims go to trial or you apply for a default judgment with itemized proof, crediting payments and any deposit you kept. The court's booklet says late fees are usually not allowed after the tenant has left and that prejudgment interest is generally not awarded on rent if late fees were charged. A judgment for unpaid rent or damage against a former tenant can be collected from the tenant's permanent fund dividend without the usual 20% exemption.

title: No Alaska Self-Cure as Rent
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant act has no provision letting you fix a tenant's breach yourself and bill the cost as rent. Your remedies for a tenant's breach are actual damages, an injunction, and termination on the statutory notice tracks. You may enter to make necessary repairs, on at least 24 hours' notice and with the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold; in an emergency you may enter without consent. You can then claim the reasonable cost as damages. That cost is not rent, which Alaska defines as the uniform periodic payment due you, so its nonpayment cannot support a seven-day nonpayment eviction even if the lease calls it additional rent. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, you may deduct it from the deposit only as damage caused by the tenant's breach of the statutory tenant duties, not for normal wear and tear. Itemize and bill it promptly.

title: No Alaska Liquidated Damages Rule
bodyText:
Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on liquidated or agreed damages in residential leases: nothing authorizes or caps a fixed amount owed for a tenant's breach. General contract law decides whether a fixed charge is a reasonable estimate of loss or an unenforceable penalty.

The landlord-tenant act leans toward actual loss. Your remedies are actual damages and an injunction; the statutory multipliers, such as up to one and one-half times actual damages for a wilful bad-faith holdover, are tied to actual damages; where the deposit statute applies (rent of $2,000 a month or less), the deposit can be kept only for accrued rent and damage from the tenant's breach of statutory duties; and a lease may not limit either side's legal liability.

This library therefore avoids fixed damage amounts in Alaska leases. An early-termination option the tenant chooses is a different question; see the Alaska early-termination row.

title: No Alaska Rent Lockout
bodyText: You may not lock out a tenant who is behind on rent, even if the lease says you may; Alaska has no opt-in lockout procedure. A landlord may not take possession by action or otherwise, including by wilfully cutting off utilities or other essential services, except after abandonment or surrender, in circumstances beyond your control due to energy conditions, or as the landlord-tenant act permits, which for unpaid rent means the seven-day notice and a court eviction. A lease term allowing a lockout waives the tenant's rights and is unenforceable. A tenant who is locked out may recover possession or end the lease and recover up to one and one-half times actual damages. See the Alaska self-help eviction row.

title: No Alaska Minor Defendant Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no rule barring you from naming a minor as an eviction defendant, and no penalty for doing so. The court's booklet tells you to name everyone listed on the lease and all other adults living in the home, which leaves minor children off the complaint, and the writ of assistance removes all persons holding the premises, so children living with an evicted tenant need not be named. If a minor is a party, for example a minor who signed the lease, special rules apply: the summons must be delivered to the minor and also to a parent or guardian, and you cannot use the court's standard default form against a defendant under 18; get legal advice. A lease signed by a minor also raises contract-capacity questions under general law. The practical rule is to name every adult occupant and leave children off.

title: Alaska Nonpayment Notice
bodyText:
To evict for unpaid rent, give the tenant written notice of the nonpayment and that the rental agreement will terminate if the rent is not paid within seven days. If the tenant does not pay in full within seven days, the tenancy ends unless you agree to let the tenant stay.

This notice is your notice to quit. State the rent owed, the date and time to pay, the date and time the tenancy ends, a direction to move out by then, and that you may sue for possession.

Day one is the day after delivery; count weekends and holidays. Serve it by handing it to the tenant, leaving it at the premises if the tenant is absent, or registered or certified mail; mailing adds three days, so give ten.

One notice is enough for any one default. Demand only rent: late fees, interest and other charges are not rent, and the court's form warns that a tenant can't be evicted for nonpayment of late fees.

The court's notice form CIV-725 is a safe template. A lease cannot waive or shorten this notice, and the lease itself cannot serve as the notice.

title: Alaska Notice Fees Not Offered
bodyText: Alaska has no statute allowing, capping or banning a fee for preparing or serving a notice to quit, and this library offers no notice-service-fee clause for Alaska. Such a fee is not rent, which Alaska defines as the uniform periodic payment due you, so it cannot be included in the amount demanded in a seven-day nonpayment notice or support a nonpayment eviction. A fee framed to cover a lawyer's work on the notice would also run into the ban on lease promises to pay your attorney fees, and a flat fee could be attacked as a penalty. What you can recover is your court costs if you win the eviction case, such as the filing fee and the process server's fee, within the limits set by court rule, plus attorney fees under the prevailing-party rule. Keep receipts for service costs.

title: No Alaska Notice-to-Quit Waiver
bodyText: Your lease may not waive or shorten the notice to quit Alaska requires before you sue for possession. Except for the nonpayment notice, which itself serves as the notice to quit, and a court nuisance-abatement order, you may not start an eviction case without first serving a notice to quit. Each period is a statutory minimum: seven days to pay rent, at least 10 days for a curable breach, at least 30 days before the rental due date to end a month-to-month tenancy, and so on. A lease term giving up or shortening those notices waives the tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant act and is unenforceable, and wilfully using a lease you know contains such a term lets the tenant recover actual damages. You may agree to give longer notice than the law requires. An eviction filed on a short or missing notice will be dismissed or delayed, so check every date before serving.

title: Alaska Nuisance Abatement
bodyText: Alaska's nuisance-abatement law reaches rental property used for prostitution, illegal gambling, controlled or imitation controlled substances, or illegal alcohol delivery in a dry area. Anyone who maintains, uses, owns or leases a place used for those activities is guilty of maintaining a nuisance. The attorney general must, and a citizen or a home rule municipality may, sue to enjoin the nuisance, the person maintaining it, and the owner, lessee or agent of the building. If the court finds a nuisance, its abatement order must end the lease (if the tenant had notice of the case), remove and sell the fixtures and contents used in the nuisance, and close the building to all use for a year unless released sooner. The order terminates the rental agreement, and an occupant who stays can be evicted without a notice to quit. An owner not in contempt can get the premises released by paying costs and posting a bond to keep the nuisance from recurring for a year. Contempt fines become a lien on the property. Acting promptly on illegal activity protects you.

title: No Alaska Possession Bond
bodyText: Alaska has no statutory bond by which a tenant promises to deliver possession at the end of the term, enforced by a confessed judgment, and a rental agreement may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement, so that device is unavailable. The bonds Alaska's eviction law knows run the other way. A tenant who wants the eviction hearing continued for more than two days must give an undertaking with court-approved sureties for the rent that may accrue, and a tenant who appeals may be required to post a bond to stay in the property while the appeal is pending. To recover possession at the end of a term, serve a notice to quit and file an eviction if the tenant stays; a wilful, bad-faith holdover adds up to one and one-half times your actual damages.

title: Alaska Property After Eviction
bodyText: After a judgment for possession, if the occupants do not leave by the court's deadline, a peace officer acting under a writ of assistance removes them and their possessions; law enforcement may charge a fee. The writ makes you, the plaintiff, responsible for the return, storage or disposal of any personal property left on the premises after the removal, in accordance with applicable law, and it cites Alaska's abandoned-property statute. The cautious course is to follow that statute: give written notice to remove the property by a date at least 15 days after delivery or mailing, store it with reasonable care, and sell or dispose of it only as that procedure allows. Alaska law sets no separate inventory duty, no special rule for pets left behind, and no statutory immunity for you when the writ is executed. A person who stays or returns after removal without your consent may be committing criminal trespass.

title: Alaska Paying to Stop Eviction
bodyText: Alaska's right to save a tenancy by paying is short. After your written nonpayment notice, the tenant may stop the eviction by paying the rent in full within seven days (ten if you served the notice by registered or certified mail, the only mail service a notice to quit allows). If the tenant does not, the tenancy terminates unless you agree to let the tenant stay. Late fees and interest are not part of the amount the tenant must pay. You may accept a partial payment after giving the notice and extend the eviction date accordingly, but accepting rent knowing of a default can waive your right to end the lease for that breach unless you agree otherwise after the breach, and the court's booklet tells tenants an accepted partial payment waives termination for that nonpayment. If you take a partial payment, sign a written agreement with the tenant at that time that states the new deadline and preserves your notice. An older statute may also let a tenant who pays all arrears, interest and costs before judgment stay; its reach is unsettled.

title: Alaska Counterclaims and Rent into Court
bodyText: When you sue for possession for nonpayment, or for rent while the tenant still lives there, the tenant may counterclaim for any amount recoverable under the lease or the landlord-tenant act. If the court finds the defense supported by the evidence, it may reduce the rent to reflect the lost value while you were out of compliance, continue the case for a reasonable time so you can fix the violation, order the tenant to pay into court all or part of the rent accrued and accruing, or order the tenant to vacate during repairs that cannot be made otherwise, with reinstatement afterward. If rent is paid into court and the violations are not cured within six months, the court enters judgment for the tenant and refunds the money or uses it to make the dwelling fit. If they are cured, the court decides what each side owes, and if no rent remains due the tenant wins on possession. Paying rent into court is a court option, not a condition of the tenant's defenses, and a tenant who has moved out may counterclaim without paying into court.

title: Alaska Application Misstatements
bodyText:
The library's rental-application clause lets you treat a materially false application as a material lease breach.

In Alaska that breach follows the ordinary track: a written notice to quit giving at least 10 days (three more if you serve it by registered or certified mail, the only mail method allowed), and the lease continues if the breach can be remedied and the tenant remedies it, so record why a particular misstatement cannot be cured.

Alaska has no statute letting either side void a lease for fraud; general contract law applies.

Two Alaska rules limit what can count as false. You may not ask about or record an applicant's sex, marital status, changes in marital status, race, religion, physical or mental disability, color or national origin, so an answer you were not allowed to ask for cannot be a breach. And a person whose criminal record was sealed by the agency because it resulted from mistaken identity or false accusation may deny the record and the arrest, charge or conviction it shows, so a 'no' answer about that record is not a misrepresentation.

title: No Alaska Repair-Cost Termination
bodyText: Alaska gives neither you nor the tenant a right to end the lease because repairs would cost too much compared with the rent. Your duty to make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable does not end because a repair is expensive, and no lease, assignment or financing document may let anyone collect rent free of that duty. If a needed repair is not made, the tenant has remedies: written notice ending the lease if a breach materially affecting health and safety is not fixed in 10 days, damages, essential-services remedies, and rent reduction in a court case. Your lawful exits are the ordinary ones: end a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' written notice, or, if you in good faith will substantially alter or demolish the building or take the unit out of residential use for at least six months, use the optional Alaska owner-recovery clause with at least 30 days' notice.

title: Alaska Retaliation Rules
bodyText: You may not retaliate by raising rent, cutting services, or bringing or threatening an eviction because the tenant complained to you of a habitability violation, tried to enforce rights under the landlord-tenant act, organized or joined a tenants' union, or complained to a government agency that enforces housing, wage, price or rent controls. A tenant who proves retaliation may recover possession or end the lease, recover up to one and one-half times actual damages, and defend an eviction. After a proper notice to quit you may still seek possession if the tenant is behind in rent; code compliance requires work that would deprive the tenant of the unit; the tenant is committing waste or a nuisance or using the unit illegally; you in good faith want it for personal use, major remodeling or demolition, or to end residential use for six months; or a good-faith buyer represents one of those purposes (for the code, personal-use, remodeling, end-of-residential-use and sale grounds the tenant does not unlawfully hold until at least 30 days after the notice to quit, or any longer period the lease sets). A rent increase is allowed if tied to substantial tax or cost increases incurred at least four months earlier, a capital improvement, or comparable rents. There is no presumption period; document your reasons.

title: No Alaska Seasonal Tenancy Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no special rules for seasonal or vacation rentals. The landlord-tenant act excludes transient occupancy in a hotel, motel, lodging or other transient facility, unless the arrangement was created to avoid the act, and excludes an employee whose right to occupy depends on working substantially on services, maintenance or repair of the premises. Any other seasonal rental of a home, residence or sleeping place is governed by the act like any other tenancy: habitability, entry and eviction rules all apply, and the deposit rules apply where rent is $2,000 a month or less. A fixed seasonal term ends on its end date, but if the tenant stays you must serve a notice to quit before filing an eviction; a seasonal rental without a definite term is week to week or month to month. Seasonal worker housing for employees whose jobs are not maintaining the premises is not excluded by the employee rule. Municipal short-term rental ordinances may add requirements.

title: Alaska Self-Help Eviction Ban
bodyText: Alaska bans self-help eviction. You may not take possession of a rental unit by action or otherwise, including by wilfully cutting off electricity, gas, water, sanitary or other essential services, except after abandonment or surrender, in circumstances beyond your control due to energy conditions, or as the landlord-tenant act permits through a notice to quit and a court eviction. No one may enter land or a dwelling by force; even a lawful entry must be peaceable. If you unlawfully remove or exclude a tenant, for example by changing the locks or removing belongings, or wilfully interrupt essential services, the tenant may recover possession or end the lease, and either way recover up to one and one-half times actual damages, plus return of recoverable prepaid rent and deposit if the lease ends. The tenant may also get an injunction, and prevailing-party attorney fees apply. A lease term permitting lockouts or shutoffs is unenforceable. After judgment, only a peace officer acting under a writ of assistance removes the occupants.

title: Alaska Servicemember Protections
bodyText: Alaska extends the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act's provisions on consumer transactions and the temporary suspension of civil liabilities to members of the state's organized militia, such as the Alaska National Guard, while on active duty for the state by the governor's order. Treat federal lease-termination and eviction-stay protections as possibly reaching Guard members on state orders, not only those on federal duty; how far the state extension reaches is not settled. Alaska's own relocation-orders termination right covers internet, gym, satellite radio and television contracts, not leases, so lease rights come from federal law. In an eviction, the court's default form requires a sworn statement of each defendant's military status and suggests checking the Defense Department's SCRA website, and you cannot use the standard default form against a defendant in active military service; get legal advice before seeking a default against a servicemember.

title: No Alaska Late-Benefit Defense
bodyText: Alaska has no eviction defense, stay or continuance for a tenant whose Social Security, other public benefit, or housing voucher payment is late or interrupted. The seven-day nonpayment rule applies whatever the reason the rent is unpaid, and a continuance of the hearing needs good cause and, beyond two days, an undertaking for the rent that will accrue. You may choose to accept a partial payment after your notice and extend the eviction date, but accepting rent with knowledge of the default can waive your right to terminate for it; use a written agreement signed after the breach. If the tenant is in a federal program such as the Housing Choice Voucher program, or your loan is federally backed, federal rules may require longer notice before filing, and the court's affidavit form asks about it.

title: Alaska Tenant Termination Rights
bodyText: Alaska lets a tenant end a lease early, without your agreement, in these cases. For your material breach of the lease, or a habitability breach materially affecting health and safety, the tenant may give written notice ending the lease at least 20 days after you receive it unless you remedy within 10 days; if, in the absence of due care by you, substantially the same breach recurs within six months after that notice, the tenant may terminate on at least 10 days' written notice. The tenant may not terminate for a condition the tenant, family or guests caused. Other rights: on at least 10 days' written notice if you fail to deliver possession; by vacating after a fire or casualty that substantially impairs the unit; after an unlawful ouster or wilful utility interruption; on 10 days' notice after unlawful or harassing entry; and on 30 days' notice if you reject a proposed subtenant without a statutory ground. Alaska has no statute letting a tenant end a lease for your fraud or for an omitted lease statement; general contract law applies. Federal law gives servicemembers lease-termination rights.

title: Alaska Has No Tenancy at Will
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant act has no tenancy at will. Unless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, a residential tenancy is week to week if the tenant pays weekly rent and month to month in every other case. End a week-to-week tenancy by written notice at least 14 days before the termination date, while rent is current, and a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 30 days before the rental due date named in the notice; the same notices bind the tenant. The eviction statute mentions an estate at will only for property outside the act, such as commercial or agricultural property. Someone living in your residential unit with no valid rental agreement and without your consent is removed by a notice to quit and an eviction case, not as a tenant at will. If you let a person move in and accept rent, expect a periodic tenancy.

title: No Alaska Tenant Bankruptcy Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations have no rule of their own on what happens when a residential tenant files for bankruptcy: nothing says whether you may continue an eviction, collect past-due rent, or enforce a lease term that ends the lease because of the filing. Federal bankruptcy law decides those questions, including the automatic stay. One Alaska rule touches it: a new promise to pay a debt discharged in bankruptcy is enforceable only if it is in writing and signed. If a tenant tells you about a bankruptcy filing, pause collection calls, deposit deductions for pre-filing rent, and eviction steps, and get advice on federal law before going further. Keep collecting current rent only as that advice allows.

title: Alaska Tenant-Caused Damage
bodyText:
Alaska makes the tenant responsible for damage the tenant causes. A tenant may not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let anyone else do so, and must leave the unit at move-out in substantially the same condition except normal wear and tear, which never includes damage from negligence, accident or abuse by the tenant, household or guests.

You may recover actual damages and, where rent is $2,000 a month or less, deduct the damage from the deposit with an itemized notice under the deposit statute.

Deliberate damage over $400 by the tenant or someone in the tenant's control allows a no-cure notice ending the tenancy in 24 hours to five days.

Fault also limits tenant remedies: a tenant may not terminate for, or use the essential-services remedies for, a condition the tenant, family or guests caused.

The fire-and-casualty statute has no such exception: even after a fire the tenant caused, the tenant may vacate and end the lease or keep the usable part at reduced rent. Your remedy is damages; whether they include lost rent is a question for case law.

title: No Alaska Tenant Death Rule
bodyText:
Alaska's landlord-tenant act says nothing about a tenant's death: the lease does not end automatically, and there is no special reentry, property-release or contact-person procedure.

General rules apply. Deal with the tenant's personal representative or heirs about rent, belongings and the deposit; probate law decides who has authority.

A periodic tenancy can be ended by the usual written notice, at least 30 days before a rental due date for month to month or 14 days for week to week.

Do not take back the unit or remove belongings on your own unless the unit has been surrendered or abandoned; abandonment requires belongings left, seven days' absence without the absence notice, and a rent default, and property left after the tenancy ends follows the 15-day abandoned-property procedure.

Naming an emergency contact in the lease is lawful and useful, but the contact gets no authority over the tenant's property from the lease alone. Co-tenants who remain keep their tenancy.

title: Alaska Periodic Termination Notice
bodyText: To end a periodic tenancy in Alaska, give written notice: for week to week, at least 14 days before the termination date, available while rent is current; for month to month, at least 30 days before the rental due date named in the notice, so the end date must fall on a rent due date. The same notices bind the tenant, and you need no reason, subject to the retaliation and fair housing rules. A fixed term ends at its expiration without a termination notice, but if the tenant stays you must serve a notice to quit before filing an eviction. A lease cannot shorten these periods; it may lengthen them. If you mail a notice, add three days to be safe. If the tenant has paid rent in advance, you cannot sue for possession until that prepaid period runs. Longer notice applies in some cases: 180 days before a condominium conversion, and 30 days for properties with federally backed loans or in covered federal housing programs.

title: Alaska Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: A person whose use of the unit rests only on a tenant's rights, such as a guest or someone the tenant let in, gains no rights under the landlord-tenant act just by being there. To remove someone in possession without a valid rental agreement and without your consent, serve a written notice to quit; if the person stays, the person is unlawfully holding and you can file an eviction case against anyone wrongfully in possession. Alaska has no separate procedure for police or a sheriff to remove squatters on your affidavit outside court. Criminal trespass covers a person who enters or remains unlawfully in a dwelling or premises not open to the public without privilege, but whether officers will act when the occupant claims a right to be there is a local practice question. Do not remove anyone yourself by force or lockout: if the person turns out to be a tenant, the self-help ban applies, and any entry must be peaceable. Be careful before accepting money from an occupant, which can create a tenancy.

title: Alaska Waiver by Accepting Rent
