bodyText: Accepting rent while you know the tenant is in default, or accepting performance that differs from the lease or later-adopted rules, waives your right to terminate the rental agreement for that breach, unless you and the tenant agree otherwise after the breach has occurred. A lease clause written in advance saying acceptance is never a waiver does not meet that test, because the agreement must come after the breach. The nonpayment statute separately lets a landlord who has served the seven-day notice accept a partial payment and extend the eviction date. How that permission fits with the waiver rule is unsettled, and the court's booklet tells tenants that an accepted partial payment after a notice to quit waives termination for that nonpayment. Cautious course: once you have served a notice, either decline payment or accept it only under a written agreement signed after the breach that states the new deadline and that your right to terminate is preserved. The waiver covers only that breach, not a later one.

title: No Agreed Actual-Notice Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no landlord-tenant rule requiring "actual notice" and no provision letting you and the tenant agree on an extra method, such as a text message, that counts as a statutory notice. Alaska instead fixes how key notices are given. A notice to quit must be in writing and served by handing it to the tenant, leaving it at the premises if the tenant is absent, or sending it by registered or certified mail; mailing adds three days to the tenant's deadline. Your notice of intent to enter must come at least 24 hours ahead but has no set form. A lease may add texts or e-mail for routine messages if both of you agree to deal electronically, but an added method never replaces a method the law prescribes.

title: Foreclosure Disclosure Not Required
bodyText:
Alaska's statutes and regulations do not require you to tell tenants or applicants that the property is in foreclosure, a tax proceeding or another claim against your title.

Tenants hear about a nonjudicial foreclosure another way: within 10 days after recording the notice of default, the trustee must mail a copy by certified mail, or deliver it personally, to any person actually in physical possession of the property, which includes your tenants. Federal law separately protects tenants after a foreclosure sale.

Telling tenants and applicants about a pending foreclosure is still good practice. Alaska law also does not require a tenant to pass on court papers or notices about the property; ask for that in the lease if you want it.

title: No Automatic Renewal Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no statute governing automatic renewal clauses in residential leases: no bold-type rule, no opt-in requirement and no reminder notice before renewal. The automatic-renewal rules found in Alaska law cover other contracts, such as rental-purchase agreements for household goods and royalty contracts. If your lease has no renewal clause and the tenant stays on after the term with your consent, the tenancy becomes month to month (week to week if rent is paid weekly), and either of you can end it with the ordinary written notice: at least 30 days before a rent due date for month to month, 14 days for week to week. If you do use a renewal clause, state the renewal term, the opt-out deadline and any rent change plainly, and remind the tenant before the deadline.

title: Other Rules Alaska Does Not Have
bodyText: Some rules found in other states are missing, or narrower, in Alaska. (1) No statute gives you a special right to end a lease because the rental application was false. Make accuracy of the application a lease term, so a material falsehood is a breach you handle with the 10-day notice to cure or quit. (2) Alaska has a narrow detector shield, not an insurance one: if you did not know and had not been told that a smoke or carbon monoxide detector needed repair or replacement, your failure to repair or replace it may not be considered evidence of negligence in a later lawsuit for death, property loss or injury. No statute limits what an insurer may do. (3) Double-letting and payment-method fees have no special Alaska statute either; see those topics.

title: Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: Alaska's statutes, regulations, court rules and 2025-2026 session laws were searched, not only the landlord-tenant act, for three things landlords ask about. (1) There is no squatter-specific removal procedure. A person who stays in possession without a valid rental agreement and without your consent is removed by serving a notice to quit and filing an eviction case; criminal trespass law also reaches someone who enters or remains unlawfully in a dwelling, but the police decide whether it applies. Never use self-help. (2) There is no duty to give a receipt for rent, even rent paid in cash; give one anyway. (3) There is no statewide landlord registration or rental license, so registration is not a condition of winning possession for an individual owner. An out-of-state entity is different: a foreign limited liability company must register with the state before conducting affairs here and may not maintain an eviction or other court action until it has registered, and a foreign corporation transacting business here without a certificate of authority may not maintain an action until it obtains one; the lease stays valid either way (AS 10.50.605, 10.50.675, 10.06.705, 10.06.713 and 10.06.715). Those statutes do not say whether renting out property is conducting affairs or transacting business, so register before you file. Check local rules.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Alaska has not moved its protective-order laws. Domestic violence protective orders are in AS 18.66.100 - 18.66.180, and stalking and sexual assault protective orders are in AS 18.65.850 - 18.65.870; 2026 legislation still cites both ranges. The older domestic violence injunction sections in AS 25.35 were repealed and point to AS 18.66, and a trespass definition still mentions orders issued under that former chapter. A domestic violence protective order may remove and exclude the abuser from the victim's residence regardless of who owns it, and may give the victim possession of essential personal items, including a pet. If a tenant shows you such an order, follow it. Alaska's landlord-tenant act itself cites no protective-order statute.

title: Electronic Leases, Signatures and Notices
bodyText:
Alaska's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets you sign and keep the lease electronically, but only with a tenant who has agreed to do business electronically; the circumstances can show agreement, and the lease's electronic-signature clause helps.

A tenant who agreed may still refuse to do later transactions electronically, and the lease cannot waive that right. An electronic record satisfies a writing requirement only if the tenant can print or store it; if you block printing or saving, the record cannot be enforced against the tenant.

The Act does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a tenant's primary residence, to the extent federal law excludes them, and where another law prescribes how a notice is sent, that method still governs. Serve notices to quit on paper as the eviction statute requires.

title: No Emergency Contact Law
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour contact or telephone number. What you must give, in writing at or before the start of the tenancy, is the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or agent authorized to receive notices and legal papers, and you must keep that information current. Give an emergency number anyway. Tenants need to reach you about heat, water and other essential services, and if a tenant cannot reach you after reasonable effort in an emergency, the tenant may change the locks without your written agreement and need only give you keys and written notice within five days.

title: No Energy Data Release Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations have no building energy-benchmarking program and no provision letting a lease clause authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you. The energy-use reporting rules found in Alaska law apply to state energy grant and audit programs, not to rentals. If you need a tenant's usage data, for example for an efficiency program or a lender, ask the tenant for a separate written authorization that names the utility, the account and the data, and ask the utility what form it accepts.

title: Changing the Lease After Signing
bodyText:
Alaska has no statute letting you amend an existing lease by notice to bring it into line with a new law, so a clause requiring changes to be in a signed writing gives up no statutory right; new laws apply on their own terms.

Three Alaska rules matter. First, the rental agreement includes all agreements, written or oral, so put side deals in writing or they may still bind you.

Second, it also includes valid rules you adopt; a rule adopted after the tenant signs binds the tenant only if you give reasonable notice of it and it does not substantially modify the lease.

Third, an unsigned lease can still take effect if you accept rent without reservation, or the tenant takes possession and pays rent without reservation, but for no more than one year.

title: Governing Law
bodyText:
Alaska's landlord-tenant act applies to every rental agreement for a dwelling unit in Alaska, wherever the agreement was made, and a lease may not waive the act's rights or remedies. A lease of an Alaska home should therefore name Alaska law, as the library's governing-law clause does; choosing another state's law would not displace the act.

Alaska has no statute on venue clauses in residential leases. The court's eviction booklet says an eviction case must be filed in the judicial district where the property is located, and in district court if past-due rent and property damage total $100,000 or less.

The clause's reference to local law covers any that apply.

title: Mediation and Arbitration
bodyText:
Alaska lets you and the tenant agree to mediate, or to submit to binding arbitration, disputes about either party's obligations under the rental agreement.

If you agree, the agreement's scope must be in the signed rental agreement, referred to in it, or attached to it; the library's optional mediation and arbitration clauses do this. Alaska's arbitration act makes an arbitration agreement in a record enforceable like any other contract.

No statute requires mediation or a pre-suit meeting before an eviction, and none says what an informal-resolution clause must leave out. Because a lease cannot waive the tenant's statutory rights or remedies, don't let a pre-suit step delay the statutory notices or possession cases, and don't add any promise that the tenant pays your attorney fees.

The court's Eviction Diversion Program offers free mediation before or after you file.

title: No State Landlord Registration
bodyText: Alaska has no statewide landlord registration or rental license, and no rule that an out-of-state owner must hire an Alaska broker. Two state rules still apply. First, collecting rent or managing property for someone else generally requires an Alaska real estate license; owners managing their own property, resident managers, individuals managing a total of four or fewer residential units for others, and individuals managing without a fee are exempt. Second, Alaska requires a business license to engage in a business; whether your rental activity needs one is not settled here, so check with the Department of Commerce, Community, and Economic Development. An out-of-state landlord may file a designation of an Alaska agent for service of process. An out-of-state limited liability company or corporation must also register with the state (a foreign LLC before conducting affairs here, a foreign corporation by obtaining a certificate of authority before transacting business) and may not maintain an eviction or other court action until it does (AS 10.50.605, 10.50.675, 10.06.705 and 10.06.713); see `edu-nonresident-landlord-agent-ak`. Cities and boroughs may have their own programs.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in or treating a blank as a breach. The only Alaska blank-space rule found is for retail installment contracts, where a seller may not get the buyer's signature on a contract with blanks in essential terms. Complete every blank before signing anyway, because the law fills gaps in ways you may not intend: with no agreed rent the tenant owes fair rental value, rent is payable at the unit unless you agree otherwise, and with no definite term the tenancy is month to month (week to week if rent is weekly). Strike through any blank that does not apply.

title: No Statutory Duty to Give a Lease Copy
bodyText: Alaska does not require you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and not doing so is not a defense the tenant can raise. Alaska deals instead with leases one side never signs or delivers. If you don't sign and deliver a lease the tenant signed and delivered to you, your accepting rent without reservation makes it binding as if you had signed. If the tenant doesn't sign and deliver one you signed and delivered, the tenant's taking possession and paying rent without reservation does the same. A lease given effect this way lasts no more than one year. Give every tenant a signed copy anyway; the court's eviction booklet expects you to bring the lease as proof at the hearing.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Alaska statute or regulation requires a tenant to initial a particular lease term, such as a notice period longer than the law requires, for it to bind the tenant; as far as the statutes go, the tenant's signature on the lease is enough. Signatures do matter in a few places: the tenant must acknowledge by signature the accuracy of a premises condition statement and contents inventory, a tenant repair agreement for a unit other than a single family residence must be a separate writing signed by both of you, and a tenant needs your written agreement before changing locks outside an emergency. Initials beside unusual terms remain useful evidence that the tenant saw them.

title: Lease Length Limits
bodyText: Alaska sets no maximum length for a residential lease, but how the lease is made can limit it. If you accept rent without reservation on a lease the tenant signed but you never signed and delivered, or the tenant takes possession and pays rent without reservation on one you signed but the tenant never did, the lease takes effect, but for no more than one year even if it states a longer term. A lease for longer than one year is also unenforceable unless it, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against. With no definite term, the tenancy is month to month, or week to week if rent is paid weekly.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: Alaska sets no minimum type size for a residential lease, and no statute or court rule keeps you from relying on a lease, or part of one, because the print is small. The print-size rules found in Alaska law apply to other documents, such as motor vehicle dealers' price stickers. Two related rules apply to your lease rules: they must be posted prominently on the premises, and a rule binds the tenant only if it is explicit enough to tell the tenant fairly what to do or not do. Use a readable type size throughout, so no tenant can claim a term was hidden.

title: Agents for Out-of-State Landlords
bodyText: If you live outside Alaska, or are a corporation not authorized to do business here, and you rent an Alaska dwelling, you may designate an agent in Alaska to accept service of process. The agent must be an Alaska resident or a corporation authorized to do business here, must be the same person you name in your written owner-and-manager disclosure (given at or before the start of the tenancy) as your agent for notices and service, and the designation must be in writing and filed with the commissioner of commerce, community, and economic development. If you file none, or the agent can't be served in Alaska, a tenant may serve the commissioner instead, if the tenant immediately mails the papers to you by certified or registered mail. An out-of-state entity has a further duty. A foreign limited liability company must register with the state, naming an Alaska registered agent, before conducting affairs here; until it does it may not maintain an eviction or other court action, and while it has no registered agent the commissioner is its agent for service, so a tenant may sue it by serving the commissioner (AS 10.50.605, 10.50.615, 10.50.645 and 10.50.675). A foreign corporation may not transact business here until it has a certificate of authority, may not maintain an action until it gets one, and is liable for back fees and taxes plus a penalty of up to $10,000 a year; its leases stay valid (AS 10.06.705, 10.06.710, 10.06.713 and 10.06.715). These statutes do not say whether renting out property counts as conducting affairs or transacting business, so register before you need to file. No Alaska statute requires an in-state broker or tax withholding from rent paid to you.

title: How Alaska Notices Must Be Delivered
bodyText:
Alaska sets delivery rules notice by notice.

A notice to quit, including the seven-day nonpayment notice, must be in writing and either handed to the tenant, left at the premises if the tenant is absent, or sent by registered or certified mail; if you mail it, add three days to the tenant's deadline.

No statute says who must deliver it; usually you or your manager do, and whoever delivers or posts it should be ready to testify.

Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, the itemized deposit notice and refund must be mailed to the tenant's last known address.

Electronic delivery works only between parties who agreed to it, and Alaska's electronic transactions law does not reach eviction, default or cure notices for a primary residence to the extent federal law excludes them. Lease-agreed methods may add to, but never replace, the statutory ones.

title: Extra Terms in Move-Out Notices
bodyText: Alaska has no statute governing a move-out notice form you ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep such a form to the move-out date and the forwarding address you need for the deposit refund. A form that slips in new obligations, such as a cleaning charge or a release of the tenant's deposit rights, invites a dispute, and a term in which the tenant gives up rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act is unenforceable. Remember the tenant's notice ending a month-to-month tenancy must be written and given at least 30 days before the rental due date it names, or 14 days for a week-to-week tenancy.

title: Where Alaska Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Several Alaska rules apply only if, or unless, the lease says so, and a silent lease takes the default. Rent is due at the unit, monthly at the start of each month, unless you agree otherwise. The tenant needs your consent to sublet unless you agree in writing to allow it, and must use the unit only as a dwelling unless agreed otherwise. The lease may cap the number of occupants. Where no well or utility water serves the premises, the lease may state that the tenant waives your duty to supply running or hot water. In a one- or two-family residence you may agree in writing that the tenant handles trash, water, heat, locks and detectors, but the detector statute still requires you to provide working smoke detectors, and carbon monoxide detectors where the unit contains or is served by a fuel-burning appliance or device, has an attached garage or carport, or is adjacent to a parking space, at each occupancy. The abandoned-property procedure and the abandonment-termination right apply unless otherwise agreed, and a waiver for accepting rent after a breach can be avoided only by an agreement made after that breach.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Alaska has no plain-language or readability law for residential leases: no readability test, no attorney general preapproval, and no required statement listing the rights a tenant gives up. Alaska's plain-language rules cover other documents, such as health care price lists, utility tariff notices and installment sale contracts. What Alaska polices is content. A lease term that waives the tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant act, authorizes a confession of judgment, limits or excuses either side's liability, requires indemnity, or makes the tenant pay your attorney fees is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease with such a term, the tenant may recover actual damages. Write the lease clearly anyway; your rules bind tenants only if they are explicit enough to tell tenants what to do.

title: Small Landlords and Property-Type Thresholds
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant duties do not change with how many units you own; there is no small-landlord exemption. Several rules turn instead on the property or the rent. The deposit limits, trust-account and refund rules do not apply where rent exceeds $2,000 a month, and only in a unit renting for more than $2,000 may the tenant agree to maintain the facilities and appliances you supply. In a one- or two-family residence you may agree in writing that the tenant takes on certain duties, while in other units tenant repair work needs a separate signed agreement supported by consideration. Alaska's fair housing statute does not reach renting a room in a home you live in and share (federal fair housing law, not read here, has its own exemptions). The one portfolio count is licensing: an individual managing four or fewer residential units for others needs no real estate license.

title: Renter's Insurance Is Unregulated in Alaska
bodyText:
Alaska neither requires renter's insurance nor limits your ability to require it. There is no rule on the tenant's choice of insurer, proof deadlines, force-placed coverage or fees for it, and no required statement that you will not insure the tenant's belongings.

Two limits shape an insurance clause. A lease may not excuse or limit your liability or make the tenant indemnify you, so the clause can require coverage but cannot shift onto the tenant or the tenant's insurer your own legal duties, such as keeping the premises fit and habitable.

And a tenant's failure to carry required insurance is a lease breach; if it is material, you may serve a written notice to quit naming the breach and a termination date at least 10 days after service (three more if you serve it by registered or certified mail, the only mail method allowed), which the tenant can defeat by getting the coverage before that date.

Letting the tenant choose the insurer avoids disputes.

title: Changes of Manager, Sale and Foreclosure
bodyText: Alaska keeps tenants able to find who is responsible. The written disclosure of the manager's and the owner's or agent's names and addresses must be kept current and binds any successor landlord, owner or manager; a manager who never makes it becomes the landlord's agent for notices, service and the landlord's duties. Unless otherwise agreed, an outgoing manager is released only for events after written notice to the tenant that the management ended. On a sale, the deposit-on-sale rules apply, and you may show the unit to buyers and lenders with 24 hours' notice. Selling a single-family home or duplex, or granting a lease with an option to buy one, requires the seller's disclosure statement before the buyer's written offer, unless the buyer and seller agree in writing that the disclosure law will not apply or the sale is the first transfer of a never-occupied property. In a deed of trust foreclosure the trustee notifies occupants.

title: What Alaska's Landlord-Tenant Act Covers
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant act governs every rental agreement for a dwelling unit in Alaska, wherever made, and applies statewide to any lease entered into, extended or renewed since March 19, 1974. Unless an arrangement was set up to avoid the act, it does not govern: residence in an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services; occupancy by a buyer under a contract of sale; members' housing run by a fraternal or social organization; transient occupancy in a hotel, motel, lodgings or other transient facility; housing for an employee whose occupancy depends on working substantially on the premises; condominium owners and cooperative proprietary lessees; mainly agricultural premises; and public or nonprofit transitional or supportive housing programs. Mobile home park lots are covered, with special rules this library does not address.

title: Leases Over One Year Must Be in Writing
bodyText: In Alaska a lease for longer than one year is unenforceable unless it, or a note or memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against or that party's agent, and an agent signing for you needs written authority. Only a lease for a term of one year or less can create an interest in real property without a signed writing. A long oral lease can still be enforced in some cases, such as full performance by one side accepted by the other, or the other party admitting the agreement in court. Recording matters too: a lease for one year or longer that is not recorded is void against a later good-faith buyer who records first, though it stays valid between you and the tenant.

title: Forms Alaska Supplies
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations supply no lease form and no verbatim lease text. The landlord-tenant forms come from the court system: notices to quit for nonpayment of rent (CIV-725), nonpayment of utilities (CIV-726), violation of the rental agreement (CIV-727), intentional damage (CIV-728) and illegal activity (CIV-729); the eviction complaint (CIV-730); the affidavit of compliance with the federal 30-day notice requirement (CIV-731); the confidential information sheet (CIV-732); and the eviction booklet (CIV-720). A notice to quit need not be on the court form, but it must contain what the statute requires, such as the breach, any cure and its deadline, and the termination date. One statute requires a state form: having an abandoned vehicle removed from private property takes a written request on a form the state prescribes.

title: Tenant Portals and Online Payments
bodyText: Alaska has no statute on tenant portals as such. Rent is payable at the time and place you and the tenant agree, so the lease may name an online portal as the place to pay. Signatures and notices are different. Alaska's electronic transactions law applies only where both sides agreed to deal electronically, and a tenant who agreed may refuse to do later transactions electronically; a lease cannot waive that right, so a clause requiring every future signature or notice to go through the portal will not hold if the tenant later refuses. Anything the portal delivers must let the tenant print or save it, or it cannot be enforced against the tenant. Serve notices to quit on paper as the eviction statute requires, and mail the itemized deposit notice.

title: Protecting Tenant Records
bodyText: Alaska has no rent-ledger duty and no statute limiting what you may tell others about a tenant's rental history. Alaska's personal information law does reach landlords doing business. If someone gets unauthorized access to records holding a tenant's or applicant's name with a Social Security, driver's license or account number, you must notify each affected Alaska resident without unreasonable delay, unless after investigating and notifying the attorney general in writing you determine harm is not reasonably likely. You may collect a Social Security number for a background check or credit report, but you may not disclose it to others except as the law allows. When you dispose of records with personal information, shred or erase them, and adopt written disposal policies.

title: Changing Terms of a Periodic Tenancy
bodyText: Alaska has no statute setting a notice period for changing lease terms other than rent, and no rule that a change must be offered as a new tenancy after a full termination notice. During a fixed term, you can change terms only with the tenant's agreement, under a change the lease itself reserves, or by adopting a rule, which binds the tenant only after reasonable notice and only if it does not substantially modify the lease. For a month-to-month tenancy, the cautious course is to give written notice at least 30 days before a rent due date, the same notice that would end the tenancy, and make the change effective on that date; use 14 days for a week-to-week tenancy. Treat an increase in an existing fee the same way.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: As of October 16, 2026, none of Alaska's core landlord-tenant statutes is scheduled to expire. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the eviction statutes and the fair housing provisions carry no repeal or expiration date, and no 2025 or 2026 session law amends, repeals or sunsets them. The only 2026 act that refers to the landlord-tenant act borrows its definition of dwelling unit for an optional municipal property tax exemption for converting short-term rentals to long-term rentals. Because this answer reflects the law through the 2026 session, check for new session laws each year.

title: No Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: Alaska does not require you to translate a lease, a notice or any other landlord-tenant document, and has no rule triggered by advertising or negotiating in another language. The translation rules found in Alaska law concern other matters, such as foreign documents filed for bar admission. If a tenant does not read English well, consider giving a translated copy or summary of the lease and key notices, and say in the lease which version controls. Federal language-access rules for federally assisted housing may apply to subsidized units.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Many Alaska landlord-tenant notices must be in writing, and a lease cannot downgrade them to oral notice, because it may not waive the act's rights or remedies. In writing: your disclosure of the manager and owner or agent; the itemized deposit notice, which must be mailed (where the deposit section applies, rent of $2,000 a month or less); notice of a sale or of the end of a manager's role; every notice to quit, including the seven-day nonpayment notice; notices ending a periodic tenancy; your notice ending the lease after a tenant refuses access; your rejection of a proposed subtenant; and the tenant's notices of a repair breach, of essential services cut off, of ending the lease for undelivered possession, and of an emergency lock change. Some notices have no form rule, such as your 24-hour notice of entry and the tenant's notice of leaving after a fire; writing them is still wise.

title: Animals Left in a Rental
bodyText: Alaska's statutes give you no special right to enter a unit to check on or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. The general entry rules apply: at reasonable times with at least 24 hours' notice, without consent in an emergency, and at reasonably necessary times while the tenant is away more than seven days. If you believe an animal is being neglected or abused, complain to animal control or a peace officer; an officer who seizes the animal must notify the owner in writing. Alaska's abandoned-property procedure does not mention animals, so the cautious course is to call animal control rather than treat a pet as property to sell or discard. Ask tenants with pets to name an emergency caretaker.

title: Service Animals in Alaska Rentals
bodyText:
Alaska's service-animal rule for public accommodations also binds landlords, except when you rent a room in a home you live in and share.

A service animal is a dog or miniature horse trained to do work or tasks for a person with a disability, including a psychiatric disability.

If the need isn't obvious, you may ask only whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it performs; you may not ask about the disability itself or require certification, registration, a vest or ID. For an alert animal you may ask for a health care provider's written verification.

You may not charge a pet deposit, pet rent or other surcharge, though you may charge for damage the animal causes if you charge others for damage. You may exclude an animal that is out of control, not housebroken, or a significant risk that cannot be reduced.

Emotional support animals fall under federal fair housing law.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Alaska has no state fact sheet on pets and eviction that you must give a tenant who has a dog or cat, at signing or later, and its eviction statutes have no special rule for animals left in a unit. If a tenant is evicted or leaves an animal behind, ask the tenant, or someone the tenant names, to collect it right away. If the animal is at risk, contact animal control or a peace officer, who can place it in protective custody and must notify the owner; don't treat the pet as abandoned property to sell or discard. Note that a domestic violence protective order may award a pet to the victim regardless of who owns it.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Rent and Pet Fees
bodyText:
An Alaska pet deposit is a security deposit with its own limit. For a tenant with a pet that is not a service animal, you may take an extra deposit of up to one month's rent on top of the regular two-month limit; account for it separately, apply it only to damage the pet causes, and return the rest with the itemized notice on the usual deadline.

Where rent exceeds $2,000 a month, none of the deposit limits or rules apply. Alaska sets no limit on monthly pet rent, but a fixed charge paid every period with the rent may itself be rent.

A nonrefundable pet fee is not addressed by statute; money you hold as security for pet damage is a deposit whatever you call it, so treat it as refundable.

title: Pet Rules in Alaska
bodyText:
Alaska law does not require you to allow pets, gives no tenant group, including seniors, a right to keep one, and sets no breed or size rules; service animals are the exception.

You may refuse a proposed subtenant because of proposed pets. Your pet terms belong in the lease; a pet rule adopted after signing binds the tenant only with reasonable notice and if it does not substantially change the lease.

If a tenant materially breaks the pet terms, serve a written notice to quit with a termination date at least 10 days after service (three more if you serve it by registered or certified mail, the only mail method allowed), which a cure before that date defeats; if, in the absence of due care by the tenant, substantially the same breach recurs within six months after that notice, you may end the lease on at least five days' written notice to quit.

Don't enter just to remove a pet: outside an emergency, entry needs 24 hours' notice and a lawful purpose. Never seize a tenant's animal or other belongings, and the lease cannot require indemnity or excuse your liability for pet problems.

title: Penalties for Refusing a Service Animal
bodyText: Alaska makes it a class B misdemeanor to intentionally prevent or restrict a person with a physical or mental disability from being accompanied by a certified service animal, or to charge extra for the animal, in a common carrier, place of public accommodation, or other place to which the general public is invited. The statute does not mention housing, and whether it reaches a rental home is doubtful, though it may reach a leasing office open to the public. In housing itself, refusing a service animal or charging extra for one is civil discrimination under Alaska's human rights law and its service-animal regulation, which applies to landlords except for a shared room in a home you live in, and the deposit statute bars an extra pet deposit for a service animal. Federal fair housing law also applies.

title: No Service-Animal Misrepresentation Penalty
bodyText: Alaska has no crime or civil penalty for misrepresenting a pet as a service or assistance animal, in housing or anywhere else. The nearest rule is a traffic regulation barring a person who is not legally blind from using a white cane or guide dog to get the pedestrian right-of-way. Your protection is the service-animal rule itself: where the need is not obvious, you may ask whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it performs, and you may exclude an animal that is out of control, not housebroken, or a significant risk that cannot be reduced. For an alert animal you may require a licensed health care provider's written verification.

title: No Tenant Right to EV Charging
bodyText: Alaska has no right-to-charge statute: a tenant has no legal right to install an electric vehicle charger at a rental, and you are not required to allow, accommodate or pay for one. Whether to permit charging, and on what terms, is your decision; put any permission in a signed writing that covers installation, cost, electricity and removal. If you supply a charger or outlet for tenants, it becomes a facility you supplied, which you must keep in good and safe working order. The only Alaska statute that mentions electric vehicle charging lets municipalities finance improvements, including charging stations, on commercial or industrial property.

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: Alaska has no statute on who owns, or who must remove, an electric vehicle charger a tenant installed when the tenancy ends, because tenants have no statutory charging right. If you allow a tenant to install one, agree in writing who owns it, whether the tenant must remove it and restore the area, and who pays for both. Without such an agreement, the general move-out rule applies: the tenant must leave the premises in substantially the same condition as at the start, except for normal wear and tear. Removable equipment the tenant leaves behind is handled under the abandoned-property procedure, with written notice giving at least 15 days to remove it.

title: No EV Charger Installation Rules
bodyText: Alaska sets no landlord-tenant rules for a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger: no registration with you, insurance, electrician or separate-metering requirement, and no list of conditions you may or must impose. Because the tenant has no right to install one, any conditions are yours to set in a signed agreement, for example a licensed electrician and any required permits, payment for the equipment and the electricity, proof of insurance, and removal at move-out. Apply your conditions evenly to all tenants. Absent your agreement, the tenant must use the electrical system reasonably and may not damage or remove any part of the premises.

title: No Shared-Area EV Charging Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no statute on tenant electric vehicle charging in shared parking at a rental property: nothing on reserving a charging space, charging tenants for an installation in a common area, or sharing a charger among tenants. These are matters for your parking rules or a written agreement. Two general rules apply. You must keep common areas clean and safe, and keep any shared charging equipment you supply in good working order. And a rule about a shared charger binds tenants only if it serves a permitted purpose, such as a fair distribution of facilities held out for tenants generally, applies to all tenants fairly, is clear, and tenants had notice of it.

title: Parking Areas at Alaska Rentals
bodyText:
Parking areas you hold out for tenants are part of the premises under Alaska's landlord-tenant act, so your duty to keep common areas clean and safe reaches shared lots, and a lease may not excuse or limit your liability for them.

You may still designate where tenants park and adopt parking rules.

Three more Alaska rules affect parking. You may not adopt or enforce a rule that bars someone who may legally have a firearm from keeping it in, or locked in, a vehicle legally parked on your property. A unit with an attached garage or carport, or next to a parking space, must have a carbon monoxide detector. And parking in a space reserved for persons with disabilities without a permit or special plate is an infraction with a fine of at least $125.

title: Giving Notice of Parking Rules
bodyText:
Alaska does not require you to deliver parking or towing rules before the lease is signed, use a particular heading, limit the vehicle information you ask for, or tie a parking permit to the lease term.

Parking rules are rules under the landlord-tenant act, so they must be posted prominently on the premises, and a rule binds a tenant only if it serves tenants' convenience, safety, health or welfare, protects your property or fairly distributes facilities; is reasonably related to that purpose; applies to all tenants fairly; is clear; does not evade your duties; and the tenant had notice of it when signing.

A parking rule adopted mid-lease binds only after reasonable notice and only if it does not substantially modify the lease.

title: Storage Space Leased With a Unit
bodyText:
Alaska has no self-service storage act. A storage space you lease with a dwelling is part of the premises, so the landlord-tenant act governs it.

That matters in two ways. First, a landlord's lien or security interest in a tenant's household goods is unenforceable, and distraint for rent is abolished, so you may not hold or sell stored belongings to collect rent; don't rely on the general lien for people who store property for hire either, since that is the cautious reading.

Second, when a tenancy ends and belongings remain in storage, use the abandoned-property procedure: written notice giving at least 15 days to remove them, then a public sale or, for items of little value, disposal.

title: Towing Vehicles from Rental Property
bodyText:
Alaska regulates private-property towing mostly through the tow company.

A towing business gets a lien for towing and storage charges when it tows at the direction of the person entitled to possession of the property where the vehicle is parked without consent; it must notify the owner by certified letter within seven working days and may sell an unclaimed vehicle after 30 days on 20 days' notice.

For an abandoned vehicle, such as a registered vehicle left on private property more than 24 hours or a wrecked or junk vehicle, without your consent, a peace officer or authorized employee may remove it on your written request on the state form. A vehicle left 30 days without consent is presumed abandoned, and you may claim title after notice.

State law sets no signage or rate rules; municipal ordinances may.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring or regulating parking offered separately from rent, and no rule that new buildings unbundle parking. You may include parking in the rent, charge for it separately, or lease it under a separate parking agreement. If you charge a fixed monthly parking fee with the rent, it may count as rent, which matters for the seven-day nonpayment notice; a separate parking agreement with its own payment terms keeps the charge clearly apart. Either way, parking areas held out for tenants, or promised to the tenant, are part of the premises, so your common-area duties still apply.

title: Marijuana in Alaska Rentals
bodyText:
Alaska lets adults 21 and older possess up to one ounce of marijuana and grow up to six plants, three of them mature, with no more than 12 plants in one dwelling however many adults live there; using marijuana in public stays illegal.

The same law says it does not stop anyone who owns, occupies or controls private property from prohibiting or regulating the possession, use, display, growing or sale of marijuana on that property. Your lease or rules may therefore ban or limit smoking, vaping, edibles or growing.

Alaska's medical marijuana law gives registered patients a defense to prosecution but no housing protection, so a rule may treat medical and adult use alike.

Smoking marijuana counts as smoking under the smoke-free law, which already bars it in enclosed common areas of apartment buildings. A rule adopted after signing binds only with reasonable notice and if it does not substantially modify the lease, so put any ban in the lease itself.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on hotel, motel or short-stay guests displaced by a disaster, such as a rule letting them stay without becoming tenants or limiting how they may be removed. The landlord-tenant act does not govern transient occupancy in a hotel, motel, lodgings or other transient facility, unless the arrangement was created to avoid the act. Whether a long stay by a displaced household turns into a tenancy covered by the act, with its notice-to-quit and court process, is not settled by statute. State disaster programs provide individual assistance and temporary housing help, and relocation payments apply when a state project displaces people, but none of them sets rules for private landlords. If you house displaced people, decide at the start whether the stay is transient lodging or a tenancy, put it in writing, and use a written rental agreement for anything residence-like.

title: Grills and the Fire Code
bodyText:
Alaska has no statute aimed at grills on rental balconies, but the state fire code reaches larger buildings.

The Department of Public Safety's fire and life safety regulations cover residential buildings with four or more dwelling units, and conditions or activities outside those buildings likely to injure people or property. Those regulations adopt the 2021 International Fire Code, including its general open-flame requirements, so the code's limits on open-flame cooking devices near such buildings apply there. Read the adopted code, or ask the fire marshal, before allowing charcoal or gas grills on balconies or decks.

Anchorage, Fairbanks, Juneau and other cities may enforce their own fire codes.

The statute behind those regulations names residential buildings of four or more units, but the fire-code regulation itself says it regulates 'all occupancies and buildings', so do not assume a house, duplex or triplex is outside it; in any case the lease can set your own grill rules.

In any building your lease may be stricter, for example banning grills within a set distance of the building, and the tenant may not deliberately or negligently damage the premises.

title: Firearms and Your Lease
bodyText: Alaska has no statute that bars a landlord from restricting firearms in a rental unit, and none that requires a restriction. The state constitution's right to keep and bear arms limits the state and its political subdivisions, not private landlords, and state law reserves firearm regulation to the state, so cities may not adopt their own firearm rules except as statutes allow. One rule reaches you directly: no person may adopt or enforce a policy or rule that prohibits someone who may legally possess a firearm from having it in a motor vehicle, or from keeping it locked in a vehicle legally parked on another person's property. A lease or parking rule therefore cannot ban firearms in tenants' or guests' vehicles in your lot, and you are not liable for injury or damage from a firearm stored in someone's vehicle under that rule. A restriction inside units or common areas is an ordinary lease term; state it clearly and apply it to everyone.

title: Guests in Alaska Rentals
bodyText:
Alaska has no statute on how long a tenant's guests may stay, what you may charge for guests, or when a guest becomes a tenant.

Several rules frame a guest clause. A person whose use of the premises rests only on the tenant's rights, and who has not individually acquired a tenant's rights, gains no rights under the landlord-tenant act just by being there. The tenant may not let people on the premises with the tenant's consent unreasonably disturb neighbors, may not knowingly permit anyone to damage the premises, and may not let the number of occupants exceed what the lease allows.

Damage caused by guests through negligence or misuse is not normal wear and tear, so it can be deducted from the deposit.

A reasonable guest-stay limit tied to the lease's occupancy terms is an ordinary lease term, enforced through the 10-day notice for material noncompliance. Be careful about accepting rent from a long-staying guest.

title: No Guest Rights Statute
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations give a tenant's guests, visitors, caregivers or service providers no statutory right of access to a rental building, and they neither bar nor cap a fee for guests. Alaska's rules run the other way: a person whose use of the premises rests only on the tenant's rights gains no rights under the landlord-tenant act by being there, and the tenant answers for guests who damage the unit or unreasonably disturb neighbors. A guest fee is therefore a contract term. If you charge one, state it in the lease, keep it reasonable and apply it evenly, and remember that a one-off fee is probably not rent, because rent is the uniform periodic payment, so the seven-day nonpayment notice may not reach it. Federal fair housing law may require you to allow a live-in aide as a reasonable accommodation.

title: No Crime-Free Lease Statute
bodyText: Alaska has no crime-free lease statute. Nothing requires a lease to make tenants cooperate with police, requires you to evict after police calls, or bars a lease from penalizing a tenant for calling for help. What Alaska has is a municipal option. A city or borough may by ordinance charge the owner of residential property, including multifamily housing, a fee when police respond an excessive number of times in a year, capped at the actual cost. The ordinance must give you actual notice of police contacts and a warning, must count a notice to quit among the corrective actions, and must excuse the fee if you act promptly. No fee may be charged for calls involving potential child neglect, domestic violence or stalking. Your tenant may not unreasonably engage in, or let others engage in, conduct that results in such a fee. Don't penalize tenants, especially victims, for calling for help. Some reporting duties bind you as they bind anyone. If you or your staff witness the murder, kidnapping or sexual assault of a child under 16, or an assault causing a child serious physical injury, you must report it to the police in a timely manner (failing to is a class A misdemeanor); witnessing the murder, kidnapping or sexual assault of an adult brings a duty to report as soon as reasonably practicable (failing to is a violation). Both duties have defenses for danger and for stopping the crime (AS 11.56.765 and 11.56.767). Anyone who has knowledge of a death that appears to have been caused by unknown or criminal means, suicide, accident or poisoning, that occurred suddenly in apparent good health or unattended by a physician, or in other listed circumstances, must notify a peace officer and immediately notify the state medical examiner, and the body may not be moved without the medical examiner's permission, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit (AS 12.65.005). The child-abuse and vulnerable-adult reporting duties bind listed professionals and caregivers, not landlords as such, though anyone may report (AS 47.17.020 and 47.24.010).

title: No Candidate Access Rule
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations give political candidates, campaign workers and petition circulators no right to enter an apartment building, gated community or other multi-unit residential property to campaign, and they do not require you to set aside a voter information area. Access to your building's interior, grounds and common areas is governed by your lease and posted rules. If you allow canvassing or literature in common areas, allow it on the same terms for every candidate and cause, put the terms in a written rule posted on the premises, and keep it reasonable, explicit and fairly applied to all tenants so it is enforceable. Visitors a tenant invites to the tenant's own unit are governed by your guest terms. Municipal election rules may add requirements; check them before an election.

title: No Window Unit Right
bodyText: Alaska has no statute giving a tenant the right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and no rule on how a lease may restrict one. Alaska's habitability duties cover heat, not cooling: you must supply heat and running and hot water insofar as energy conditions permit, and keep in good and safe working order any air-conditioning you supply or are required to supply. If you supply an air conditioner, maintain it; the tenant must use it reasonably. If you don't, a lease may allow, limit or ban tenant-installed units, for example by requiring that window units be installed safely and supported, not block a required exit window, and be removed without damage at move-out. A tenant who installs one must not damage the premises and must leave them in substantially the same condition, except for normal wear and tear. A tenant with a disability may ask for an accommodation under federal law.

title: No Plug-In Solar Right
bodyText: Alaska has no statute giving tenants a right to install plug-in, balcony or other portable solar devices, and no law voiding lease, covenant or association restrictions on solar energy systems. Solar appears in Alaska law mainly as a building-code item and as equipment a utility may finance on the customer's bill. A lease may therefore allow, limit or prohibit tenant solar devices. If you allow them, require that devices be listed for the use, mounted without penetrating the roof or exterior unless you agree, kept clear of exits, and removed with any damage repaired at move-out. Connecting a device that feeds power into the building's wiring or the grid is governed by electrical codes and the utility's interconnection rules; require the tenant to get any approval first. If you supply the device, it becomes a facility you must maintain.

title: No Recycling Notice Requirement
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation requiring you to provide recycling at a rental or to tell tenants where and how to recycle. Your duty is the general one: provide and maintain appropriate receptacles and conveniences for removing ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste, and arrange for their removal. In a one- or two-family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant takes over that duty. The tenant must dispose of all waste from the unit in a clean and safe manner. If your hauler or municipality offers recycling, a posted rule telling tenants what goes where is enforceable if it meets the rules statute's tests, including notice at signing or reasonable notice of a later rule. Some municipalities have their own solid-waste and recycling ordinances.

title: No Religious Display Statute
bodyText: Alaska has no statute protecting a tenant's display of religious or cultural items, such as an item on the entry door or doorpost, and none limiting how a lease or association may restrict them. Alaska fair housing law reaches the question indirectly: you may not discriminate because of religion in a term, condition or privilege of a rental, and you may not ask about or record an applicant's religion. A display rule that singles out religious items, or that is enforced only against one faith, invites that claim. Apply any limit on door, window or exterior displays to all items equally and for neutral reasons, such as preventing damage or keeping exits clear, and consider allowing small items that do not damage the door. Federal fair housing law has similar religion protection.

title: When Your Rules Bind Tenants
bodyText:
You may adopt rules about the tenant's use and occupancy of the premises, and valid rules become part of the rental agreement, but only if they meet Alaska's tests.

Post them prominently on the premises.

A rule binds a tenant only if it promotes the tenants' convenience, safety, health or welfare, protects your property from abusive use, or fairly distributes services and facilities; is reasonably related to that purpose; applies to all tenants fairly; is explicit enough to tell the tenant what to do or not do; does not evade your obligations; and the tenant had notice of it on signing.

A rule adopted later binds if you give reasonable notice of it and it does not substantially modify the lease; no lease clause is needed for that.

If you accept performance that departs from a rule adopted after signing, you waive termination for that breach unless otherwise agreed after the breach.

title: Smoke From Other Units
bodyText: Alaska has no statute on secondhand smoke drifting between units, and none that lets a lease make a tenant accept smoke drift or give up claims for it. A clause in which the tenant waives claims, or excuses you from liability, for smoke from other units runs into Alaska's ban on lease terms that waive the tenant's rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act or that exculpate or limit either party's liability. Such a term is unenforceable, and knowingly using it exposes you to the tenant's actual damages. The smoke-free law already bars smoking in an enclosed common area of an apartment building or multiple-family dwelling, which covers shared hallways whether or not staff work there, and outdoors within 20 feet of an entrance, open window or air intake of such an area. Your better tools are a no-smoking lease term or rule and the tenant's duty not to unreasonably disturb neighbors.

title: Snow and Ice
bodyText:
Alaska has no statute that assigns snow and ice removal at a rental; the general rules decide it.

You must keep all common areas of the premises clean and safe, which in winter includes shared walks, stairs, entries and parking, and that duty stays yours toward every tenant even if one tenant agrees to help.

In a single family residence you and the tenant may agree in writing, including in the lease, that the tenant performs specified maintenance tasks such as clearing the walks and driveway. For any other unit, including a duplex, the agreement must be in a separate writing signed by both of you, supported by adequate consideration, made in good faith, and not a condition of the lease.

Many cities require owners to clear abutting sidewalks; check local ordinances. If the lease says you provide plowing and you don't, the tenant may claim a rent reduction.

title: No Tenant Flag or Sign Statute
bodyText: Alaska has no statute giving tenants, or condominium and homeowners' association members, a right to display the United States flag, other flags, or political or yard signs, and none limiting how a lease may restrict them. Alaska's flag statute governs display at state institutions and schools, not homes. Because no statute protects a tenant's display, a lease or posted rule may regulate flags and signs, for example by size, placement, method of attachment and preventing damage. Keep any rule content-neutral and even-handed; a rule aimed at religious displays, or enforced against one group, invites a fair housing claim. In a rented condominium or planned-community home, the association's declaration and rules may limit displays too, so check them and pass them on.

title: Tenant Security Cameras
bodyText: Alaska has no statute on tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells, so the lease controls installation: you may require consent, limit mounting to methods that do not damage the premises, bar cameras aimed into other units or private areas, and require removal and repair at move-out. Criminal laws set outer limits for everyone. Knowingly viewing or recording the private exposure of another person's genitals, anus or female breast is a crime, with an affirmative defense only for a security surveillance system with posted notice used for crime prevention. Recording a conversation with a device requires the consent of a party to it, so a doorbell that records neighbors' conversations raises risk. Installing a device to observe or record events in someone's residence can be part of stalking. The same limits apply to cameras you install in common areas, and you have no right to place one inside a unit.

title: Waterbeds
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no rule on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture: no tenant right to have one, no insurance or deposit rule, and no limit on a lease ban. A lease may therefore allow, condition or prohibit waterbeds. If you allow them, you may require written consent, a proper frame and liner, and placement that respects the floor's load. You may not collect extra deposit money for a waterbed beyond the deposit cap: where rent is $2,000 a month or less, prepaid rent and security deposits together may not exceed two months' periodic rent, and only a pet deposit may be added on top. Requiring renters insurance is a contract term no statute addresses. Damage from a leaking bed caused by the tenant's negligence is the tenant's responsibility and is not normal wear and tear.

title: No Association Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Alaska does not require a lease of a condominium, cooperative or planned-community unit to disclose the association's obligations, or require you to give the tenant the declaration, bylaws or rules. The disclosure duties in Alaska's common interest ownership act run to buyers: a selling unit owner must give the purchaser those documents and a resale certificate. For a tenant, delivery still matters. Your own rules bind a tenant only if the tenant had notice of them on signing, or reasonable notice of a later rule that does not substantially modify the lease, and the tenant's occupancy-limit duty reaches limits in a covenant restricting your use of the property. So give the tenant the association rules that affect the unit with the lease and get a signed receipt; the library's Alaska association-compliance clause does this. Older horizontal property regimes, formed before 1986, bind tenants to their declaration and bylaws directly.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no bed bug disclosure requirement: you need not tell prospective tenants about past infestations, and no statute sets inspection or treatment timelines or assigns treatment costs. The general rules apply. You must keep the premises fit and habitable and common areas clean and safe, so a known infestation must be treated. The tenant must keep the unit as clean and safe as its condition permits and may not negligently damage the premises, and may not unreasonably refuse entry for inspection or treatment, which you schedule on 24 hours' notice except in an emergency. Before a pesticide is applied inside a leased unit, the applicator must notify the tenant, by posted notice or verbally with the date and time, pesticide name and re-entry instructions. Telling applicants about a current infestation you know of is still the safer course; concealing it invites a dispute.

title: No Occupancy Certificate Disclosure
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring you to give tenants a certificate of occupancy or a notice about one, and no state rule barring rent for a unit without one. Certificates of occupancy are issued by municipalities with building codes. In Alaska statutes and regulations they appear only in other settings, such as proof of completion for housing finance loans, the documents a condominium developer turns over to the association, and one way to show a condominium unit is substantially complete. If your municipality requires a certificate, renting a unit without one can violate local code, and a unit that cannot lawfully be occupied may not meet your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable. Check local requirements before renting converted space such as a basement or garage apartment, and fix any problem before the tenant moves in.

title: No Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no defective or corrosive drywall disclosure requirement for leases or sales. If you know a unit has drywall that corrodes wiring or plumbing or gives off sulfur odors, the general duties apply: you must keep the premises fit and habitable and keep the electrical, plumbing and other facilities you supply in good and safe working order, and the tenant may use the statutory repair remedies if you do not. A real estate licensee who helps you lease the unit must disclose known material information about its physical condition that substantially affects it. Disclose known problems in writing before signing, and repair them.

title: No Electric Submetering Disclosure
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation requiring a lease disclosure when you submeter electricity or bill tenants for it, and no prescribed form or rate limit for landlord billing. The fuller answer, including the risk that reselling metered service could bring you within the public-utility definitions, is in the library's Alaska row on utility submetering disclosure. In short: state in the lease which utilities you bill, how you measure or allocate them, when payment is due and how the tenant can see the readings or source bills; never cut off service to collect; and remember that billed utility charges are probably not rent, because rent is the uniform periodic payment, so the seven-day nonpayment notice may not reach them.

title: No Flood Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant whether a rental is in a flood zone, has flooded before, or needs flood insurance. Alaska's residential seller disclosure statement covers sales, and also a lease with an option to purchase a one- or two-family home: if you give a tenant an option to buy, deliver the completed Real Estate Commission disclosure form, by mail or in person, before the tenant makes a written offer, unless you both agree in writing that the chapter will not apply. A real estate licensee who helps you lease must disclose known material information about the property's physical condition. After a disaster, a renter who receives a state flood grant may have to keep flood insurance on the unit's contents. Telling tenants about known flooding and recommending contents insurance is good practice; floodplain rules are local.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Alaska does not require an owner facing foreclosure to tell a prospective tenant before signing a lease, or to tell current tenants that a foreclosure has started. Notice comes from the trustee instead: in a deed of trust foreclosure, within 10 days after recording the notice of default the trustee must mail it by certified mail to, among others, any person actually in physical possession of the property, or deliver it personally. After the trustee's sale, the buyer is entitled to possession against anyone claiming through the borrower after the deed of trust was recorded, which can include a tenant whose lease came later. Federal law generally protects bona fide tenants. If your rental is in default, tell prospective and current tenants in writing, keep your owner and manager disclosure current, and don't sign new leases you may not be able to honor.

title: No Good Cause Notice
bodyText: Alaska has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so there is no notice telling a tenant whether the unit is covered by one. You may end a month-to-month tenancy with written notice at least 30 days before the rental due date named in the notice, or, while rent is current, a week-to-week tenancy with written notice at least 14 days before the termination date, and a fixed-term lease ends on its date. Two limits apply. You may not end a tenancy, raise rent or cut services in retaliation for a tenant's complaint about conditions, use of statutory rights, tenant organizing or complaint to a government agency, although listed grounds such as nonpayment or a good-faith plan to occupy the unit yourself remain available after a notice to quit (for the owner-occupancy ground the tenant does not unlawfully hold until at least 30 days after that notice, or any longer period the lease sets). And you may not act for a reason fair housing law forbids. Federally assisted housing has its own good-cause rules.

title: No Contamination Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring you to disclose hazardous-substance or radioactive contamination to a tenant before signing, and no rule requiring recorded environmental restrictions to be written into residential leases. Two contamination rules still reach tenants. When an environmental covenant restricts the use of contaminated land, a copy must be provided, as the environmental department requires, to each person in possession of the property, and the covenant runs with the land. Anyone proposing a notice of activity and use limitation must give written notice to affected persons in possession, and the limitation stays in place for later owners until terminated. If either affects your rental, for example by barring wells or digging, put the restriction in the lease so the tenant's use complies. Property determined to be an illegal drug manufacturing site may not be leased until it is found fit for use.

title: Renting a Condominium or HOA Unit
bodyText:
Alaska's common interest ownership act does not cap association lease-approval fees, does not let an association collect rent directly from your tenant when you fall behind on assessments, and does not limit the tenant information an association may request.

The declaration controls leasing: it must state any restrictions on the use, occupancy and alienation of units, which can include rental limits, and the association may adopt rules and charge fees for services. The declaration may also give lessees the vote on specified matters, with the right to notice of meetings and access to records on those matters.

Before you rent a unit, read the declaration, bylaws and rules, follow any leasing procedure they set, and budget for any fees.

Older horizontal property regimes, formed before 1986, bind tenants to their declaration and bylaws directly. Whether a new rental restriction binds an owner who did not vote for it was not resolved here.

title: Association Rules and Fines
bodyText:
When you rent a unit in a condominium, cooperative or planned community, the association's rules govern the unit, but the association's remedies run against you as owner.

Alaska's common interest ownership act lets the association, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, levy a reasonable fine against the unit owner for violating the declaration, bylaws, rules or regulations; the fine is a lien on the unit, and the association may seek an injunction.

Your lease cannot make the tenant indemnify you for that liability, because Alaska bars lease terms that require either party to indemnify the other. You can recover from the tenant only your actual damages for the tenant's breach of a lease promise to follow the association's rules, and that promise binds best when the tenant received the rules at signing.

Antenna and satellite dish limits come from federal rules.

title: No Code-Order Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring you to give prospective tenants copies of outstanding inspection, code-violation or condemnation orders. Where a municipality has adopted an unfit-dwelling ordinance, the Alaska Housing Finance Corporation may, after a hearing, find a dwelling unfit for human habitation and order the owner to repair it or to vacate and close it, or to remove or demolish it if repair would cost too much. Renting a unit under such an order is unlikely to meet your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable, and exposes you to the tenant's statutory remedies. If code-required work would deprive the tenant of the unit, you may recover possession after a notice to quit even after a tenant complaint, but the tenant does not unlawfully hold until at least 30 days after that notice (or any longer period the lease sets). A real estate licensee who helps you lease must disclose known material information about the property's physical condition. Tell prospective tenants about open orders in writing; local codes may require it.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Alaska does not require residential landlords to carry liability insurance, and it has no statewide rental registration that asks for proof of coverage. Where Alaska law does require liability insurance, it is for other activities, for example a regulation may require commercial pesticide applicators to carry it. Your lender, an association's declaration or a housing program may still require coverage, and a lease may require the tenant to carry renters insurance, a contract term no statute addresses. Keep in mind that a lease cannot shift your liability to the tenant: Alaska bars lease terms that excuse or limit either party's liability or require either to indemnify the other, and knowingly using such a term exposes you to the tenant's actual damages. Insurance, not lease language, is how you manage that risk.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate
bodyText: Alaska has no state lead-safe certificate, lead registry or lead inspection requirement for rental housing, and no certificate to attach to the lease. The lead rules for ordinary rentals come from federal law: for housing built before 1978, the lead disclosure, pamphlet and Lead Warning Statement in the library's lead-based paint row, and federal renovation rules for work that disturbs paint. Alaska's own lead rules cover other settings. Licensed care entities, such as child care and assisted living homes, and licensed foster homes must not use lead-based paint and must keep painted surfaces free from flaking; plumbing installed or repaired in buildings connected to a public water system must be lead-free; and labs and health care providers report elevated blood lead results to the state. If you also run a licensed care or foster home in the unit, those licensing standards apply to you.

title: No State Lead Notices
bodyText:
Beyond the federal lead disclosure for housing built before 1978, Alaska requires no state lead notice, tenant-rights packet, inspection certificate or renewal re-notice for rentals.

Give the federal disclosure, the Lead Warning Statement and the federal pamphlet before a pre-1978 tenancy begins, using the library's lead-based paint row; whether the federal rules call for a new disclosure at renewal was not reviewed here.

Alaska has no state lead agency program that issues orders or notices to landlords, and no statute ties lead paint to a tenant termination right or a retaliation presumption. Lead hazards are handled under your general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable, and the general bar on retaliating against a tenant who complains about conditions or to a government agency.

title: Meter Conservation Charges
bodyText: Alaska lets a utility finance a renewable energy system, efficiency or storage device, or conservation system in an occupied building through an on-bill financing agreement repaid by a meter conservation charge on the utility bill. For rental property, the utility may recover those costs through a meter conservation charge only if you, the landlord, are responsible for the entire utility bill, including the charge. So the charge cannot be put on a tenant's own account, and Alaska needs no notice-to-tenant or rent-deduction procedure for it. The charge must appear as a separate line item, and the utility may disconnect service for nonpayment of it after following the usual disconnection rules, which matters to tenants in a unit whose bill you pay. The utility records a notice of the agreement, which is not a lien, and can recover the balance from a later owner of the building.

title: Illegal Drug Lab Properties
bodyText: Alaska controls property where illegal drug manufacturing is found. When qualified law enforcement determines a site is an illegal drug manufacturing site, it must notify you, post the property, at the main entry of a single family dwelling or at the unit's door otherwise, and notify the environmental department, which lists the property online. Within four days you must pass the notice to any property manager or rental agent. Until the department determines the property fit for use, you may not lease or rent it, and no one may occupy it after the fourth day following posting, except for testing or cleanup. A lease made in violation is voidable by the tenant, and knowingly renting or allowing occupancy is a class A misdemeanor; filing a court action to remove occupants within four days is a defense. Fitness requires certified testing, and cleanup if needed. The listing stays online five years afterward, but no statute requires disclosing a cleared site to tenants.

title: No Military Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant that a rental is near a military installation or airport, or within an air installation noise or accident potential zone, and no tenant right to end a lease over a missing disclosure. If your rental is near a base or an airfield, the local zoning code may include notice or overlay rules, so check with the municipality or borough. Aircraft noise and overflights can matter a great deal to a tenant, so if they are significant, say so before signing to avoid a later dispute over whether the tenant was misled. A real estate licensee who helps you lease must disclose known material information about the property's physical condition, which may or may not include noise.

title: No Mold Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation requiring a mold disclosure, a mold information pamphlet, or mold testing in rental housing, and no state indoor mold standard. Mold is handled under the general duties. You must keep the premises fit and habitable and keep the plumbing, heating and ventilating facilities you supply in good and safe working order, so leaks and ventilation failures that cause mold are your repairs. The tenant must keep the unit as clean and safe as its condition permits, use facilities such as bath fans reasonably, and not negligently damage the premises, so mold from the tenant's own neglect can be charged as damage rather than wear and tear. If you use a premises condition statement, note any mold or water staining at move-in. A real estate licensee who helps you lease must disclose known material information about the property's physical condition.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring you to tell prospective tenants about a former military ordnance or munitions site nearby, a planned demolition of the building, or a shared utility meter. Related rules still matter.
