If code-required work, or a good-faith plan to substantially alter, remodel or demolish the building, would take the unit, you may recover possession after a notice to quit even after a tenant complaint, but the tenant does not unlawfully hold until at least 30 days after your notice to quit (or the longer notice period your lease sets), plus three days if you serve it by registered or certified mail, even in a week-to-week tenancy; a month-to-month tenancy also needs the notice at least 30 days before a rental due date. If a master-metered utility account in your name goes unpaid, the electric utility must give each tenant served by the master meter notice before disconnecting. If you bill tenants for a shared meter, explain the method in the lease. Disclose a planned demolition before signing a lease that would run past it.

title: Owner and Manager Disclosure
bodyText:
At or before the start of every tenancy, give the tenant in writing the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises, and of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner to accept service of process and to receive and receipt for notices and demands.

Keep the information current; the duty binds every later landlord, owner or manager.

Alaska's consequence is agency, not a bar to eviction: a person who fails to disclose becomes the agent of each landlord for service, notices and demands, and for performing the landlord's duties under the act and the lease, including spending the rent collected for that purpose, and a manager who fails to disclose is treated as a landlord.

No statute bars an eviction because the disclosure was missing, but make sure your notices come from the disclosed person. If you live outside Alaska, any in-state agent you designate for service must be the same person you disclose.

title: Pesticide Notices
bodyText: Alaska requires notice before pesticides are applied in rental housing. No one may apply a pesticide inside a dwelling unit leased to another person without first notifying the tenant, either by posting a written notice at each entrance to the treated area that meets the state's posting rules, or verbally, giving the date and time, the pesticide's name, and when the area may safely be reentered under the label. Common areas of an apartment building or other multi-family dwelling of more than four units are public places: pesticides may be applied there only by a licensed or otherwise authorized applicator, with a notice posted at each customary access point immediately before application and kept up at least 24 hours or until reentry is safe. Records of those applications must be kept two years. Certain products, such as rodenticides in tamper-resistant bait stations and ready-to-use gels, are exempt from common-area posting. No pest-control disclosure is required before signing.

title: No Private Well Testing Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation requiring you to test a private well serving a rental, or to give well test results to tenants or buyers. Your duties are the landlord-tenant act's: supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, insofar as energy conditions permit, and keep the plumbing and sanitary facilities you supply in good and safe working order. Where the premises have no well or utility water connection, the rental agreement may specifically state that the tenant waives your duty to supply running or hot water. A single family residence in an undeveloped rural area, or where public sewer or water has never been connected, is exempt if it had no running water or sanitary facilities from a private system when the rental began. Water that is unsafe to drink can make a unit unfit, so testing a well before each tenancy and sharing the results is prudent.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65. No statute or regulation requires you to warn tenants that a building or unit contains chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, and there is no private enforcement scheme for missing warnings. Alaska's chemical-related rules for rentals are narrower: notice to the tenant before pesticide is applied inside a leased unit, licensed application and posting before pesticide use in common areas of multi-family buildings of more than four units, and the bar on leasing property identified as an illegal drug manufacturing site until it is found fit for use. Federal lead-based paint disclosure applies to housing built before 1978. Disclose known hazards in writing anyway.

title: No Property Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: Alaska does not require you to tell tenants what part of the rent pays property taxes. One program touches it. A resident who rents a permanent home and is at least 65, a disabled veteran, or at least 60 and the widow or widower of an eligible person may apply to the state by January 15 for a property tax equivalency payment based on the prior year's rent, if the rental is in a municipality that levies property tax; payments are reduced pro rata if appropriations fall short. The applicant proves rent with receipts, cancelled checks, or a rent certificate form completed by the landlord. No statute requires you to fill out the certificate, but doing so helps an eligible tenant. Charges for food, care or other services not tied to shelter and utilities do not count. A substantial property tax increase can also justify a rent increase that would otherwise look retaliatory, if the increase reasonably matches the net tax increase.

title: No Radon Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation requiring a radon disclosure, radon test or radon mitigation for rental housing, and no floor-level rule. The only radon reference in Alaska's statutes and regulations is a drinking water definition. Radon-resistant construction depends on the building code your municipality has adopted, and the text of the model codes was not reviewed here. Testing is not a legal requirement, but it is inexpensive. If you have test results, share them with tenants, and if a test shows elevated levels, address them as part of your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable. A real estate licensee who helps you lease must disclose known material information about the property's physical condition.

title: Alaska Lease Disclosure Checklist
bodyText: Alaska's required written items for a residential lease are few. At or before the tenancy starts, disclose in writing the names and addresses of the manager and of an owner or agent for service and notices. If you take prepaid rent or a security deposit, tell the tenant the terms under which you may withhold it, unless rent exceeds $2,000 a month. The lease must require the tenant to tell you of an anticipated absence of more than seven days. A waiver of your water-supply duty, allowed only where there is no well or utility water, must be stated specifically in the lease. If you agree to mediate or arbitrate, put its scope in, refer to it in, or attach it to the lease. For housing built before 1978, give the federal lead disclosure. Granting an option to buy a one- or two-family home requires the seller disclosure statement. Alaska has no required state form, cover page or renewal notice.

title: No Rights Guide Delivery Duty
bodyText: Alaska does not require you to give tenants a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights, at signing or at renewal, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one. The state does publish guidance. The attorney general must prepare and update an information pamphlet on landlord and tenant rights and on how to complain to the appropriate public agencies, and the Real Estate Commission sells an information pamphlet on landlord and tenant rights. The court system's eviction booklet points readers to the handbook What the Landlord and Tenant Act Means to You, available from the Department of Law. Handing tenants the handbook is optional good practice; it does not replace the disclosures the law does require, such as your owner and manager disclosure.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation requiring you to give tenants a copy of a health, sanitary or housing code variance or waiver, or to attach one to the rental agreement. A local variance does not change your duties under the landlord-tenant act, which require you to keep the premises fit and habitable and to supply running water and reasonable hot water and heat insofar as energy conditions permit. If a variance or approved alternative affects the unit, such as a hauled-water system, a holding tank or an alternative heat source, describe it in the lease so the tenant knows what to expect. The act's own water exception works only if the rental agreement specifically states that the tenant waives your duty to supply running or hot water, and only where the premises have no well or utility water connection.

title: No Sex Offender Registry Notice
bodyText: Alaska does not require a lease to include a sex offender registry notice, and does not require you to tell tenants that a registered offender lives in the building or nearby. The registry is public. The Department of Public Safety keeps a central registry of sex offenders and child kidnappers and may release an offender's name, address, photograph, crime and compliance status, and it maintains a registry website. The seller disclosure form for one- and two-family homes must tell buyers that they are responsible for checking whether a convicted sex offender lives nearby and where to find that information, and that form also applies if you give a tenant an option to buy. No Alaska statute bars you from using registry information to screen applicants, but apply any criminal-history criteria consistently.

title: No Lease Font or Placement Rules
bodyText: Alaska has no rule requiring a single-family home lease to state occupancy terms, or any other term, in a particular type size or on the first page. Alaska's occupancy rule is substantive instead: a tenant may not let the number of people occupying the premises exceed the number allowed by applicable law, by a covenant limiting your use of the property, or by the rental agreement. So state your occupancy limit plainly in the lease itself, and check any covenant or association rule that limits occupancy of the home. Alaska sets no minimum type size for leases; use a readable size throughout. Keep occupancy limits reasonable and consistent with fair housing law, including the federal protection for families with children.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring a landlord to tell a tenant about public access to a shoreline, beach or tidelands next to a rental, or about limits on the tenant's own access. Alaska's shoreline rules govern state land. For example, when the state leases shoreland, tideland or submerged land to the owner or lessee of adjoining upland, the lessee's right of access is nonexclusive unless the state grants an exclusive right. Whether the public may cross or use land next to your rental depends on title, recorded easements and state land law, not on your lease. If a recorded easement or public access route crosses the property, or the tenant's waterfront use is limited, say so in the lease so the tenant is not surprised.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection
bodyText: Alaska does not bar housing discrimination because of a tenant's source of income, and does not require you to accept housing choice vouchers or other rental assistance. Alaska's fair housing statute protects against discrimination because of sex, marital status, changes in marital status, pregnancy, race, religion, physical or mental disability, color and national origin; it does not list source of income or public assistance. If your rental is financed by the Alaska Housing Finance Corporation, the loan requires you not to discriminate because of sex, marital status, changes in marital status, pregnancy, parenthood, race, religion, color, national origin or status as a student, which also does not include source of income. You may decline voucher participation, but apply income and screening criteria evenly, and never use a voucher policy as cover for a decision based on a protected trait. Municipal ordinances, including Anchorage's, should be checked.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation requiring a lease to say whether a building has fire sprinklers, or requiring a sign about a missing system. Sprinklers are a fire-code matter. The state fire code, which applies to residential buildings with four or more dwelling units, adopts the International Fire Code with Alaska changes, and the adopted code calls for automatic sprinklers in buildings with apartment-type (Group R-2) occupancies, except buildings no more than two stories high, including basements, that contain four or fewer dwelling units or 16 or fewer sleeping rooms. Fire protection systems and extinguishers must be inspected, tested and serviced annually and after any use or damage, with reports kept on the premises. Telling tenants whether the building is sprinklered, and where extinguishers and exits are, is good practice; municipal codes may require more.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Other Events
bodyText: Alaska has no statute on whether a landlord acting alone must disclose a death, crime or illness connected with a rental. For real estate licensees, including property managers, a statute sets the rule: a licensee must disclose known material information about the property's physical condition, but that duty does not imply a duty to disclose, unless other law requires it, events on the property that might affect whether someone wants to buy or lease it. The one exception runs to buyers: before a buyer makes or accepts an offer, a licensee must disclose a murder or suicide on the property within one year before the licensee first showed it, if the licensee knows of it. The statute does not extend that exception to tenants. Never answer an applicant's direct question falsely, and do not refuse a tenant because of a disability, which fair housing law protects.

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText: Alaska has no statute requiring an employer-landlord to give an employee a signed disclosure of occupancy and vacating terms, or to offer a rental agreement when the job ends. The key rule is scope: the landlord-tenant act does not govern occupancy by your employee whose right to occupy is conditioned on employment substantially for services, maintenance or repair to the premises, such as a resident manager or caretaker, unless the arrangement was created to avoid the act. Other employee housing, and any separate rental agreement, generally falls under the act, including its notice-to-quit and court process. If you deduct board or lodging from an employee's pay below minimum wage or overtime rates, state labor rules require that it be customarily furnished, reasonable and without profit, and preceded by written notice describing it, stating the weekly deduction and stating that accepting the lodging and deduction is voluntary, and that the employee give signed written acceptance. Put the occupancy terms, and what happens when the job ends, in writing.

title: No Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Alaska requires no state-agency statement of tenant rights in or with the lease: no attachment, no first-page placement, no signature on each page, and no rule barring a suit until one is given. The state publishes guidance you may share, including the attorney general's information pamphlet on landlord and tenant rights and the court system's eviction booklet. What Alaska requires instead is accuracy in the lease. A rental agreement may not waive the tenant's rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act, authorize a confession of judgment, excuse or limit either party's liability or require indemnity, or make the tenant pay your attorney fees. Such terms are unenforceable, and if you wilfully use a lease containing terms you know are prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: Alaska has no statewide tenant protection act like California's, so there is no notice telling tenants that rent caps or just-cause rules apply. Alaska has no state rent control, no just-cause eviction law, and no general tenant right to buy the building when you sell it. The one purchase right is limited to conversions: when a building is converted to a condominium or other common interest community, each residential tenant gets written notice at least 180 days before having to vacate, an offer to buy the unit for 90 days, and then a right of first refusal. Otherwise you may end a periodic tenancy with the statutory written notice, subject to the bans on retaliation and discrimination.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Act
bodyText: Alaska has no truth-in-renting act requiring a statement in the lease, or penalizing a landlord simply for offering a lease with terms that violate clearly established tenant rights. Its own rule is narrower but similar. A rental agreement may not provide that either party waives rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act, authorizes anyone to confess judgment, accepts the exculpation or limitation of liability or indemnifies the other, or agrees to pay your attorney fees. Such a term is unenforceable, and if you wilfully use a rental agreement containing a term you know is prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages. Remove prohibited terms rather than relying on a severability clause to save the rest of the lease.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Alaska requires no utility disclosure attachment to the lease, such as a form explaining how a shared bill is apportioned, a water submeter certificate, or a notice of energy-improvement charges on the bill. If you apportion or submeter utilities, the library's Alaska rows on utility apportionment and submetering disclosure explain the limits; put the method, the utilities covered, the due dates and how tenants can see the bills in the lease itself. If a utility on-bill financing charge applies to your rental, Alaska puts it on your account, not the tenant's: a utility may assess a meter conservation charge on rental property only if you are responsible for the entire utility bill, including that charge.

title: No Alaska Accessory Dwelling Unit Law
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations contain no accessory dwelling unit law: nothing stops a city or borough from restricting backyard cottages, garage apartments or in-law units, nothing requires municipalities to allow them, and nothing bans owner-occupancy conditions. Whether you may build or rent one is a question for your local zoning code. Once you rent an accessory unit, the landlord-tenant act applies to it like any other dwelling unit: it reaches every rental agreement for a dwelling unit in Alaska, and a dwelling unit is any structure or part of a structure used as a home by one household. One fair housing detail: renting a room in your own home where you live and share common living areas with the renter is outside the state fair housing rental ban, but a self-contained accessory unit is a separate dwelling and is not covered by that exception.

title: No Alaska Alarm Tampering Fee
bodyText: No Alaska statute or regulation authorizes or caps a lease fee for a tenant who removes or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide detector, so the library does not offer a set tampering fee. The tenant's duty is fixed by law: keep the devices working by keeping charged batteries in battery-operated devices and testing them periodically, if possible, and never permanently disable them. That duty is part of the tenant's statutory obligations, so you may recover your actual damages, such as the cost of a replacement detector and its installation, and a breach that materially affects health and safety can support a 10-day notice to cure or quit. Violating the detector statute is also a class B misdemeanor for smoke detectors and a lesser violation for carbon monoxide detectors. Charge actual costs, not a fixed penalty.

title: Asbestos in Alaska Rentals
bodyText: Alaska's statutes and regulations do not require you to disclose asbestos to tenants, inspect a rental for it, or notify tenants before asbestos work. The state's asbestos abatement program covers public schools and the University of Alaska. One rule reaches any building, including yours: if asbestos-containing material risks releasing fibers and you hire someone to abate it, a contractor must have an approved employee certification plan before taking the job, and no one may be employed to abate an asbestos health hazard unless certified in an approved program. A contractor who breaks these rules faces civil penalties and misdemeanor charges. Your general duty to keep the premises fit and habitable still applies. Federal asbestos rules also govern renovation and demolition. If you suspect asbestos, hire a certified contractor and tell tenants about the work and any precautions.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate
bodyText: Alaska has no law requiring periodic engineering inspections of balconies, decks, porches or exterior stairways in rental buildings. Your ordinary duties still cover them: you must keep the premises fit and habitable and keep common areas clean and safe. For buildings with four or more dwelling units, the state fire code regulations also apply, and a state fire and life safety officer who finds a building hazardous because of a lack of repairs, blocked exits or another cause must order the condition remedied; if the order is not met, the building can be posted as unsafe to occupy. Your city or borough may have its own building or property maintenance code. Inspect elevated wood structures regularly, especially after freeze-thaw seasons and heavy snow loads, and repair rot and loose railings promptly.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Your Alaska lease cannot contract around the casualty or mitigation rules. If fire or another casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, the tenant may move out and end the lease as of the move-out date, or, if staying is lawful, vacate the unusable part and pay rent reduced in proportion to the lost rental value; rent is accounted for as of the casualty date, and you must return the deposit and prepaid rent recoverable under the deposit statute. The act also makes every aggrieved party mitigate damages, and if a tenant abandons, you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent at fair rental value. A lease term waiving any right or remedy under the landlord-tenant act is unenforceable, so clauses keeping full rent due after a casualty or excusing you from re-renting do not work. See the Alaska casualty termination row.

title: Children in Alaska Rentals
bodyText: Alaska does not require your lease to say anything about children living in the unit. Alaska's fair housing rental ban lists sex, marital status, changes in marital status, pregnancy, race, religion, physical or mental disability, color and national origin, but not familial status or parenthood, even though the Human Rights Act's purpose and civil-rights sections name parenthood. Two other rules do protect families: if your rental property is financed through an Alaska Housing Finance Corporation loan program, the loan requires you not to discriminate against tenants or applicants because of parenthood, pregnancy or student status, and the federal Fair Housing Act protects households with children. The sublease statute lets you reject a proposed subtenant because of the number of household members under 18, but that ground may conflict with federal law. Treat families with children equally and base any occupancy limit on the unit, not on the occupants' ages.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: An Alaska lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the rental agreement, meaning it may not let you or your lawyer obtain a judgment against the tenant without a contested case. Such a term is unenforceable, and if you knowingly use a lease containing it, the tenant may recover actual damages. The bar works both ways: the tenant's lease cannot authorize a confession against you either. Alaska still allows confessed judgments outside a lease: a person may confess judgment in a signed, sworn writing made in person or through an attorney-in-fact, and the court rules set the form. That route is not a lease term, and a confession built into a lease adds nothing. Recover possession and money through the ordinary eviction and damages case instead.

title: Alaska Consumer Protection Act and Rentals
bodyText: Alaska's Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Act makes unfair or deceptive acts in trade or commerce unlawful, and a person who loses money or property because of one may sue for three times actual damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus full reasonable attorney fees, within two years of discovering the loss. Whether the act reaches residential leases is unsettled: it speaks of goods and services, and it exempts acts regulated by a state statute unless that statute does not prohibit the practice, but the exemption never covers the practices the act lists. One listed practice is representing that an agreement confers rights, remedies or obligations it does not, or that the law prohibits. The cautious course is to assume the act applies: advertise units accurately, describe the lease truthfully, and keep terms the landlord-tenant act prohibits out of your lease.

title: Victim Address Confidentiality in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska has no domestic violence lease-termination statute, so it has no matching landlord duty to keep a victim-tenant's status or new address confidential. A new state address confidentiality program, in effect since July 1, 2026, lets victims of domestic violence, stalking or sexual assault who have a protective order or meet department standards, and their household members, use a state-designated post office box as their mailing address. State and municipal agencies must accept that substitute address; the statute does not say private landlords must. Disclosing confidential program information is a class A misdemeanor in listed cases, including knowingly telling the respondent of a protective order. If a tenant or applicant gives you a program address, accept it for mail and notices that may be mailed, keep the tenant's physical address out of anyone else's hands, and never share it with the person the tenant is protected from.

title: No Alaska Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: Alaska has no statute giving tenants an express, non-waivable right to call police or emergency services, and none voiding lease terms that penalize such calls. The closest rule runs through local police-response fees. A city or borough may charge the owner of residential property a fee when police respond an excessive number of times in a year, but never for calls involving potential child neglect, domestic violence or stalking, and the owner must get notice and a warning and is not liable if it promptly takes the corrective action the ordinance defines, which can include a notice to quit. Your tenant may not unreasonably cause such a fee, and you may recover actual damages if the tenant's conduct does. Do not write lease terms that discourage tenants from calling for help; a tenant who calls in an emergency is not acting unreasonably.

title: No Eviction Penalty Statute
bodyText: Alaska has no statute aimed specifically at lease clauses that impose a penalty because of an eviction notice or eviction case. Other Alaska rules reach most such clauses anyway. A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees; instead, the prevailing party in any case arising out of the landlord-tenant act or a rental agreement is allowed attorney fees by statute. Your money remedies for a tenant's breach are actual damages and an injunction, plus a claim for rent and possession after termination, and the act's multipliers are tied to actual damages. Alaska has no statute authorizing a fixed fee for serving a notice or filing a case, so the library offers none. Leave out flat eviction charges, notice fees and penalty rent; claim your actual losses and court-awarded fees in the case itself.

title: No Liability Waivers or Indemnity
bodyText: An Alaska lease may not excuse or limit either side's liability arising under the law, and may not make either side indemnify the other for that liability or its costs. The bar runs both ways, so a clause saying you are not liable for injuries, theft, water damage or utility failures is unenforceable, as is a clause making the tenant hold you harmless or defend claims against you. Knowingly using a lease with such a term lets the tenant recover actual damages. Your protection comes from the statutes themselves: you are not liable for loss of abandoned property you store unless caused by your deliberate or negligent act; if you did not know and were not told a detector needed repair, that failure is not evidence of negligence; and after a good-faith sale and written notice to the tenant, you are released for later events, except for deposits. Carry liability insurance and encourage renters insurance instead.

title: Alaska Fair Housing Rules
bodyText: Alaska's Human Rights Act makes it unlawful for an owner, lessee, manager or anyone else with the right to rent real property to refuse to rent, or to discriminate in a term, condition or privilege of a rental, because of sex, marital status, changes in marital status, pregnancy, race, religion, physical or mental disability, color or national origin, which includes ancestry. You also may not ask about or record most of these traits, falsely say a unit is unavailable or refuse a showing because of them or age, or advertise a preference based on race, color, religion, disability, sex or national origin. Alaska adds marital status and pregnancy to the federal list but does not list familial status, source of income, sexual orientation or gender identity; the federal Fair Housing Act and some city codes go further. Two state exceptions exist: housing commonly known as for singles or married couples only, and renting a room in your own home where you live and share common living areas. Never advertise a preference, even then.

title: Fair Housing Complaints and Penalties
bodyText: If someone believes you discriminated in renting, they may file a written complaint with the State Commission for Human Rights within 300 days after the act, or after a continuing practice stops, or sue you in superior court, which may stop the practice, order any appropriate relief including money, and hear a class action. Commission staff investigate, and if they find substantial evidence they try to settle the matter by conciliation; a signed agreement is binding. After a hearing that finds discrimination, the commission may order you to rent the unit, a like unit or the next vacancy to the person, award actual damages including the costs of alternative housing, storage and moving, and award reasonable attorney fees, but it may not award noneconomic or punitive damages. Wilful discrimination is also a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500, up to 30 days in jail, or both. Respond to any complaint promptly and keep written records of your rental decisions and reasons.

title: Which Fire Codes Apply in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska's state fire code is a set of Department of Public Safety regulations, not statutes. The statute directs fire and life safety standards for public and commercial buildings and for residential buildings containing four or more dwelling units. The regulations adopt the 2021 International Building Code and the 2021 International Fire Code, with Alaska amendments, plus the 2021 existing-building and mechanical codes. The building code's scope excludes detached one-, two- and three-family dwellings and certain townhouses. Before building, altering or changing the use of a covered building, plans must be reviewed and approved, and a covered building built or altered since December 5, 1956 may not be occupied without approval. The state fire marshal may defer review and inspection to qualified cities, so your local fire department may enforce. If an inspector orders a hazard corrected in a leased building, the order goes to the tenant unless the fix would become part of your real property; then it goes to you. Smoke detectors are required in every dwelling unit regardless of size.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Alaska Rentals
bodyText: No Alaska statute requires you to retrofit an existing rental with fire sprinklers or to tell tenants whether a building has them. Sprinkler rules come from the state fire code. Buildings that contain an R-2 occupancy, as the adopted International Building Code classifies occupancies (the class that usually covers apartment buildings; Alaska's regulations don't reproduce the code's definitions, so confirm a building's class with the fire official), need an automatic sprinkler system unless the building is no more than two stories including basements and contains four or fewer dwelling units, or 16 or fewer sleeping rooms; fire walls may divide a structure into up to three separate buildings for this purpose. An unsprinklered small residential building with more than 10 occupants needs one-hour rated corridors. Where a building has a sprinkler or other fire protection system, it must be inspected, tested and serviced at least annually, and the reports kept on the premises. Cities may not require sprinklers in all new single-family homes or duplexes unless they adopt an ordinance after extra notice and at least three public hearings.

title: Foreign Ownership and Leasing in Alaska
bodyText:
Alaska has no law barring foreign individuals, companies or governments, including foreign adversaries, from owning, buying or leasing private real property, so a residential lease to a foreign person is not restricted by state law.

Two narrow rules exist. Exploration and mining rights on state land may be held by citizens and by aliens only if their country grants like privileges to United States citizens. And when an interest in real property is created for a nonresident alien, the written instrument must say so and give the alien's name and address.

The one-year exception sits in the subsection's writing requirement; whether the nonresident-alien statement is also excused in a written lease of one year or less is not settled, so the cautious course is to include it in any written lease to a nonresident alien.

Ask every tenant the same neutral question about it, and never treat applicants differently because of national origin. Federal foreign-investment rules may separately apply to owners.

title: Code Editions Fixed by Alaska Rules
bodyText: Several Alaska safety rules point to an outside code at a named edition, so a newer national edition does not apply until the state amends its regulations. The state fire code adopts the 2021 editions of the International Building Code, International Fire Code, International Existing Building Code and International Mechanical Code, and parts of the 2021 International Fuel Gas Code, each with Alaska amendments. Single-station smoke detectors required in every dwelling unit must meet NFPA 72, 2019 edition, and the building code's smoke alarm placement rules; the statute itself only says detectors must be a type, and installed in a manner, approved by the state fire marshal. Electronic records of monthly fire extinguisher inspections follow NFPA 10, 2021 edition. By contrast, the electrical and plumbing codes are incorporated as adopted by other state regulations as amended from time to time. Check your city's code too: a city that enforces fire rules under a state deferral may use its own editions.

title: The One Habitability Duty a Lease Can Waive
bodyText: Only one Alaska habitability duty can be removed by the lease itself. Where the premises have no well and no water from a direct public utility connection, the rental agreement may specifically state that the tenant waives your duty to supply running water or hot water. Every other duty stays with you: a lease term waiving the tenant's rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act is unenforceable, and no lease may let you collect rent free of the duty to keep the premises fit. Separate written agreements can shift some tasks, such as trash, heat, locks or repairs, to the tenant, but they reassign the work rather than erase the standard, and in buildings other than a single family residence they need a separate signed writing supported by adequate consideration. Alaska has no rule letting a tenant accept substandard conditions for a stated rent reduction. See the Alaska rows on modifiable habitability duties and the water-supply waiver.

title: No Alaska Immigration-Status Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no statute on immigration or citizenship status in rental housing: nothing bars you from asking about it, nothing protects it as a class, and nothing makes it unlawful to rent to a person who is not lawfully present. National origin, which includes ancestry, is protected, and you may not ask about or record an applicant's national origin, so questions about where someone is from or a demand for papers from only some applicants can become national-origin discrimination. If you need identity or income documents, ask every applicant for the same ones and accept any reasonable proof. One narrow rule may require the question: a written lease made with a nonresident alien must say so and give the alien's name and address (the statute's one-year exception sits in its writing requirement, so whether a written lease of one year or less is excused is not settled), so ask that neutrally of every tenant. Federal fair housing law also protects national origin.

title: Jury Waivers Not Offered
bodyText: The Alaska Constitution preserves the right to a jury of twelve in civil cases where more than $250 is in controversy, to the same extent as at common law, and the court rules keep that right inviolate. On a claim over $250, including the damages part of an eviction case, either side may demand a jury in a signed writing served no later than 10 days after the last pleading on the issue; a party who does not demand one waives it, and the parties may later agree in writing or in open court to a trial by the judge. No Alaska statute or rule addresses a jury waiver written into a residential lease before any dispute arises, and whether one is enforceable has not been settled here. Because a waiver adds little when a party who wants a judge can simply not demand a jury, the library does not offer an Alaska lease jury waiver.

title: Penalty for Knowingly Using Prohibited Terms
bodyText: If you wilfully use a lease containing a term you know Alaska prohibits, the tenant may recover actual damages. The rule is two-way: a tenant who knowingly uses such terms against you owes the same. The prohibited terms are waivers of rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act, confessions of judgment, clauses excusing, limiting or indemnifying either side's legal liability, and promises that the tenant pays your attorney fees; each is unenforceable whether or not you knew. Alaska adds no extra statutory penalty, such as months of rent, on top of actual damages, but the prevailing party in a case arising out of the lease is allowed attorney fees, and a lease that states rights or obligations the law prohibits may also draw a consumer protection claim, whose reach to leases is unsettled. Review your lease against the prohibited list before each use.

title: What an Alaska Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Alaska has no single list of required lease contents, but scattered rules put specific items in or with the lease. The rental agreement must require the tenant to notify you of an anticipated absence of more than seven days. In writing, at or before move-in, you must disclose the name and address of the manager and of an owner or agent for service of process and notices. Where rent is $2,000 a month or less, you must tell the tenant the terms and conditions under which you may withhold prepaid rent or the deposit. Some items are required only if you use them: a premises condition statement and inventory become part of the agreement when signed; tenants are bound by a rule adopted before signing only if they had notice of it at signing and it meets the statute's purpose and fairness tests, and by later rules only with reasonable notice and if they do not substantially modify the agreement; a water-supply waiver must be stated specifically; a mediation or arbitration agreement must be included, referenced or attached; and a lease longer than one year must be in a signed writing, with a nonresident alien statement where it applies. Federal lead-paint disclosure applies to older housing.

title: Alaska Has No Separate Habitability Waiver Bar
bodyText: Some states put habitability in a separate part of their statutes with its own clause voiding any waiver of that part. Alaska has no such separate part. Its habitability duties sit inside the general landlord-tenant act, and one rule covers the whole act: a lease may not make either side waive or forgo rights or remedies under the act, and such a term is unenforceable. A second rule protects habitability specifically: no lease, assignment, deed or security instrument may let anyone collect rent free of the duty to keep the premises fit. The only changes allowed are the ones the act itself permits, such as terms that apply unless otherwise agreed, the water-supply waiver for premises without a well or utility water, and written task-shifting agreements. See the Alaska rows on modifiable habitability duties and the one waivable habitability duty.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no plain-language, readability or consumer-contract statute for residential leases, and no dollar-ceiling consumer-contract law that reaches them. The only readability rule in the consumer protection act covers installment sales of goods or services, whose written terms must be stated in readable, clear and unambiguous language. What Alaska polices is content: terms the landlord-tenant act prohibits are unenforceable, and your rules bind tenants only if they are explicit enough to fairly tell tenants what they must or must not do. Write the lease in short, plain sentences anyway; a clear lease is easier to enforce and less likely to mislead. See the Alaska row on plain-language lease law for the full search.

title: Pools at Alaska Rentals
bodyText: Alaska has no statute or regulation requiring a residential landlord to fence a pool, install a pool barrier or gate, or give tenants a pool safety notice. The state's pool rules cover public swimming pools and spas: a public swimming pool is one at least two feet deep at any point, operated by an owner, lessee or operator and intended for public use. Those pools need plan review and approval (the pre-occupancy inspection rule applies to pools built or extensively remodeled after December 23, 1993), a certified operator, daily water-quality records, a ring buoy and a life pole. A residential spa or hot tub is excluded from the spa definition. Whether a pool limited to residents of an apartment complex is intended for public use is not settled by the rules; ask the Department of Environmental Conservation before opening one. Keep any pool or hot tub secured and supervised, and check your local code.

title: Terms an Alaska Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: An Alaska lease may not make either side waive rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act, authorize a confession of judgment, excuse, limit or indemnify either side's legal liability, or promise that the tenant pays your attorney fees. Those terms are unenforceable, and knowingly using them lets the other side recover actual damages. That list is not the whole story. No lease may let you collect rent free of your duty to keep the premises fit. Sublease restrictions beyond the statutory grounds are unenforceable. A lien on the tenant's household goods is unenforceable and distraint for rent is abolished. A waiver of the tenant's exemptions from collection is unenforceable. In a building other than a single family residence, you may not make a separate repair agreement a condition of the lease. And a waiver of your acceptance-of-rent rule counts only if agreed after the breach, so pre-signed non-waiver language does not work. Alaska has no specific rule on home-warranty deductibles or repair fees; charge only for damage the tenant causes.

title: Alaska Bans Even Asking
bodyText: Alaska goes beyond banning discrimination: it is unlawful to make a written or oral inquiry, or to keep a record, of the sex, marital status, changes in marital status, race, religion, physical or mental disability, color or national origin of a person seeking to rent. That reaches application forms, screening questions, showings and notes in your files. Ask for the names of all adults who will live in the unit, not how they are related; leave out marital status, spouse fields and titles such as Mrs.; and do not ask about birthplace, ancestry, religion or health. If a tenant asks for a disability accommodation, ask only what you need to evaluate that request. One statute pulls the other way: a proposed subtenant's written offer must state age and marital status, so take that information only in that form and never base a decision on marital status. Pregnancy and age are not on the inquiry list, but you still may not refuse to rent because of pregnancy.

title: No Alaska Sex Offender Residency Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no statewide residency restriction for registered sex offenders: no distance limit from schools or child care, no ban on two registrants living together, and no duty on a landlord to screen for, or refuse, registrants. Registry information is public in part, including name, address, photograph, conviction and compliance status, through the Department of Public Safety. One rule touches rentals with a purchase option: a transfer of a single-family home, or a building with two single-family dwellings, by a lease with an option to purchase is covered by the property disclosure law, and the disclosure statement must tell the buyer that they are responsible for finding out whether a convicted sex offender lives nearby and where to get that information, unless both sides agree in writing that the disclosure law will not apply. If you screen for criminal history, apply one written standard to every applicant.

title: No State Owner-Occupancy Rental Limit
bodyText: Alaska has no statewide law limiting the rental of homes in single-family zones to owners who live on the lot. Zoning is left to cities and boroughs, so check your local code before renting a house, a duplex unit or a second unit on the lot. The one place owner-occupancy shows up in state law is housing finance: several Alaska Housing Finance Corporation loan programs are defined around owner-occupied single-family homes, duplexes and small multiplexes. If your mortgage came through one of those programs, its owner-occupancy terms may limit renting out the property, so read your loan documents before you lease. Your homeowners association covenants may also restrict rentals.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no rule requiring you to install covers on steam radiators when a tenant asks, and no required radiator-cover lease rider or annual notice. Your general duties still apply: you must keep the heating facilities you supply in good and safe working order and supply heat at all times, insofar as energy conditions permit, unless heat comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control with its own utility connection. If a tenant with young children asks for a cover on a hot radiator, providing one is a sensible safety repair, and your city's housing code may say more.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: Alaska has no statute on refusing a subsidized or voucher tenancy because of the program's inspection, and none on a subsidized tenant's refusal of a program inspection. Source of income is not a protected class under Alaska's fair housing law, so state law does not require you to accept housing vouchers, though some cities may, and you may not use a voucher policy as a cover for discrimination on a protected trait. If you take part in a program, its federal inspection rules apply under your program contract. Inside the unit, Alaska's entry rules still govern: the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to an inspection, you must give at least 24 hours' notice except in an emergency or where impracticable and enter at reasonable times, and if the tenant refuses lawful access you may seek an injunction or end the lease on 10 days' written notice and recover up to the greater of actual damages or one month's rent.

title: Sharing Tenant Information
bodyText: Alaska has no statute generally barring you from disclosing a tenant's or applicant's information, such as rental history, phone number or payment record, and no consent rule for sharing it. One firm limit applies: a person doing business may not disclose an individual's Social Security number to a third party, except in listed cases such as consumer credit reports, background checks, identity verification, fraud prevention or disclosures the law authorizes. The state constitution recognizes a right of privacy, but whether it restricts private landlords is not settled. If a tenant is enrolled in the state's address confidentiality program, never reveal the tenant's physical address. Share tenant information only for a legitimate purpose, such as answering a reference request the tenant authorized. The Alaska tenant records row covers data-breach notice and safe disposal of records.

title: Tenant Organizing in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant act has no express right for tenants to form associations, meet in common rooms or distribute flyers, and no rules on organizer access. It does protect organizing through the retaliation ban: you may not raise rent, decrease services, or bring or threaten an eviction because a tenant organized or joined a tenants' union or similar organization. A tenant who proves retaliation may recover possession or end the lease, recover up to one and one-half times actual damages, and defend an eviction. You may still evict for the act's listed reasons, such as unpaid rent, after a proper notice to quit. Building rules on common areas must apply to all tenants fairly and be reasonably related to their purpose, so don't adopt rules aimed at tenant meetings. Your city may have more protections.

title: Tenant Screening in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska has no tenant-screening statute: no rule on when you may check criminal history, no look-back periods, no limit on minimum-income tests, and no negligence shield for renting to someone with a record. Several rules still shape screening. You may not ask about or record an applicant's sex, marital status, race, religion, disability, color or national origin. You may collect a Social Security number for a background check. The state criminal records repository may release conviction information to anyone, but not nonconviction information such as arrests without a conviction. A person whose record was sealed as mistaken identity or false accusation may deny it, and the court system's public website drops criminal cases 60 days after an acquittal or a dismissal that was not part of a plea deal. From January 1, 2027, state agencies will not release, on the person's request (from January 1, 2028, without a request), an adult's sole conviction in a case for possessing less than one ounce of marijuana. An applicant's credit freeze does not cover agencies whose files serve only tenant screening. Federal credit-reporting and fair housing rules also apply.

title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states require a lease notice telling tenants a property is exempt from statewide rent caps or just-cause eviction rules. Alaska has no such notice because it has neither law to be exempt from: there is no statewide rent control or rent-increase cap, and no statewide rule that you must have cause to end or not renew a residential tenancy outside mobile home parks. A month-to-month tenancy ends on 30 days' written notice before a rent due date, and a week-to-week tenancy while rent is current on 14 days' written notice. What does limit you is the retaliation ban: you may not raise rent, cut services or bring or threaten an eviction because a tenant complained, enforced rights, joined a tenants' union or complained to an enforcement agency. Check your city or borough for local rules.

title: No Alaska Lease Unconscionability Statute
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant act has no unconscionability section, so no statute lets a court refuse to enforce a residential lease or a lease term because it was unconscionable when made. Alaska's unconscionability statutes cover other contracts: sales of goods, leases of goods such as furniture or equipment, and contracts of a condominium or other common interest community association. A court may still apply the general contract doctrine of unconscionability to a residential lease, but no published Alaska decision was searched for this row. Most one-sided terms are already handled by the act's own rules: waivers of statutory rights, confessions of judgment, liability waivers and indemnities, and tenant promises to pay your attorney fees are unenforceable, and rules must be reasonable and fairly applied. Keep terms balanced and plainly stated.

title: Renting to Veterans in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska has no tax credit, deposit waiver or other incentive paid to landlords for renting to veterans. One state program helps veteran tenants directly: a resident who rents a permanent home and is a disabled veteran, at least 65, or a qualifying surviving spouse at least 60, may apply for a property tax equivalency payment based on the rent paid, if the legislature funds it. The application must include rental receipts or other proof of rent paid, so expect such tenants to ask you for receipts or a rent statement each year; provide them promptly. State law also directs the state housing corporation to build and operate moderate-cost rental housing for veterans and other residents. Servicemember protections, such as lease termination on deployment, are covered in the Alaska servicemember rights row.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Alaska has no rule setting a maximum or minimum water heater temperature for rental housing, and no duty to reset a unit's water heater before a new tenant moves in. Alaska's temperature limits apply elsewhere: licensed child care facilities and foster homes must keep hot water at fixtures between 100 and 120 degrees Fahrenheit, and public showers must be supplied at 100 to 120 degrees. For rentals, your duty is to supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, insofar as energy conditions permit, unless the hot water comes from an installation in the tenant's exclusive control with its own utility connection. Setting a unit-only water heater at about 120 degrees before each move-in is a sensible scald-prevention practice, and your local plumbing code may say more.

title: No Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: Alaska has no requirement to install window guards, window stops or other window-fall protection in rental housing, and no window-guard lease notice. The state fire code points the other way on sleeping rooms: in addition to the ordinary exits, provisions must be made for emergency escape and rescue openings in Group R residential occupancies, and Alaska deleted two of the model code's exceptions to that rule. So if you add window guards, bars or stops for child safety, make sure any window serving as an emergency escape and rescue opening can still be opened and used from inside without special knowledge or tools; check the fire code's requirements for release devices before installing anything. Your local building code may say more.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Alaska follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (AS 45.03.311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (AS 45.01.308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the chapter, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (AS 34.03.320). That binds you and the tenant alike. Alaska's section adds that the party who is wronged has a duty to mitigate damages. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: No State Approval Rule for Leases; Restricted Native Land Is Federal
bodyText: No Alaska statute makes a residential lease of private land wait for a government officer's approval, and Alaska has no communal land system of its own. Alaska's landlord-tenant act and property title set no approval rule for leases of Native or tribal land. Land held in trust or restricted status by the United States for a tribe or an individual Indian is different, and federal law governs it. Restricted Indian land may be leased for residential purposes by its Indian owners only with the approval of the Secretary of the Interior (25 U.S.C. § 415(a)). Anyone who is not an owner needs a lease from the owners before taking possession, and possession without a required lease is a trespass that the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) may act to end, including by eviction (25 C.F.R. §§ 162.005, 162.023). A residential lease takes effect on the date BIA approves it, and it must be recorded in BIA's land titles office (25 C.F.R. §§ 162.342, 162.343). Practical step: if the home or the land under it may be a Native allotment, a restricted townsite lot or other trust or restricted land, check its status with BIA or the tribe before you sign, and don't let a tenant move in until any required BIA approval is given.

title: No Alaska Rule on a Tenant's Hunting Rights
bodyText: No Alaska statute says whether a tenant who rents a home with land gets the right to hunt or fish on it, or keeps that right with the owner. Alaska's landlord-tenant act doesn't govern a rental of premises used primarily for agricultural purposes (AS 34.03.330(b)(7)). Two rules shape the question. Under the criminal trespass law, a person who enters or remains on unimproved and apparently unused land that is not fenced or enclosed, without intent to commit a crime, is privileged to do so unless notice against trespass is given personally by the owner or another authorized person, or by conspicuous posting (AS 11.46.350(b)). And the law against obstructing hunting protects only lawful hunting, which on private land means hunting with the private landowner's permission (AS 16.05.790(f)(2)). Neither law says whether a tenant in possession can give or refuse that permission. So settle it in the lease: say whether the tenant may hunt or fish, or let others do so, where and when, and whether you or others will keep using the land for hunting. If you want people kept off unfenced land, post it.

title: Recording a Lease in Alaska Is Optional but Protects Longer Leases
bodyText: Alaska doesn't require you to record a residential lease, and an unrecorded lease is valid between you and the tenant (AS 40.17.080(b)). Recording matters only against later buyers and lenders. A conveyance of real property, other than a lease for a term of less than one year, is void as against a later good-faith buyer for value (including a lender taking a security interest) whose conveyance is recorded first; it stays valid against anyone with actual notice of it (AS 40.17.080(b)). So a lease of one year or longer can be cut off by a later buyer or lender who records first without knowing of it. A recorded document is constructive notice of its contents to later buyers and secured lenders (AS 40.17.080(a)). Instead of the whole lease, you may record a memorandum of lease signed by both parties, giving the parties' names and addresses, the lease date, a description of the property, the start and end dates (or how they are fixed) and the conditions of any renewal, extension or purchase rights; it has the same effect as recording the lease (AS 40.17.120). Record in the recording district where the property is, with the recording fee (AS 40.17.020(a), 40.17.030(a)). No Alaska statute ties notice to a relative's lease the way Nebraska's does. Practical step: for an ordinary lease shorter than a year, don't bother; for a lease of a year or more, or one with a purchase option, consider recording a memorandum of lease.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages
bodyText: Alaska's landlord-tenant act sets no deadline of its own for a landlord's suit against a tenant, so the general limits in AS 09.10 apply. An action upon a contract, which includes a suit for unpaid rent or other money owed under a lease, must be brought within three years (AS 09.10.053). An action upon a sealed instrument gets 10 years, and an action for waste or trespass upon real property gets six years (AS 09.10.040(a), 09.10.050). Which of these a court applies to a tenant's damage to the unit is case law, so treat three years from each missed payment or each damage claim as your deadline. A tenant's acknowledgment or promise to pay extends the period only if it is in writing and signed by the tenant (AS 09.10.200). That rule doesn't alter the effect of a payment, and when a past due payment is made on an evidence of indebtedness, the period runs from the last payment (AS 09.10.200, 09.10.210); whether a partial rent payment restarts the clock on a lease debt is case law, so don't count on it. If the former tenant leaves Alaska, the time the tenant is out of the state is not counted (AS 09.10.130). The rules are the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies.

title: No Special District Statement Required in an Alaska Lease
bodyText: No Alaska statute requires a residential lease to say that the property lies in a special taxing, assessment, utility or improvement district, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges or rules. Alaska's landlord-tenant act lists what a landlord must disclose (who manages the property and who receives notices), and a district statement isn't among them (AS 34.03.080). Any district taxes or assessments on the property fall on you as owner, not on the tenant. If the lease passes a district charge through to the tenant, state it in the lease as a fixed charge or part of the rent.

title: Student Housing in Alaska
bodyText: Alaska has no statute written for student leases, parental guarantees or academic-year terms, so a lease to a student follows the same rules as any other lease. The one student-related rule is an exclusion: Alaska's landlord-tenant act doesn't govern residence at an institution, public or private, if it is incidental to the provision of educational (or medical, geriatric, counseling, religious or similar) services, unless the arrangement was created to avoid the act (AS 34.03.330(b)(1)). Occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in the part of a structure operated for the organization's benefit is excluded the same way (AS 34.03.330(b)(3)). A privately owned house or apartment that you rent to students is not residence at an institution, so the act applies in full. If you rent to a student under 18, have an adult sign or guarantee the lease.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText: Alaska's criminal trespass law lets you keep a non-tenant (a former tenant, a troublemaker, a tenant's ex) out of parking lots, hallways and other common areas. A person commits criminal trespass in the second degree, a class B misdemeanor, by entering or remaining unlawfully in or upon premises (AS 11.46.330); entering or remaining unlawfully in a dwelling is first-degree trespass, a class A misdemeanor (AS 11.46.320). 'Enter or remain unlawfully' means being on premises that are not open to the public when the person is not otherwise privileged to be there, or failing to leave premises that are open to the public after being lawfully told to leave, in person, by the person in charge (AS 11.46.350(a)). In an apartment building each unit counts as a separate building (AS 11.81.900(b)). A tenant's invited guest is generally there with the tenant's permission, so a ban reaching into the tenant's own unit is enforced against the tenant through the lease, not by trespass. For unfenced, unimproved land, give the person notice in person or post the land (AS 11.46.350(b)). Practical step: give the person a written notice that he or she may not enter the property, keep a copy and a photo of any posting, and give a copy to the police.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Alaska)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Alaska property law doesn't use, so the rule about leases granted by a usufructuary doesn't arise in Alaska. The closest Alaska interest is a life estate (for example, a surviving spouse who holds a home for life while the children own the remainder). No Alaska statute in the property title says what happens to a residential lease signed by a life tenant when the life estate ends; that is case law. The cautious course if you lease as a life tenant: say so in the lease, keep the term short or month-to-month, and have the remainder owners sign the lease or agree in writing that it will continue if your life estate ends first. The same applies to every tenancy type.
